The Cao-Dong School.
Chan Master Dongshan Liangjie Wuben of Ruizhou, whose Dharma lineage descends from the fourth generation under Qingyuan,
was the son of the Yu family of Kuaiji. In his youth, he followed a teacher to recite [the scriptures].

In the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*, upon reaching the passage "no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind," he suddenly touched his face with his hand and asked the Master, "I have eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth;
why does the sūtra say they do not exist? The Master was startled and marveled at him.
He said, "I am not your teacher," and immediately pointed him toward Mount Wuxie to pay respects to Chan Master Mo, under whom he received the tonsure.

At the age of twenty-one, he went to Mount Song to receive full ordination and began his travels. His first destination was Nanquan, where he arrived just as they were preparing a vegetarian feast for the anniversary of Mazu’s passing.
Nanquan asked the assembly, "Tomorrow we shall offer a memorial feast for Mazu; I wonder, will Mazu come? No one in the assembly could answer.
The Master came forward and replied, "I shall come once I have a companion. Nanquan said, "Although this boy is of late birth, he is quite fit for carving.

The Master said, "Preceptor, do not treat the noble as lowly. He next visited Muzhou Daoyuan and asked, "Recently I heard the story of National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang regarding 'insentient things preaching the Dharma,' yet I have not yet fathomed its subtlety. Muzhou said, "Disciple, do not merely memorize it."
"Is it so? the Master asked. Dongshan said, "I remember it. Miaoyan said, "Try reciting it once for me. Dongshan then recounted it:
A monk asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas? The National Teacher said, "Walls, tiles, and rubble are it. The monk said, "Are walls, tiles, and rubble not insentient?
The National Teacher said, "They are. The monk said, "Can they preach the Dharma? The National Teacher said, "They preach constantly."

He preached with fervor without ceasing. A monk asked, “Why do I not hear it? The National Teacher said, “It is you who do not hear; it cannot be that you hinder others from hearing. The monk asked, “I wonder, who is it that can hear it? The National Teacher said, “The various sages can hear it. The monk asked, “Does the Master hear it as well? The National Teacher said, “I do not hear it. The monk asked, [“Why not? The National Teacher said, [“Because I have nothing to hear. The monk asked, [“Then what about the Buddhas and patriarchs? The National Teacher said, [“They too do not hear it. The monk asked, [“In that case, who hears it? The National Teacher said, [“Only those who have no ears can hear it. The monk asked, [“How can one come to have no ears? The National Teacher said, [“When you have no ears, you will naturally hear it. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘having no ears’? The National Teacher said, [“To have no ears means to have no self. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘having no self’? The National Teacher said, [“To have no self means to have no mind. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘having no mind’? The National Teacher said, [“To have no mind means to have no thoughts. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘having no thoughts’? The National Teacher said, [“To have no thoughts means to be free from all mental activity. The monk asked, [“If there is no mental activity, how can one attain liberation? The National Teacher said, [“Liberation is precisely this absence of mental activity. The monk asked, [“Is there then no distinction between the enlightened and the unenlightened? The National Teacher said, [“There is no distinction at all. The monk asked, [“If there is no distinction, why do people suffer? The National Teacher said, [“Suffering arises from the deluded grasping of the mind. The monk asked, [“How can one sever this deluded grasping? The National Teacher said, [“By realizing that there is nothing to grasp, one severs it. The monk asked, [“What is the ultimate state of non-grasping? The National Teacher said, [“Non-grasping is the state where the mind is like empty space. The monk asked, [“Can one describe this state? The National Teacher said, [“It cannot be described. The monk asked, [“Can one point to it? The National Teacher said, [“It cannot be pointed to. The monk asked, [“If it cannot be described or pointed to, how can one know it? The National Teacher said, [“Knowing it is precisely not knowing it. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘not knowing’? The National Teacher said, [“Not knowing is the true knowing. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘true knowing’? The National Teacher said, [“True knowing is the realization that there is nothing to be known. The monk asked, [“If there is nothing to be known, is this not nihilism? The National Teacher said, [“Nihilism is the view that there is nothing at all. True knowing is the realization that all things are originally thus. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘originally thus’? The National Teacher said, [“‘Originally thus’ means that from the very beginning, there has been neither birth nor death, neither coming nor going, and nothing to be attained or lost. The monk asked, [“If this is so, then what is the purpose of the Buddha’s teachings? The National Teacher said, [“The Buddha’s teachings are merely expedient means to guide sentient beings back to their original nature. The monk asked, [“How does one return to one’s original nature? The National Teacher said, [“By casting off all views and attachments, one returns to one’s original nature. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘casting off all views and attachments’? The National Teacher said, [“To cast off all views and attachments is to realize that the mind is fundamentally empty and still. The monk asked, [“If the mind is fundamentally empty and still, how can one benefit others? The National Teacher said, [“Though the mind is empty and still, its compassionate response is inexhaustible. This is called the great function of the Way. The monk asked, [“How can one manifest this great function? The National Teacher said, [“By acting spontaneously according to the needs of the moment, without premeditation or calculation. The monk asked, [“If one acts without premeditation, will one not fall into confusion? The National Teacher said, [“Confusion arises from seeking. When there is no seeking, there is no confusion. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘no seeking’? The National Teacher said, [“No seeking is the state where the mind is free from desire and attachment. The monk asked, [“If one is free from desire and attachment, is this not a state of indifference? The National Teacher said, [“Indifference is the enemy of the Way. True freedom from desire is not indifference, but rather a state of active engagement with the world while remaining inwardly detached. The monk asked, [“How can one engage with the world while remaining inwardly detached? The National Teacher said, [“By viewing all phenomena as illusions and dreams, one engages with them without clinging. The monk asked, [“If one views all phenomena as illusions and dreams, will one not become detached from the world? The National Teacher said, [“Detachment is not the goal. The goal is to transform the world through compassion, using the illusory nature of phenomena to liberate other illusions. The monk asked, [“How does one use the illusory nature of phenomena to liberate other illusions? The National Teacher said, [“By teaching that all phenomena are empty and illusory, one leads sentient beings to see through their own delusions and return to their original nature. The monk asked, [“If all phenomena are empty and illusory, is there then no such thing as good and evil? The National Teacher said, [“Good and evil are relative concepts. From the perspective of ultimate reality, there is neither good nor evil. The monk asked, [“If there is neither good nor evil, why do people fear the consequences of their actions? The National Teacher said, [“Fear arises from ignorance. Those who understand the truth of emptiness have no fear of karmic retribution. The monk asked, [“How can one understand the truth of emptiness? The National Teacher said, [“By practicing the Way with single-minded devotion, one will gradually penetrate the truth of emptiness. The monk asked, [“What is the practice of the Way? The National Teacher said, [“The practice of the Way is simply to maintain mindfulness in every thought and action, never allowing the mind to wander from the truth. The monk asked, [“How does one maintain mindfulness in every thought and action? The National Teacher said, [“By being aware of the arising and ceasing of each thought, one maintains mindfulness. The monk asked, [“What is meant by the ‘arising and ceasing of thoughts’? The National Teacher said, [“Thoughts arise like clouds in the sky and cease like mist vanishing. They have no substance and no origin. The monk asked, [“If thoughts have no substance and no origin, how can they cause suffering? The National Teacher said, [“Suffering arises when one clings to thoughts as real. When one sees that thoughts are empty and illusory, there is no suffering. The monk asked, [“If there is no suffering, is there then no need for liberation? The National Teacher said, [“Liberation is not something to be attained. It is the realization that one was already liberated from the very beginning. The monk asked, [“If one was already liberated from the beginning, why do people seek enlightenment? The National Teacher said, [“People seek enlightenment because they are unaware of their original nature. Once they realize their original nature, there is nothing more to seek. The monk asked, [“What is meant by ‘original nature’? The National Teacher said, [“Original nature is the mind that is unborn and undying, beyond all conceptualization and expression. The monk asked, [“If the mind is unborn and undying, how can one speak of birth and death? The National Teacher said, [“Birth and death are merely names given to the flow of conditioned phenomena. In the ultimate sense, there is no birth and no death. The monk asked, [“If there is no birth and no death, is there then no such thing as the cycle of rebirth? The National Teacher said, [“The cycle of rebirth exists only for those who are deluded. For those who have realized the truth, there is no cycle of rebirth. The monk asked, [“If there is no cycle of rebirth, what happens to the merit
The Master said, "Since you did not hear it, how could you know that the insentient can preach the Dharma? The National Teacher said, "I am fortunate indeed that I did not hear it.
Had I heard it, I would have been equal to the various sages, and you would not have heard me preaching the Dharma.

The monk said, "If that is so, then sentient beings have no share [in the Dharma]. The National Teacher said, "I preach for the sake of sentient beings; I do not preach for the sake of the sages. The monk—
[The monk] asked, "What happens after sentient beings hear it? The National Teacher said, "They are then no longer sentient beings.
The monk asked, "On what scriptural authority is 'insentient things preaching the Dharma' based? The National Teacher said, "It is evident that words do not encompass the scriptures;

this is not something spoken by a gentleman. Have you not seen that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'The lands preach, sentient beings preach, and all things of the three periods of time preach'? Having finished citing this, the Master [continued].

"Is that so? Muzhe asked. Baizhang said, "From here, going toward Shiling in You County, Liling, there is a man of the Way named Yunyan whose hermitage is connected to yours.

Dongshan said, "He once asked me, 'When a student wishes to follow his teacher, what should he do?

Having concluded the preceding account of causes and conditions, he asked, "Who is it that hears the insentient preaching the Dharma? Yanguan replied, "The insentient hear it.

"How truly marvelous! The insentient preaching the Dharma is inconceivable. If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to understand;
only when hearing through the faculty of sight does one come to know it. The Master asked Yunyan, "I have residual habits that I have not yet exhausted.
Yunyan said, "What have you been doing? The Master replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. Yunyan said, "Have you attained joy yet? The Master replied, "Joy..."
Joy is not non-existent; it is like finding a single bright pearl atop a heap of refuse. The Master asked Yunyan, "What is it like when you intend to meet me?

[The Master] had not yet determined where he would stay. [Nanquan] said, "Do not go south of the Hu Lake. The Master said, "Do not say 'do not';

He intended to instruct him, saying, "What is the nature of this sickness that resides in your mind? The Master replied, "How great or small is the sickness of one who speaks of the Buddha-realm and the Path-realm?
At first, there was no response. The next day, [the student] suddenly passed away. At that time, people called the Master "The Teacher Who Killed the Head Seat.
From the end of the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, he received and guided students at Mount Xinfeng; subsequently, his teachings flourished in Gaoyang, Yuzhang.

At Dongshan, he provisionally opened up the five ranks (*wuwei*) to skillfully receive those of the three capacities. He extensively expounded the single sound (*yiyin*) to widely propagate it for the myriad types of beings.
Horizontally drawing his precious sword, he cut through the dense forest of various views; wondrously harmonizing with the great penetration, he severed the myriad ends of artificial fabrication.

Furthermore, he attained Cao Shan’s profound clarification of the ultimate meaning and his wondrous chanting of excellent principles. Therein, the Way conformed to the relationship between ruler and subject, and the partial and the correct were mutually interwoven. By means of this...
Thus, the profound tradition of Dongshan spread throughout the world; consequently, the masters of all quarters collectively honored it, calling it the Caodong School.

"What is 'directing'? The Master said, "What is it when you are eating? "What is 'serving'?
The Master said, "What is it when you are carrying a load on your back? "What is 'merit'? The Master said, "What is it when you have set down your hoe?
"What is 'shared merit'? The Master said, "No appearance. "What is 'merit of merit'? The Master said, "Not shared."
He then presented this verse: "The Sage Ruler has always been like the Dharma-Emperor Yao; He governs the people with propriety, bending his dragon-waist.
Sometimes he passes through the midst of a bustling market; Everywhere there is civilization—hail to the Sagely Court! Washing clean and applying thick makeup—for whom?
Amidst the cries of the cuckoo, it urges people to return home. The myriad flowers have all fallen, yet its wailing never ends; It continues to cry out deep within the chaotic peaks."
Flowers bloom on withered trees; a spring beyond kalpas. Riding backward upon a jade elephant, one pursues the qilin.

Now, hidden high beyond a thousand peaks, the moon is bright and the wind is clear—a most auspicious day. Sentient beings and Buddhas do not encroach upon one another; the mountains are naturally high and the waters naturally deep.
Amidst ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, what is clarified? Where the partridge cries, the hundred flowers are fresh. As soon as the horns appear...

"I am already incapable. To even conceive of seeking the Buddha is a source of great shame. For vast, empty kalpas, no one has recognized [this]. Would you be willing to travel south to consult the fifty-three masters?

Because Cao Shan was about to take his leave, the Master then entrusted him, saying: "While I was at the place of my former teacher Yunyan, I personally received the seal of the *Precious Mirror Samādhi* (*Baojing Sanmei*).
Having exhausted the essential points of the matter, I now transmit it to you. The verse says: "Such a Dharma as this, the Buddha..."
The Patriarch entrusted it secretly; you have now obtained it. You should protect it well. Like snow held in a silver bowl, or the bright moon hidden among the herons—their natures are not the same.
When mixed, their locations are known; the meaning does not reside in the words. When the responsive mechanism arrives, it also departs; movement creates a nest of habitual patterns.
To falter or linger is to turn one's back or touch upon it—both are wrong. It is like a great mass of fire; as soon as it takes on form or color, it belongs to defilement. Night.

Half-light reveals itself; at dawn, it is not yet manifest. It serves as a model for all things and employs means to uproot all suffering. Although it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not without expression.

It is like standing before a precious mirror, where form and reflection behold one another. You are not that [mirror], and that [mirror] is precisely you. Like an infant of the world, the five characteristics are fully complete;
there is no going and no coming, no arising and no abiding. It is harmonious and peaceful, and yet it exists.

Phrases and non-phrases ultimately yield no substance, for the words have not yet reached their ultimate rectitude. The six lines of the hexagram *Lí* (Fire) intermingle through the shifting of the biased and the correct;

they are layered to form three, and through transformation, they become five. It is like the taste of the *chí* herb, or like a vajra-pestle: the center is perfectly correct while the flanks are subtly held in tension. Striking and singing are raised together;
it penetrates both the fundamental principle and the common path. It carries both the way and the road; when applied with precision, there is auspiciousness—this must not be violated.

It is contrary [to worldly logic], yet it is natural and wondrous. It does not belong to delusion or enlightenment. Through causes, conditions, and the timing of seasons, it is silently manifest. Subtly, it enters the infinitesimal; vast, it transcends all spatial dimensions.
A deviation of even a hair’s breadth would fail to accord with the musical scales. Now, there are sudden and gradual approaches, established as doctrinal orientations based on conditions.

Once these orientations are distinguished, they serve as the very compass and square. When the orientation is penetrated and the goal reached, the True and Constant flows forth; externally tranquil, it is active within.

Shaking [the head]. Tethering colts and subduing rats—the former sages took pity on these and established the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving). Following their delusions, they took black for white;

once those inverted perceptions were extinguished, they sincerely pledged themselves to accord with the ancient tracks. Please observe the ancients: when the Buddha-way was about to be perfected, he gazed at the tree for ten kalpas.
Like a tiger with a missing tooth, like a horse with a white left hind hoof (*zhù*, pronounced *zhù*), because of such inferiority, the treasure...
How rare and precious! Because there is something startling and extraordinary. The wildcat and the white ox—Hou Yi, with his skillful strength, shot an arrow that hit the mark at a hundred paces.
When the tips of the arrows meet directly, what has skillful strength to do with it? A wooden man sings; a stone woman dances. This is not reached by consciousness or cognition;
how could it admit of thought or deliberation? A subject serves his ruler; a son obeys his father. Not to obey is not filial; not to serve is not to assist. [The Emperor] remained hidden...
Practice in secret application; appear as if foolish and dull-witted. If you can merely maintain continuity, you are called the "Lord among Lords. The Master further said:
"In the age of the Dharma’s decline, many people possess only dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*). If one wishes to discern the true from the false, there are three kinds of leakage:

first, the leakage of views (*dṛṣṭi-lepa*), where the faculty does not leave its station and falls into a sea of poison; second, the leakage of emotion (*sneha-lepa*), which stagnates in preferences and aversions..."

The first is dwelling in partiality and deficiency. The second is dwelling in stagnation and obstruction. The third is dwelling in perversion and inversion. The third [of the three faults] is called "leakage in speech": when investigating the subtle, one loses the fundamental source;

when the spiritual capacity is dim regarding the beginning and end, turbid wisdom flows on. One should understand these three seeds. Furthermore, there are three summary verses. The first, "Both the Strike and the Call are Practiced," states:
The golden needle and double lock are both prepared; The converging paths are hidden yet fully encompassed. The precious seal is wondrous as it faces the wind; Layer upon layer, the brocade seams.
Opening: Unfurling the two golden locks of the profound path. A verse says: Alternating light within darkness, the effort is equal yet turning toward awakening is difficult.

When strength is exhausted, one forgets advancing or retreating; the golden locks form a net that covers everything. Three: Not falling into the ranks of ordinary beings or sages (also titled "Neither Entering Principle nor Phenomena"). A verse says: Neither entangled with phenomena nor principle, the returning illumination cuts off all subtlety.
Turning one's back on the wind, there is neither skill nor clumsiness; like lightning or a flash of fire, it is difficult to pursue. Ascending the hall.
The Way is mindless and accords with people; people are mindless and accord with the Way. If you wish to understand the meaning within this, there is one who is old and one who is not old.

(Later, a monk asked Caoshan, "What is 'one who is old'? Shan said, "Not supporting. The monk asked, "What is 'one who is not old'? Shan said, "A withered tree. The monk then related this to Xiaoyao Zhong, who said, "The three obediences and six virtues."
He asked the monks, "What is the most painful thing in the world? They replied, "Hell is the most painful. The Master said, "Not so.
To be under these robes [in this human form] and not clarify the Great Matter—this is called the greatest suffering.

While walking with his senior teacher, Mi, the Master pointed to a monastery by the road and said, "Inside there, someone is talking about the mind and nature. The Senior Teacher asked, "Who is that? The Master said, "By your venerable self..."
A questioner asked, "I have attained the state where death is fully transcended. Baizhang said, "Who is it that speaks of mind and nature? The teacher replied, "To find life within death.
He then asked a monk, "What is your name? The monk replied, "So-and-so. The teacher said, "Who is that which is your true host?"
Jian replied, "I have respectfully responded. Master Ci said, "How bitter, how bitter! People of the present age are for the most part like this;
they merely recognize that which is behind the donkey and before the horse, taking it to be themselves. This is precisely why the Buddha-dharma is sinking.
They have not yet distinguished the host within the guest—how then can they discern the host within the host? A monk then asked, "What is the host within the host?"
The Master said, "Upādhyāya, speak for yourself. [The Upādhyāya] said, "If I were to speak, I would be the host within the guest" (Yunju spoke on his behalf:
"If I were to speak, I would not be the host within the guest"). "What is the host within the host? The Master said, "To speak thus is easy;
to maintain continuity is very difficult. He then presented this verse: Alas, I see those who study the Way nowadays, By the thousands and tens of thousands, all recognizing the gatehead.
"It is just like entering the capital to pay court to the Sovereign; one stops as soon as one reaches Tongguan.
The Master was unwell and ordered a novice to convey this message to Yunju, instructing him: "If he should ask whether the Master is at ease, simply say, 'The path to Yunyan is about to be cut off.
When you deliver these words, you must stand far away, for I fear he might strike you. The novice took his instructions and departed.

As he was delivering these words, before the sound had even faded, Yunju struck him with a staff. The novice remained speechless. (Tongan Xian spoke on his behalf, saying: "In that case, one branch of Yunyan’s lineage has not fallen.
Yunchi Xi said: "Venerable sir, tell me, is Yunyan's path cut off or not? Choushou Chou said: "What was the intention behind the Ancients striking this one blow?
When the Master was about to pass away, he addressed the assembly, saying: "I have a reputation for idleness remaining in the world; who can rid me of it? The assembly all remained silent.

"Yes. At that time, the śrāmaṇera came out and said, "Please tell me the Dharma-name of the Master. The Master replied, "I have long since discarded my worldly name. (Shishuang said, "No one can obtain his approval.

Yunju said, "If there were such a 'leisurely name,' it would not be my late teacher's. Caoshan said, 'From antiquity to the present, no one has been able to discern it. Shushan said, 'The dragon possesses the mechanism of emerging from the water; no one can discern it.')
A monk asked, "When the Master is unwell, is there anyone who does not fall ill? The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "Does this one who is not ill still look after the Master?
The Master said, "The old monk has his share of looking after him. The monk asked, "In what way, Master, do you look after him?
The Master said, "When the old monk looks, he sees no illness. The Master then asked the monk, "Having left this shell-and-leakage body..."
"Son, where will you meet me? The monk had no reply. The Master presented this verse: "Students as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, not one has attained awakening;
The fault lies in seeking the path of another’s tongue. If you wish to forget form and obliterate all traces, Exert yourself with earnest diligence in walking through space.
He then ordered his hair to be shaved and his body washed. Donning his robes and sounding the bell, he took leave of the assembly and sat upright, passing away.

At that time, the great assembly wailed and lamented for so long that the sun moved across the sky without ceasing. The Master suddenly opened his eyes and said to the assembly, "For those who have left the household life, not being attached to things is true cultivation.
To toil through life and cherish death—what benefit is there in such grief? He further instructed the administrators to prepare a meal for the ignorant.
Although the assembly’s longing did not cease, it took seven days for the food and utensils to be fully prepared; the Master then joined the assembly.
When the fast was concluded, he said, "In the monastic life there is no [mundane] business; generally, at the moment of departure, one must not cause commotion.

He then returned to his quarters, sat upright, and passed away. This occurred in the third month of the tenth year of the Xiantong era. He was sixty-three years of age and forty-two years since his ordination.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Wuben, and his stupa was named Huijue.
Chan Master Caoshan Benji of Fuzhou was the dharma heir of Chan Master Dongshan Jia of the fifth generation under Qingyuan.
He was the son of the Huang family in Putian, Quanzhou. In his youth, he studied Confucianism. At the age of ten...
9. He went to Lingshi in Fuzhou to leave the household life. At twenty-five, he received full ordination. He then visited Dongshan, who asked, "What is your name, Layman?
The Master replied, "Benji. Dongshan said, "Who is that? The Master replied, "He is not named Benji. Dongshan held him in high esteem.
Thereafter, he stayed in the master's quarters for several years before taking his leave. Dongshan then secretly transmitted the teachings of the Dongshan school to him.
The Master asked again, "Where have you been going? The Master said, "I go to the place of non-alteration. Shan said, "In the place of non-alteration, how can there be going?
The Master said, "Going itself is also non-alteration. He then went to Caoxi to pay homage at the ancestral pagoda and returned to Jishui.
As the community heard of his reputation, they invited him to open a Dharma hall. Since the Master’s aspiration had always been to emulate the Sixth Patriarch, he was accordingly named [Huineng].
Shanwei was his secular surname. During a period of banditry and unrest, he went to Yihuang. There, the lay devotee Wang Ruoyi offered him the Hewang Monastery and invited him to serve as its abbot.
The Master further renamed the Hewang Monastery as Heyu. Consequently, the Dharma seat flourished greatly and students gathered like clouds;

the lineage of Dongshan reached its peak of prosperity during the Master’s tenure. Once, when a monk asked about the essential principles of the Five Ranks of Lord and臣 (Minister), the Master said: [The text continues with the dialogue].

The Master said: "The position of correctness is the realm of emptiness; fundamentally, there is nothing therein. The partial position is the realm of form; it possesses the manifestations of the myriad phenomena.
'Correctness within the partial' means turning one's back on principle to attend to phenomena. 'The partial within the correct' means relinquishing phenomena to enter into principle.

As for the 'comprehensive and simultaneous,' it responds to all conditions in profound stillness without falling into any state of existence. It is neither defiled nor pure, neither correct nor partial. Therefore, it is called the Great Mystery."
The Way is the True School of Non-attachment. The former masters of antiquity have all deduced that this single position is the most wondrous and the most profound;

it must be examined with care and clearly distinguished. The ruler represents the position of correctness, while the minister represents the position of partiality. When the minister faces the ruler, it is "correctness within partiality"; when the ruler looks upon the minister—
"This is the 'central position with partiality. It is the merging of the Way of Ruler and Minister; it is a speech that encompasses both. A monk asked, "What is the Ruler?
The Master said, "Sublime Virtue honors the universe; lofty brilliance illuminates the great void. [The monk] asked, "What is the Minister?

The Master said, "Spiritual mechanism expands the holy Way; true wisdom benefits all living beings. [The monk] asked, "What is the Minister turning toward the Ruler? The Master said, "Not falling into any heterogeneity."
[The monk] approached, his mind focused as he gazed upon the Master’s countenance, and asked, "What is 'the ruler looking at the minister'?

The Master said, "Though the wondrous countenance does not move, its light shines without partiality. [The monk] asked, "What is 'the way of ruler and minister in harmony'? The Master said, "It is a state of total fusion, without interior or exterior."
"Harmonizing the high and the low brings about peace. The Master spoke again: "To speak in terms of ruler and subject, or partiality and rectitude, is because one does not wish to offend the Center.
Thus, it is correct that a minister addresses his sovereign but does not dare to name him directly. This is the essential core of our Dharma school. He then composed a verse, saying:

"The student must first recognize their own school; Do not conflate the Ultimate Reality with inert emptiness. The wondrous, luminous essence is entirely sensitive to being offended; [Exert] your power..."
Amidst meeting conditions without borrowing, uttering words directly so that fire cannot burn them; in secret practice, one must be identical to the ancients.
Having no body yet possessing affairs, one transcends the crossroads; having no affairs and no body, one falls into beginning and end. Again, he forms five signs. [Symbol] The verse says:
A layman must pay homage to the signs; this matter is not considered strange. Those whose families have held court rank for generations—do not speak of being a "disgraced wanderer."
At that time, the verse says: At the hour of Zi (midnight), one should abide in the position of correctness; the light is precisely present between ruler and minister.

Without having left the realm of Tuṣita, the crow and the cock walk upon the snow. The verse says: Within the flames, cold ice forms; willow flowers fly in the ninth month. The mud ox roars upon the surface of the water;
the wooden horse pursues the wind and neighs. The verse says: On the day of his initial descent into the royal palace, the jade hare could not depart.
"Without having attained the principle of non-action, why are humans and devas so slow? The verse says: "The matter and principle are hidden within the undifferentiated whole;
their first signs are ultimately difficult to clarify. Even King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda did not understand this; how could Maitreya be so alert? Chou Bunan asked:

"To 'wear fur and carry horns'—what kind of fallacy is this? The Master said: "It is the fallacy of being of that class. He asked: "To 'not sever sound and form'—what kind of fallacy is this? The Master said: [The text here is incomplete].

[The student] asked, "This is falling into conformity. [The Master] said, "Not accepting food—what kind of falling is this? The Master said, "This is falling into nobility. He then said, "To eat is simply one's fundamental task.

To know it exists yet not take it is why it is called 'falling into nobility. If one clings to it, knowing from the very beginning that there is a self and a state of sainthood, it is therefore called 'falling into categories. If, from the very beginning, one knows one's own matter and turns the light back..."
At that time, by casting aside form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharmas*), one attains tranquility and achieves success.

Later, however, if one does not relinquish attachment to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth, one will become obscured according to their influence; if one merely complies with them, they will become an obstruction.
Therefore, the six heretical teachers were your teachers; where those teachers fell, you also followed and fell. Only then may you take the food. This "food" is precisely the Right [Dharma].

"Life is food. This also refers to the gates of the six sense faculties—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—which simply means not being defiled by them. To speak of "falling" (duo) is not the same as before; even one's own fundamental matter is not accepted, so how much less so other matters? Whenever the Master speaks of "falling," he means that things are mixed and cannot be categorized as equal. As for what he calls "beginners": [The text continues: ...they do not yet understand that the Buddhas and patriarchs were originally like this. They have not yet realized that the Way is fundamentally without words or phrases. They do not know that the mind is originally pure and the nature is originally still. They do not know that all dharmas are originally empty and quiescent. They do not know that the six sense objects are originally non-existent. They do not know that the six consciousnesses are originally non-arising. They do not know that the six sense organs are originally non-dual. They do not know that the three karmas are originally non-active. They do not know that the four elements are originally non-substantial. They do not know that the five aggregates are originally non-self. They do not know that the twelve links of dependent origination are originally unconditioned. They do not know that the eighteen realms are originally non-discriminating. They do not know that the eighty-four thousand afflictions are originally non-existent. They do not know that the three poisons are originally non-poisonous. They do not know that the six paramitas are originally non-practiced. They do not know that the three bodies are originally non-attained. They do not know that the ten stages are originally non-traversed. They do not know that the four fruits of the śramaṇa are originally non-attainable. They do not know that the two truths are originally non-dual. They do not know that the four formless absorptions are originally non-absorption. They do not know that the eight liberations are originally non-liberation. They do not know that the nine successive dwellings are originally non-dwelling. They do not know that the ten totalities are originally non-totality. They do not know that the ten powers of a Buddha are originally non-powers. They do not know that the four fearlessnesses are originally non-fearlessness. They do not know that the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are originally non-unique. They do not know that the great compassion is originally non-compassion. They do not know that the three gates of liberation are originally non-liberation. They do not know that the four analytical knowledges are originally non-knowledge. They do not know that the six supernormal powers are originally non-supernormal. They do not know that the three samādhis are originally non-samādhi. They do not know that the four dharmas of a Buddha are originally non-dharma. They do not know that the twelve causal conditions are originally non-conditions. They do not know that the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma are originally non-turning. They do not know that the eighty thousand dharmas are originally non-dharma. They do not know that the three bodies are originally non-body. They do not know that the four wisdoms are originally non-wisdom. They do not know that the five eyes are originally non-eye. They do not know that the six perfections are originally non-perfection. They do not know that the seven treasures are originally non-treasure. They do not know that the eightfold path is originally non-path. They do not know that the nine successive dwellings are originally non-dwelling. Kāśyapa did not conceal [his realization]. The monk asked, "Why was it that as soon as he was born, he did not know existence? The Master said, "He was not born in the same way.

The monk asked, "How was it before he was born? The Master said, "He had never ceased. The monk asked, "Where was he when he was not yet born? The Master said, "There is no place where he is contained.
The monk asked, "What kind of person does not undergo cessation? The Master said, "It is one who cannot be extinguished. Above.
Hall. When a member of the monastic community speaks or exhales, there must be a source for it; do not treat this with levity. What kind of place is this?
How could one possibly afford to be casual? Whenever you inquire about a matter, you must recognize at least a modicum of what is good and what is bad. If you do not recognize it, [you will fail].
Whether noble or base, high or low, they do not know what constitutes an offense. They speak recklessly at will and derive no benefit.
They wander from house to house, seeking out similar words wherever they go. Therefore, I have always told my brothers: "Do not take offense at our lack of similarity;
I fear that those who study together are too numerous. Do not bring them here first; if you do, they will not be like us. You must also examine their speech."
First of all: An eighty-year-old man enters the hall; this is no child’s play, nor is it a matter of mere routine.
A single word that is off by even a hair’s breadth means a thousand miles of distance; it is difficult to grasp and hold. This is because one has not applied oneself with vigor to the place of study.
One must strike the bone and beat the marrow; there must be a source for every word. It must be like tongs, like pincers, like hooks, and like locks; you must cause them to correspond.
Only when the continuity is uninterrupted can one attain it; it is fully present in every head and clearly manifest in every object.
Is this not the attainment of the wondrous matter? This kind of study requires great meticulousness. One must investigate thoroughly until it is perfectly accurate and precisely without error.
Once you have reached this point, where is there any room for hesitation? Where is there any room for deliberation? Those who move forward toward the goal must always maintain a sense of solemn awe.
Only when one has gathered their wings can they truly begin. A person who knows this for themselves naturally understands how to guard and cherish [their speech];
they never speak recklessly, and even if they speak ten times, they will cease nine times. Why is this so? It is because they fear it may be of no benefit.

The mind of one who has realized the essence is like a fan in the month of December; it is so parched that mold forms upon the mouth. This is not a matter of forced effort, but occurs spontaneously and naturally.
If you wish to attain such a matter, you must be such a person. Since you are such a person, you need not worry about such a matter.

Such a matter is difficult to obtain. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "You all, even if you were to study and master the matters on the Buddha's side, it would already be a mistaken use of your minds.
Have you not seen how the ancients said that when they lectured, heavenly flowers fell and stones nodded? Even so, it was not of their own doing."
One's own affair. What else is there that is idle? To intend to take this finite body and mind and employ it within the infinite is like trying to fit a square block into a round hole;
how much confusion and difficulty it entails! If there were not such a matter, then even if you were to arrange flowers into patterns or cluster brocades together, they would still have no use.
As long as one has not yet departed from emotional consciousness regarding all things, one must reach the ultimate exhaustion right here. If...
If there is even a single hair’s breadth that cannot be discarded, one is immediately burdened by worldly defilements; how much more so when there are many such errors?
A deviation of even a hair’s breadth results in a transgression as vast as a mountain. As the ancients said: "If the place of study is not profound, it is entirely mundane.
Things of the inner chamber that one cannot relinquish all constitute leaks. One must directly seize the opportunity here; whether seizing upon going or coming, one must exhaust everything at once.
Only when all matters are thus resolved can one be free from error. It is like a person who has mastered every head of knowledge and penetrated every object;
such a one is merely called a "man of affairs," but is never called "noble. This shows that the path of the noble is distinct. Have you not heard it said:
"That which enters through the gate is not the treasure; a dragon is not formed upon a staff"? Do you understand? The Master [Yunmen] held him in high esteem as the Prince of Nanchang.
“I vow to be your teacher in every lifetime. In the autumn of the first year of the Tianfu era, he manifested illness.

He then entered nirvana and was posthumously titled Chan Master Hongjue.

Counting black dots: speech is not as good as silence. Seeking from others while abandoning oneself: the borrowed is not as good as the real.

"When near water, there is no water to drink. Hearing that Master Daomian An of Daguai in Fuzhou had addressed the assembly, saying, "The phrase exists and the phrase does not exist, like a vine leaning against a tree," the Master specifically crossed the mountain ridges to visit him.

There was a One-Eyed Dragon whose secret had been exposed by his son. The next day, when Guishan ascended the hall for the discourse, the Master [Dongshan] came forward and asked, "The principle of the Dharma-body is a profound mystery beyond all reach;

Yangshan said, "What is the matter that lies beyond the Dharma-body? The Master snatched away the whisk, folded it, and threw it to the ground before returning to the assembly.
Yangshan said, "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes; a patch-robed monk is hard to deceive.

Later, hearing that Master Mingzhao Qian of Wuzhou had begun teaching (Qian was blind in one eye), he went straight there to pay his respects. Mingzhao asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Min."
Zhao asked, "Have you ever been to Daopei? The Master replied, "I have. Zhao asked, "What was said there? The Master recounted the previous conversation.
Zhao remarked, "Daopei may indeed be said to be straight from head to tail, yet he simply did not meet with one who understands him. The Master, however, still did not realize it.
He asked again, "Suddenly encountering a tree that has fallen and its vines withered, where do the words return? Baizhang said, "This will cause Moshan’s laughter to become ever fresher.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "Moshan originally had a blade hidden within his smile.
He then prostrated from afar, repenting his error. One day, Baizhang asked, "A tiger gives birth to seven cubs; which one has no tail? The Master replied, "The seventh."
This fellow has no tail. When Xiangyan appeared in the world, the Master did not renege on his previous promise and went to visit him.

As Xiangyan was ascending the hall, a monk asked, "When one seeks neither the various sages nor values one's own spiritual essence, what then? Xiangyan replied, "All myriad functions cease; even the thousand sages cannot carry it.
While in the assembly, the Master made a sound of retching and said, "What words are these? Upon hearing this, Xiangyan immediately descended from his seat and said:
"Your words just now directed at this monk must have been incorrect, which led to my uncle being treated in such a manner. I do not know where the fault lies.
The Master said, "When the myriad functions have ceased, there is still something remaining; though the thousand sages do not carry it with them, it is nonetheless obtained from others."
"How can one be without fault? Yan said, "I beg you, Senior Master, to speak. The Master said, "If I am to have you speak, you must first return the rites of teacher and disciple.
Yan then prostrated himself and repeated his previous question. The Master said, "Why do you not say: 'To agree and to assent cannot both be total'?
Yan said, "If one agrees, what is it that one agrees to? If one assents, to whom does one assent? The Master said, "Agreeing is..."
He acknowledged the thousand sages; his assent was an assent to his own numinous spirit. Yan said, "If you, Master Uncle, speak in this way, you will be vomiting for thirty years from now on.
The Master went to Jia Shan. Jia Shan ascended the hall and the Master asked, "I have heard your words: 'Before one's eyes there is no dharma, yet the intent lies before one's eyes.

The pond had no reflection. The Master made a gesture as if to overturn the meditation seat. Yaoshan said, "How do you do this, Acharya?

The Master went to visit Yantou. When Yantou saw him coming, he lowered his head and feigned sleep. The Master stood before him. Yantou paid him no heed. The Master struck the meditation seat.

Baoshou laughed heartily and said, "For thirty years I have been riding a horse; today I have been knocked off by a donkey.

"What further words or phrases are there? The Master showed them a verse, saying: "I have a precious lute, entrusted to the wilderness. It is not that I do not know how to play it;

[The Master] said, "Is it not that something other than a withered stump illustrates matters above the Dharma-body? The Master said, "Yes. [The Master] asked, "Does the Dharma-body encompass everything or not?

“Does it still pertain to the Dharma-body? The Master said, “Reverend, do not seek it beside the water pitcher. The Gatekeeper then bowed.
The Master asked Jingqing, “‘To grant or to refuse—neither is complete. How do you understand this? Jingqing said, “It is entirely contained within granting and refusing.
The Master said, “If neither is complete, then how? Jingqing said, “Within this, there is no path of granting. The Master said, “Only then does it satisfy my ailment.”

is it sufficient now? The monk replied, "It is sufficient now. The Master said, "Sufficient porridge, sufficient rice. The monk was speechless. (Yunmen spoke on his behalf:
"Sufficient porridge, sufficient rice. A monk built a stupa for the Master’s remains; when it was finished, he informed the Master. The Master asked, "How much did it cost?"
He gave the money to the artisan and said, "Everything depends on you, Master. The artisan replied, "Will you give three coins to the artisan?
Or two coins to the artisan? Or one coin to the artisan? If you can say it, I will build the stupa for you myself. The monk was speechless.
Later, the monk recounted this to Master Xian of Daling Hermitage (who was Luoshan). Daling said, "Return..."
"Is there anyone who can say it? A monk said, "No one has yet been able to say it. Ling said, "When you return, tell Shushan:
'If you give three coins to the craftsman, Master, you will certainly not obtain the stupa in this lifetime.

'Serve Master Pan well. A monk drew a portrait of the Master and presented it to him. The Master said, "Does it resemble me or not?"
The monk had no reply. The Master spoke on his behalf, saying, "Let the assembly take a look. A servant of Deshan came to visit;
as soon as he prostrated, the Master seized him and said, "Do you truly agree with Qianshan’s way? The servant said, "I regret having stayed so long at Deshan; today I have no words to answer.
The Master then let go of him and said, "Feel free to respond as you wish. The servant pushed him away.
Xiong said, "Please listen to me for a moment as I offer you a word of 'circulation' (tongqi). The Master said, "That might be acceptable under Deshan’s gate, but here it is of no use whatsoever.
Xiong said, "I have long heard that Qinshan does not deal with people according to worldly custom.
The Master said, "You have brought shame upon Deshan’s reputation. Go to the meditation hall. While the Master was sitting with Yantou and Xuefeng, Dongshan came by serving tea. The Master then—

[The Master] closed his eyes. Dong said, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Dong said, "Concentration has no door; through what did you enter?
The Master went into the bathhouse and saw a monk treading a water wheel. As the monk came down to pay his respects, the Master said, "It is fortunate that it turns so smoothly;
why must you do this? The monk said, "If I did not do this, how else could it turn? The Master said, "If you do not do this..."
“Ma! What can Qianshan’s eye do? The monk asked, “What is the Master’s eye? The Master made a gesture with his hand as if brushing his eyebrows.
The monk said, “How is it that you, Master, have attained such [a state]? The Master replied, “It is I who am thus; you, however, are not thus. The monk had no reply.
The Master said, “Seeking battle without merit—what a frustrating experience! After a long silence, he asked, “Do you understand?”
Mo said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Qinshan shall carry half of it for you. The Master, along with Yantou and Xuefeng, traveled across the Jiangxi region.
Upon arriving at a tea shop to drink tea, the Master said, "Those who cannot turn their bodies and circulate their breath shall not be allowed to drink this tea.
Yantou said, "If that is the case, I certainly shall not get to drink the tea. Xuefeng said, "I am the same."
The Master said, "These two old fellows do not even recognize the 'head' (the core point) of the dialogue. The First [Master] asked, "Where have they gone?
The Master said, "An old crow in a cloth bag; though alive, it is as if dead. The First Master stepped back and said, "Look, look! The Master said, "Let us set aside Master Huo for a moment;
what about Master Cun? Master Feng drew a circle with his hand. The Master said, "I cannot help but ask. The First Master [said], "Head! (or "Huo! [implying the name of the other master].
Hehe said, "It is too far. The Master said, "There are many who have mouths but cannot drink tea. The Zen guest Jiliang came to visit.
After performing his prostrations, he asked, "What is it like when a single arrowhead pierces the three barriers? The Master said, "Let out the master of the barrier and see.
Jiliang said, "In that case, one must surely acknowledge one's faults and reform them. The Master said, "When do you wait for anything else? Jiliang said, "Excellent!"
Unable to find a place to discharge his single arrow, Liang went out. The Master said, "Come here first, Ācārya. Liang turned his head back;
the Master stepped down from the meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Setting aside for a moment the 'one shaft piercing the three barriers,' try to discharge an arrow for Qinshan and see.
As Liang hesitated, the Master struck him seven blows and said, "Just listen to this fellow who talks nonsense; he will harbor doubts for thirty years."
The monk brought this up to Tong’an Cha. Cha said, “Master Liang may understand how to release the arrow, but he has not yet hit the mark.
The monk then asked, “I wonder, how can one hit the mark? Cha replied, “Who is the Lord of Guanzhong? The monk returned and related this to the Master (Linji).
The Master said, “If Master Liang had understood in this way, he could have spared Qinshan his mouth. Nevertheless...”
Thus it is. Tong’an was not being kind-hearted; you must examine this before you can understand. A monk came for an audience.
The Master held up his fist and said, "When opened, it becomes a palm, with the five fingers spread apart. Now, as a fist, there is certainly no distinction of high or low.
Tell me, does Qingshan allow for discussion on this point? The monk stepped forward and, in turn, held up his own fist. The Master said, "Your doing so is merely..."
A man who neither opens nor closes said, "I do not yet understand how you, Master, receive people. The Master said, "If I were to receive people, it would be just like you.
The man said, "I have come specifically to visit the Master; you must at least reveal some message. The Master said:
"If you come specifically for this purpose, I must reveal it to you. The monk said, "I request it at once. The Master struck him. The monk was speechless.

The Master said, "To sit and wait by a stump for a rabbit is to waste one's mental energy. He ascended the hall, held his staff horizontally across his chest, looked at the assembly, and said, "Is there anyone?
Is there anyone? If not, then Qinshan shall sing the *Pusa-man* (Bodhisattva-mani) and depart! La-la li-li! He then descended from the seat. The Master [concluded].
He debated the principles of the Way with a Daoist master. The master established his thesis, saying: "Coarse words and subtle speech alike all return to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
The Master said: "The Daoist is a slave to the Buddha. The master said: "That is too coarse, sir. The Master asked: "Where, then, is the primary meaning? The master was speechless.
Chan Master Tongxuan of Jiufeng in Ruizhou was the son of the Cheng family from Yingzhou. Initially, he studied under Deshan; later, he attained realization upon hearing the words of Dongshan.
After he took up residence [at Jiufeng], a monk asked: "Can one's own mind and another's mind see each other? The Master said:

Regarding "sameness and difference," the Master said: "Fine and coarse linen do not ward off the cold.
This refers to Chan Master Caoshan Ji, the sixth-generation successor in the lineage of Qingyuan.
Chan Master Daoyan of Dongshan in Ruizhou once cited a statement by Caoshan, which said: "There is a person who, from the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom precipice, leaps straight down.
What kind of person is this? No one in the assembly could respond. The Master stepped forward and said, "He does not preserve [himself]. Caoshan asked, "What is there for him not to preserve?
The Master replied, "Only then can he avoid being shattered upon impact. Caoshan deeply approved of this. Later, there was a monk...
Question: "I request that you, Preceptor, secretly transmit the true mind. The Master said: "Why do you deceive me when there is no one here?

[The Master] was like a foundation stone. [A monk] asked, "Among a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks, which one is Jinfeng? The Master then scratched his forehead.

state the first phrase. The monk said, "It is still cold in the early spring; we hope the Master is well. The Master said, "Still..."
"It is here," [the monk] said. "One must not allow others to inspect it," the Master replied. "Who? the monk asked. The monk pointed to himself.

"It is no trouble being inspected by others," the Master said. He picked up his pillow and showed it to the monk, saying, "Everyone calls this a pillow, yet Jinfeng says it is not. The monk asked, "I wonder, what do you, Master, call it? The Master picked it up.
"A pillow. The monk said, "In that case, I shall follow it accordingly. The Master asked, "What do you call it? The monk said, "A pillow.

"Is it so? The Master made a gesture of bowing; the monk made a gesture of pushing away. The Master said, "This old monk’s eyes are dim; you, Dharma brother, are deaf.

The monk asked, "How many years of age are you, Preceptor? The Master said, "I do not fall within the measure of numbers. The monk asked, "Who is it that possesses long life? The Master said, "Jinpeng."
[The Master] said, "As expected, my eyes have grown dim. The Master said, "Right, right. He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk stepped forward and remained silent for a long while.
The Master said, "What masters have you visited? [The monk] said, "What kind of bowl would you have me visit? The Master said, "Jinpeng has committed an offense. [The monk] said, "Right, right.
After a long silence, the Master asked another monk, "Where have you come from? [The monk] said, "I have come from the Eastern Land. The Master said, "How so?"

The Master said, "A Persian eats black pepper. He asked a monk, "What is your surname? The monk replied, "My surname is He.
The Master said, "In the end, you have not escaped the mundane. The monk said, "It is because of you that I have attained this. The Master said, "If it is so, then the fault lies with Jingu Peak.

The monk asked, "Why did you strike me? The Master replied, "I want this story to circulate. While they were reading the scriptures, Bian Daozhe arrived.
The Master held up a scripture and made a gesture of gathering his robe, looking at him with his eyes. Biandeng lifted his sitting mat and looked back at the Master.

The Master descended from his meditation seat and twisted the monk’s ear. The monk cried out in pain. The Master said, "Today, for the first time, I have caught hold of this ignorant fellow.
The monk bowed and departed. The Master called out, "Acarya! The monk turned his head. The Master said, "If you reach the hall..."
"It must not be brought up," he said. "Why? The Master replied, "There are many who would laugh at the 'old woman’s heart' of Jingu Peak.
He ascended the hall and said, "Twenty years ago, this old monk possessed an old woman’s heart; twenty years later, I have no old woman’s heart. A monk asked:
"What is it like to have the 'old woman's mind' twenty years ago? The Master said, "When asked about the ordinary, I answer with the ordinary; when asked about the holy, I answer with the holy.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like to be without the 'old woman's mind' twenty years later? The Master said, "When asked about the ordinary, I do not answer with the ordinary."
The questioner asked, but the Sage did not answer. When the Master saw the monk approaching, he raised his hand and said, "This is the domain of a great man.
Try to convey a message for me. The monk replied, "I do not wish to deceive you, Reverend. The Master said, "To know one who practices filial piety is indeed rare.
The monk asked, "Is this not the domain of a great man? The Master said, "I, an old monk, am deceiving you, O Kalyāṇamitra."
Lei said, "It is not easy to discern the truth here. The Master said, "Truly so, truly so. The monk bowed. The Master asked, "Where did you set out from? He replied, "Just right here.
The Master said, "Not only do you deceive yourself, but you also deceive this old monk. [He then] ascended the hall for the discourse.
"If I bring it up," he thought, "I fear I will encounter malicious gossip; if I do not bring it up, I will again be met with ridicule and strangeness.
How can I navigate between these two? As soon as a monk stepped out, the Master returned to his quarters.

That evening, another monk requested further instruction, asking, "Master, why did you not answer that monk's question today? The Master said, "It was much like losing one's money and then being punished for it."
The Master asked a monk, "Do you know that single phrase of Jingu Peak? The monk replied, "I have known it for a long time. The Master said, "How so? The monk then gave a shout.
After a long silence, the Master said, "Jingu Peak’s single phrase has been shattered today. The Master continued, "In my old age, I have questioned many people;

Jian asked, "True brass does not equal gold. [The Master] asked, "What is the 'wordless word'? The Master said, "It adds no ornamental color. He asked, "When the four seas are peaceful and clear, what then?
The Master said, "He is still but a man standing at the foot of the steps. Ascending the hall, he said: "The matter lies in the meeting of the lid and the box;

Jinpeng divided his half-courtyard with another monk to dwell there. At that time, a monk came out and paid his respects. The Master said, "It is easy to meet one another;

The monk asked, “If a guest should suddenly arrive, how would you receive them? The Master said, “With a thatched gate and a grass door, I thank you for coming from afar.

"What object do you transmit? The Master said, "The golden-threaded *kāṣāya*. He asked, "What is the *prajñāpāramitā* within the casket?
The Master said, "The six hundred fascicles stored in the side-chambers of the Buddha Hall. He asked, "Where will you go after the Hundred Years [of your life]? The Master said:
A man from the Li family of Shanyang was driving an ox away. He asked, "May I permit myself to follow you, Master?
The Master said, "If you are to follow me, do not share my horns. The man replied, "Yes. The Master asked, "Where will you arrive? The man said, "Even the Buddha-eye cannot discern it.
The Master said, "If you do not let go, you too will remain in a state of confusion. [The man] asked, "What is the high and precipitous place of Lumeng?"
The Master asked, "Have you ever ascended Mount Zhu? [The monk] asked, "What is Chan? The Master said, "A phoenix enters a chicken coop.

[The monk] asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "An elephant is pulled by a lotus fiber. [The monk] asked, "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, I wonder:
will this [reality] also be destroyed? The Master said, "Looking down at the water from the edge of a cliff—suddenly..."
A scene of sorrow. A monk asked, "What is the place where the Master turns himself? The Master said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost my pillow.
A monk asked, "When one attains sudden enlightenment upon hearing a single phrase, what then? The Master said, "Who are you? The Master ascended the hall and addressed the assembly.
A single expanse of stillness, brilliantly radiant; if one attempts to seek it through conceptual thought, it is ultimately difficult to see.
In a sudden flash, one stumbles upon it, and the human mind is opened wide; the Great Matter is clearly and completely accomplished. Truly joyful! Without fetters!
Ten thousand taels of gold could never exchange for this. No matter how many sages may emerge, they all appear within its reflection.
Chan Master Huixia Liaowu of Caoshan in Fuzhou was asked by a monk, "How is it before the Buddha appeared in the world?
The Master said, "Caoshan is not as good. The monk asked, "And how is it after he appeared in the world? The Master said, "Not as good as Caoshan.
The monk asked, "When the four mountains press in from all sides, what then? The Master said, "Caoshan is within them. The monk asked, "Does he still seek to emerge? The Master said, "..."
While inside, he immediately sought to exit. A monk stood in attendance. The Master said, "The Way-farer is truly scorched by heat. The monk replied, "Yes.
The Master asked, "As for this heat, where would you go to avoid it? The monk replied, "I would avoid it within the cauldrons and the furnace coals.
The Master asked, "As for the cauldrons and the furnace coals, how would you avoid them? The monk replied, "No manifold sufferings can reach there."
A monk asked Chan Master Fayi of Ca'an in Huazhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Deep-fry the floating bubbles until they are full and eat them. The monk asked, "If the slightest intention to deliberate is already a deviation, how does one advance on the Path?
The Master said, "There is someone who constantly deliberates; why does he not deviate? The monk said, "This is still a matter concerning the Master himself. The Master said, "Red flames."
Lotus flowers bloom one by one. A monk asked, "What is the place where the Master finds his strength? The Master said, "Like one who is blind and like one who is deaf.
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "That is exactly how I study together with you."

Chan Master Caoshan Guanghui Xuanwu of Fuzhou ascended the hall. After a long silence, he said, "The Venerable Xuefeng’s way of benefiting people is like a golden-winged bird entering the sea to seize a dragon.
A monk stepped forward and asked, "I wonder, how do you act here in this place?
The Master replied, "From where have you come? Another asked, "What is the essential meaning of the coming from the West? The Master replied, "Not."
[The monk] prostrated. [The Master asked: "When shall we meet again? [The monk asked: "What is the mind that is secretly transmitted? The Master remained silent for a long while.
The monk said, "In that case, my listening has been in vain. The Master called to his attendant, "Come here and burn some incense. [The monk asked:
"An ancient said, 'Like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Take care of your eyebrows. [The monk asked: "How is it?"
[The Master] gave an indication. [The student] immediately attained non-obscuration. The Master said, "One must not add frost upon snow.
[The student] said, "In that case, it is entirely due to you, Master. The Master said, "Due to what? [The student] asked, "What is the wondrously luminous true nature?"

The Master said, "Be careful not to damage it. He ascended the hall; after a long silence, a monk stepped forward and said, "Exerting one's utmost for the sake of the assembly brings calamity from within the private door.
I wonder, will you let this pass or not? The Master remained silent. A monk asked, "An ancient said, 'I will not speak even of birth.'"
"Even at death, one does not speak of it. What is the meaning? The Master remained silent for a long while. The monk bowed. The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not.

The Master said, "It is like a cold kitchen where the rice steamer is covered in dust. He ascended the hall and, raising his staff, said, "From the beginning, all have left this single path as a skillful means to receive people.
