Now, in the imperial palace of Great Song, All are but golden branches and jade trees."
Chan Master Baoyin Lingyun of Yunmen Mountain in Yuezhou ascended the hall and said: "Last night, clouds and rain dispersed across the vast sky;

The moon shines amidst the myriad phenomena of the universe. Within these myriad phenomena, the numinous light has neither inside nor outside— How can one penetrate this single phrase of direct clarity?
He did not mention that a monk once asked Master Dage, "When the moon rises above the clouds, what then? To which Dage replied:
Three children embrace a flower drum; do not come to block my path to the goal. When the moon rises above the clouds, what worldly matter does it illuminate?
Three children embrace a flower drum; as soon as you think of it, you are already separated. Do not come to block my path to the goal;
you must have a way to emerge before you can succeed. If you have no way to emerge, you will be like a black ox lying dead.
"Water. [The Master] asked, "How do you speak a single phrase that issues from the body? [The monk] said, "No need for protracted standing.
Zen Master Yunzheng Haipeng of Huai’an Army was asked by a monk, "What is one who has great doubt? The Master said:
In Biepan Rock, they looked at one another and asked, "What is the person who has no doubts? The Master said, "Thus have I heard;
Mount Sumeru is ground to powder. He asked, "Are the meaning of the Patriarch and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? The Master said, "Bodhidharma met Emperor Wu of Liang;
Kāśyapa Mātanga encountered Emperor Ming of Han."
Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Qianming Jicong of Fuzhou, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "This question is not in vain.
The monk asked, "What is the realm of Dongchan? The Master said, "The water of concentration has never left its ancient shore;
how would the red dust of the world dare to enter the waves?"

A monk asked Zen Master Shanji of Liangshan in Dingzhou, a successor of Zen Master Liangshan Yan: "When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then? The Master said, "Do not let your eyes grow dim.
The monk asked, "At what time will you, Reverend, attain Buddhahood? The Master said, "Do not try to degrade the noble into the lowly. The monk asked, "Why? [The Master replied: "Because..."

He did not consent to accept [the position]. The Master said, "Better that good things be non-existent. Regarding the verse on Luzu’s wall-gazing, the Master said: "Luzu’s samādhi was most effortless;
as soon as he saw a monk approach, he would turn his face to the wall. If one is a person who understands the heart and reaches the Way," [then one knows this].
It is not that one understands him merely by raising an eyebrow.
Zen Master Dao-wu Chuan’s Dharma heir, Zen Master Qi-yu of Tianping Mountain in Xiangzhou, was asked by a monk: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral style does he succeed?"
"Who? the Master asked. [The monk] said, "I strike the drum on both ends. [Another] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Radishes from Zhenzhou; tea in a stone jar. A lay practitioner asked, "When the Dharma is without movement, what then?
The Master said, "You have come from Lufu. The practitioner said, "I have not taken even a single step. The Master said, "How then did you arrive here? The practitioner—

[The official] asked, "What was the Master saying in his sleep? The Master said, "I grant you twenty blows. The official asked, "Since there is no neighbor to separate us, why do we not see each other?
The Master said, "Whom should I blame? While walking along the corridor, the Master saw a monk and pointed his staff at him.
The monk stepped forward to take it, and the Master struck him.
Chan Master Daokai of Rongmushi at Tienting Monastery in Dongjing was a dharma heir of Chan Master Qing of Touzi, the eleventh generation under Qingyuan.
He was a native of the Cui clan of Yizhou; from childhood, he studied the practice of abstaining from grain.
He lived in seclusion at Mount Iyang. Later, he traveled to the capital and registered his name at Shu’tai Temple, where he received ordination after passing the *Lotus Sūtra* examination.
He then visited Touzi at Haihui Monastery and asked: "The words and phrases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are like the daily tea and rice;
is there anything else besides these for the sake of others? Touzi replied: "You speak of the Emperor’s decree within the realm; would you still require Yao, Shun, or Yu?"

Tang had none. The Master wished to offer further words, but the monk struck the Master’s mouth with his whisk and said, “From the moment you first conceived the intention [to come here], you already deserved thirty blows.
The Master immediately attained awakening; he bowed twice and then departed. The Master called out, “Come here, Ācārya! But the monk paid him no heed.
The Master said, “Have you reached the stage of non-doubt? The monk then covered his ears with his hands. Later, he served as the *dian* (administrator).

[The Master] sat. The Master’s attendant said, “Managing the kitchen duties is no easy task. The Master said, “I dare not say it is so. The attendant asked, “Are you cooking porridge or steaming rice?
The Master said, “The laborers wash the rice and set the fires; the practitioners cook the porridge and steam the rice. The attendant asked, “Then what do you do?
The Master said, “Out of compassion, the Abbot lets me remain at ease. One day, while attending on Touzi as they were walking through the vegetable garden, Touzi—
He handed his staff to the Master. The Master took it and walked along with him. The Master said, "It is only right that you should act thus.
The Master added, "Carrying the Master’s sandals and holding his staff would not be considered an excessive burden. The Master said, "There is someone traveling with us.

The Master replied, "That one person does not accept instruction. The Master then withdrew. That evening, the Master asked the Master, "The conversation from this morning was not yet finished. The Master said:
"Please, Preceptor, give me an example. The Master said, "Born in the hour of the Rabbit, born in the month of the Dog. The Teacher immediately lit a lamp and approached.
The Master said, "Your coming up and going down here has not been in vain. The Teacher said, "Being by the Preceptor's side, it is only natural that I should act thus.
The Master said, "Who does not have servants and maids in their household? The Teacher said, "The Preceptor is advanced in years; you cannot do without him."

The Master said, "To receive such earnest devotion. The teacher replied, "There is a share in repaying this kindness. Later, after he had taken up residence, a monk asked, "The song of the Hu family does not fall within the five musical notes;
its melody emerges from the azure heights. We pray that the Master will blow and sing it for us. The teacher said, "The wooden cock crows at midnight."
"The Iron Phoenix Cries at Daybreak. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then a single phrase contains the melody of a thousand ages;
those in the hall, like clouds and water, are all connoisseurs. The Master said, "A tongueless child can provide a sequel. [The monk] said, "A master of the school, the eye of humanity and heaven.
The Master said, "Stop using those two pieces of skin. [The monk] asked: "At midnight it is truly bright, yet at daybreak nothing is revealed. What is this?"

[The Master] did not reveal the underlying matter. The Master said: "The boat is full, yet empty; the fisherman sleeps among the reeds. [A monk] asked: "What is the家风 (family style) of Cao-dong? The Master said:
"The rope-bench is rotted by wind and rain; the thatch of the abbot’s quarters has begun to encroach. [A monk] asked: "What is the direct root-source?
The Master said: "Grass has already grown beneath your feet; every step falls upon a precarious slope. He ascended the hall for a discourse. During the day, he entered...
In Jeta’s Grove, under a bright moon hanging in the sky, one ascends Vulture Peak at night; yet the sun floods the eyes, crows and ravens appear like snow, and solitary geese form flocks.
Iron dogs bark as they soar toward the heavens; clay oxen fight as they enter the sea.
At such a moment, when the ten directions gather together, how can "self" and "other" be distinguished? Within the arena of the ancient Buddhas and beneath the gate of the Patriarchs—great!
A single hand reaches out from the house to receive those who come and go. Friends, tell me, what kind of matter has been accomplished? After a long silence, he said:

"I have planted an extra tree that casts no shadow, leaving it for later generations to behold. Ascending the hall, he said: "The moment one ascends this seat, one has already entered the realm of worldly toil.
To further fix one's gaze upon it is to manifest one's own flaws. The one phrase of the separate transmission is like using a thief to catch a thief."
The family does not lose its original lineage; the fox and the wildcat remain attached to their den. Therefore, True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words;

Buddhas and sentient beings are both merely metaphorical designations. Reaching this point, one turns the light back to reflect upon oneself and takes up the responsibility with a letting-go—yet even this cannot be avoided.

The cold cicada clings to the withered tree; its weeping ends, yet it does not turn back. Entering the hall [the Master said]: To call this "one phrase" is already to bury the ancestral wind (zongfeng).
To accommodate the present age, the common path has been worn away. Therefore, one borrows function to clarify the position; the application lies within the essence.

Borrowing the position to clarify the function: the essence resides within the sphere of activity. If one were to clarify both essence and function simultaneously, it would be like a door with two panels that cannot open at once;
one must focus one's intent upon both panels. Have you not heard the Old Man of Xinfeng say: "The peaks and ridges are uniquely beautiful, yet the crane does not pause its flight;

the numinous tree stands tall and remote, yet the phoenix has no place to perch"? It reaches the point where, having accomplished the work, one does not dwell therein—like a flash of lightning or a spark of fire, difficult to pursue.
In the mere interval of deliberation, the journey extends ten thousand miles. Entering the hall, [the Master] said:
"I shall not ask about what comes before the thirtieth day of the twelfth month; but as for the matter of the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, how is it?
You worthy ones, when you arrive here, even the Buddhas cannot help you, the Dharma cannot help you, the Patriarchs cannot help you, nor can the old monks of the world."
I cannot help you; this mountain monk cannot help you; even the Old Man Yama cannot help you. You must exhaust the present moment.
If you exhaust the present moment, then even the Buddha cannot do anything for you; the Dharma cannot do anything for you;
the Patriarchs cannot do anything for you; nor can the old monks of the world do anything for you.
"What can he do? Even this mountain monk cannot do anything about him; even Old Yama cannot do anything about him. Everyone, tell me:
what is the principle for exhausting the present moment? Do you understand? "Next year there will be new branches again;
the spring wind’s vexation shall never cease. Question: "What is the Way? The Master said: "A hornless clay ox."

Benyelan. Ascending the hall, he said: "The bells and drums resound, yet the message has not been heard; a single sound startles the one who was dreaming. Perfect, constant, and quiescently responsive—there is nothing else.
Who says that Avalokiteśvara has a separate gate? After a long pause, he said: "Do you understand? Do not ask the guest atop Potalaka Mountain;
the warbling of the oriole cuts through the clouds of the sea mountains. Ascending the hall, he took up his staff and said: "This..."

To fully grasp this is entirely a matter of the various Buddhas establishing their positions. Even if one were to manifest mastery over the rolling up and unfolding of phenomena—such that they surge from the east and subside in the west—one has still not dreamt of the news prior to the Seven Buddhas. You must know that there is one person who does not receive it from another.
He does not receive instructions nor does he fall into stages. If you recognize this man, the business of a lifetime of study is finished.

He suddenly called to the assembly, saying, "If you look on with fixed eyes any longer, there is no need to meet me. Ascending the hall, after a long silence, he said, "The green mountains constantly move their feet;

the stone woman gives birth to a child at night. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, he said, "Using provisional words to proclaim the Way brings it down to the present moment. Even if...
To cause a tongueless person to understand speech, and for a footless person to be able to walk—though one may strive, one still cannot yet correspond with that one person.
Do you understand? "The dragon’s roar leaves ears aching; the tiger’s cry brings but vain brooding. He asked, "What is the speech that encompasses both?
The Master said, "The wondrous function is fully deployed, encompassing the world; the wooden man takes leisurely steps as he emerges from the midst of fire. He asked again, "If it is like this..."
"What is the family style of the Master? The Master said, "Everyone sees it. [The monk] asked, "I do not understand what it is they see.

The Master said, "The eastern wall strikes the western wall. In the first year of the Daguan era, Li Xiaoshou, the Governor of Kaifeng, memorialized that the Master’s spiritual practice was preeminent within the monastic community and should be formally honored.
Accordingly, he was granted a purple robe and the title Chan Master Dingzhao. An inner court official brought [the decree].
When the imperial decree arrived, the Master finished expressing his gratitude and then set forth his own resolve.

He stated that at the time of his ordination he had made a solemn vow not to seek profit or fame, but to study the Way with single-minded devotion in order to benefit his nine generations of kin. He declared that if he were to violate this vow, he would sooner abandon his life than do so.

His parents had granted permission based on this; if he now failed to uphold his original intent and instead shamelessly presumed upon imperial favor, he would be betraying the sacred pledge he made before the Buddha.

Thereupon, he composed a memorial with full formalities. The Emperor again issued an edict to the Capital Prefect, firmly ordering him to accept [the office]. The Master resolutely maintained his refusal and would not turn back. For refusing the command, he was sentenced to punishment.

By imperial decree, he was sent to the Jikisi (Criminals Court) and the Congqingsi (Court of Light Punishment). When the officials reported this to the authorities, they intended to transfer him to Zizhou.
The authorities said, "If he is ill, he shall be exempted from punishment. When the officials questioned the Master, he replied, "I am not ill. They asked again.
"How could there be scars from moxibustion? The Master said, "In the past I was ill; today I am cured. The official ordered him to reflect on this.

The Master said, "I have fully understood your kind intention, but falsehood is not what I find at peace. Thereupon, he calmly submitted to the execution and departed. Those who followed him were like people returning to a bustling market.

Upon arriving in Zichuan, he rented a dwelling, and his disciples grew even more devoted. In the winter of the following year, an imperial edict permitted him to act as he pleased, so he built a hermitage.
At the heart of Fuyong Lake, monks and laypeople gathered like a river’s confluence. He addressed the assembly, saying:

"Those who leave the home life do so out of weariness with worldly toil and a desire to escape birth and death; they quiet the mind and cease discursive thoughts, severing all attachments. This is why it is called 'leaving the home life.
How can one allow ordinary gain and sustenance to bury one's entire life? You must cast both ends open and let go of the middle. Whether encountering sound or form..."
It is like planting flowers upon a stone; seeing profit and fame is like having grit in one's eye.

Moreover, from time immemorial, there is nothing you have not already experienced, nor is there anything about the sequence of things that you do not know. It is nothing more than turning the head into a tail, ending up exactly as it was.
Why must you cling so bitterly? If you do not cease now, when will you? Therefore, first—
The holy teaching tells people simply to exhaust this very moment. Once this moment is exhausted, what further matter remains?

If you attain a state where there is nothing in the mind, even Buddhas and Patriarchs are but enemies; all worldly affairs naturally become cool and indifferent, and only then do you correspond with that "other side.
Have you not seen how Yinyangshan refused to see anyone until his death, and Zhaozhou refused to [die] until his death?
He told others: "Pian Dan gathers acorns and chestnuts for food; Damei uses lotus leaves as clothing; the 'Paper-Robed' Wayfarer wears nothing but paper;
the Venerable Xuantai wears nothing but cloth; Shishuang established the 'Hall of Withered Trees,' where he sits and sleeps with people only to 'kill your mind';
Touzi had people prepare rice so that they might cook and eat together, desiring that they achieve economy of effort."
This is your concern. Furthermore, the various sages of antiquity have set such precedents; if you lacked superior qualities, how could you have endured them?
O virtuous ones, if you investigate this matter thoroughly, you will certainly not fail others. If you are unwilling to take it up, I fear you will find it increasingly difficult in the future.
This mountain monk’s own practice is beyond reproach, yet I am honored to preside over this mountain gate; how could I simply sit idly while wasting the constant offerings?

I have remained here, suddenly forgetting the entrustment of the former sages. Now, following the example of the ancients, I have established the regulations for the abbot’s office in consultation with everyone.
From now on, I shall no longer descend the mountain, attend formal meals, or dispatch emissaries for fundraising.
