One day, he ordered the bell to be struck at the outer gate of the three main halls to receive the head seat.

The assembly went out to welcome him; the Master had indeed arrived. He was directly invited into the head seat’s quarters to unpack his belongings. (From the *Rendiantiyanmu*, Chapter on Lingshu). Hereafter...
The Lord of Guangzhou commanded the Master to appear in the world at Lingshu. On the day he opened the hall, the Lord personally attended and said, "I, your disciple, request your instruction.

The Master replied, "Before one's eyes, there is no other path" (Fayan remarked elsewhere: "One must not fail to benefit others"). The Master then said, "Do not say that today I am deceiving everyone;
rather, having no choice, I shall create a scene of total disorder before you all. Should you suddenly encounter a person of clear vision..."
It has become a scene for laughter; now it can no longer be avoided. Let me ask you all:
since the beginning of time, what matter has there been? What has ever been lacking? To tell you that "there is nothing" is already to bury you.
Nevertheless, you must reach this very stage before you may attain it. Do not, however, ask haphazardly just to satisfy your own impulsive curiosity regarding your own mind.
The interior is pitch black and vast. Great matters lie ahead for tomorrow and the days to come.

If your fundamental understanding is hesitant and lingering, then for the time being, look toward the gateways of transformation and edification established by the ancients; look east and west and see what kind of principle this is.
Do you wish to understand? It is entirely because of your own dense and thick delusions accumulated over immeasurable kalpas that, upon hearing [the Dharma] for a single period...

When people speak of this, they immediately give rise to doubt. They ask about the Buddha, they ask about the Dharma, they ask about the "upward" and the "downward," seeking understanding and interpretation, yet they only become further estranged from the truth.
To apply the mind is already a deviation; how much more so when there are words and phrases! Is it perhaps that not applying the mind is the way?
Do not misunderstand me! What else is there? Take care. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "I have no choice but to speak."
"You all say, 'Directly beneath, there is nothing. This already constitutes a mutual obscuration. Yet you still wish to step forward, seeking understanding by chasing after words and phrases;
thus you create a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, setting forth broad challenges and difficulties, only to gain a slippery tongue.
You move further and further away from the Way—when will there ever be a time of rest? If this matter were to reside within words,"
The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon—how could these be devoid of words? For what reason, then, do you speak of a "separate transmission outside the teachings"?

If [enlightenment] were obtained through scholarly understanding or intellectual ingenuity, then even a sage of the Tenth Ground, whose preaching of the Dharma was like clouds and rain, would still be rebuked for seeing his own nature as if through a fine gauze. From this it is known that all who possess a mind are worlds apart from [true realization].
It is indeed so. Nevertheless, for one who has attained it, the fire of words cannot burn the mouth;
though speaking of matters all day long, nothing ever touches the lips or teeth, and not a single character is ever uttered.
Though wearing clothes and eating food all day long, one never touches a single grain of rice or a single thread of silk. Even so, this is still merely talk concerning the gateway of the teaching.

"You must truly attain such realization before you can succeed. If we speak from the standpoint of the Zen monk’s school, presenting one's spirit within a phrase is merely a waste of effort in idle reflection.
Even if you were to take responsibility for it under a single phrase, you would still be a dozing fellow. At that time, a monk asked, "What is this one phrase?

The Master said, "Lift it up! He ascended the hall and said, "The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of scripture—whether explained horizontally or vertically—are like the heavens..."

Bring forth the old Master below! Speak in all directions, vertically and horizontally; bring me the principle you have spoken about, even if it were no larger than the point of a needle, and let me see it.
To speak in such a manner is already like trying to cure a dead horse with medicine. Nevertheless, how many are there who have reached this realm?

I do not dare hope that you will have resonance within your words or conceal the blade’s edge within your phrases; yet, in a single blink of an eye, a thousand differences arise, while the wind remains calm.
The waves are stilled. I humbly pray that you will partake of this offering. A monk came to visit;
the Master then picked up his *kāṣāya* and said, "If you can speak, you fall within the circle of my *kāṣāya*. If you cannot speak, you remain sitting in a ghost cave. What do you say?
He spoke on the monk's behalf, saying, "I have no strength. One day, the Master struck the ritual mallet and said, "In the world of Wondrous Joy, a hundred..."
Miscellaneous fragments. [The Master] took his alms bowl toward the city of Hunan to eat porridge and rice. He ascended the hall and said:

"Brothers, you have all come from various quarters seeking out masters to resolve the matter of birth and death. In every place you have visited, surely there were venerable elders who offered compassionate and skillful words of guidance.
Is there any phrase that you have been unable to penetrate? Come forward and cite it; I shall wait for you so that this old man may [help you]."
"Everyone, let us deliberate. Is there anyone? Is there anyone? At that moment, a monk stepped forward, intending to pose a question. The Master said, "Go! Go!
The road to the Western Heaven is long, more than a hundred thousand miles. He then descended from his seat. He further cited:

When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, took seven steps, and looked around in the four directions, saying: "Above heaven and below heaven, only I..."
"Solitary Honored One. The Master said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to the dogs, so as to ensure peace throughout the world.
The Master was attending a vegetarian feast at Wende Hall when Attendant Ju asked, "Is the fruit on Lingshu mature yet?
The Master replied, "In what year did you begin to believe in the Way? A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?"
[The student] asked, "What about the mountains, rivers, and the great earth? The Master said, "There is more above this. [The student] asked, "Is there anything further above?
The Master said, "There is. [The student] asked, "What is the matter above this? The Master said, "Śākyamuni Buddha is in the Western Heaven; Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva dwells in the Eastern Land.
[The student] asked, "What is Yunmen Mountain? The Master said, "The fixed site of Mount Geng. [The student] asked, "What is the Great Cultivation? The Master said, [as before].
A practitioner asked, "The Master said, 'A single cup is held in the hand. Ascending the hall, upon hearing the sound of the bell, he said, "The world is so vast;
why does the sound of the bell wear the seven-fold robe? A monk asked, "One lifetime accumulates evil and knows not good;
one lifetime accumulates good and knows not evil. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A candle. A monk asked, "What is the Master’s [teaching] at an improper time?"
Regarding a single phrase for people, the Master said: "In the early morning they pull the plow; in the evening they drag the harrow. He cited Xuefeng, who said:
"The Buddhas of the three periods turn the Great Dharma Wheel upon the flames. The Master said:

"The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods, and the Buddhas of the three periods stand upon the ground and listen. Entering the hall, he cited a saying to instruct you to directly accept it as such.
It was already too late; you had already been struck on the head with excrement.

Even if you were to pick up a single hair-tip and suddenly perceive the entire world, it would still be like gouging out flesh to create a sore. Nevertheless, you must truly arrive at this stage before you can succeed.
If you have not yet reached this point, do not engage in empty pretense; rather, you must step back and turn toward your own fundamental root.

Push it down and investigate further: what kind of principle is this? Truly, there is not even a hair’s breadth of anything that can serve as an intellectual interpretation for you or cause you doubt.
Moreover, each of you is, in yourself, a person for whom a segment of reality exists, wherein the Great Function is manifest before you.
It does not require even a hair’s breadth of effort from you, and you would be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
It is simply that you all have shallow roots of faith and thick layers of evil karma;

thus, you suddenly sprout all these horns and carry your alms-bags across thousands of villages and ten thousand miles—why do you suffer such humiliation? Furthermore, my friends, what is lacking for you? You are great men!
Han: "Who is it that has no share? Only one can personally take this up; yet even so, it is not easy. One must not allow oneself to be deceived by others or accept their directions.
As soon as you see the old monk open his mouth, you should take a stone and shove it in his mouth.
Otherwise, you will be like flies on excrement, fighting over and pecking at it, three or five of you gathered together to deliberate in misery."
I yield to you, brothers. For all of you, the ancient masters of old had no other recourse; thus, through skillful means, they bestowed a word or a phrase to provide you with a way of entry.
Once you recognize such matters for what they are, set them aside and exert some effort of your own.
Is this not a point where you have a measure of affinity? Hurry, hurry! Time does not wait for man. As the breath goes out—
I cannot guarantee that you will even survive this inhalation. Beyond this, what other body or mind is there to be used idly elsewhere?
You must pay close attention; take care. [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "The entire universe is brought forth all at once and placed upon the lashes of your eyes.
Hearing such words as these, I do not dare hope that any of you will impulsively come forward and give this old fellow a slap. Rather, proceed slowly and examine it carefully."

Look! Is it existence? Is it non-existence? What kind of principle is this? Even if you were to attain clarity here, should you encounter the gate of a true monk, I would gladly break your legs with a mallet.
If you are such a person, upon hearing it said, "Where is there an old master appearing in the world?
you should spit right in his face, saying, "You defile my ears and eyes! If you do not possess such capability, [you are no match for me].
As soon as you hear someone mention it, you immediately try to take it upon yourself; this already falls into the secondary level of functioning.
You should look at how Master Deshan, as soon as he saw a monk enter the gate, would simply drag his staff and drive him away. Or how Master Muzhou, as soon as he saw a monk enter, would say:
"This is a settled case; I grant you thirty blows. As for the rest of them—how should they have acted?
If one is merely a hollow talker who feeds on the spittle and saliva of others,
memorizing a heap or a load of antiquated rubbish and galloping about everywhere with the lips of a donkey and the mouth of a horse, boasting that he understands "ten-turn" or "five-turn" dialogues—
even if you were to question him from morning until night for kalpas like this, have you ever even dreamed of it? Where in this is there any real exertion for the sake of others?
In such a state, there are those who even begrudge a monk his meal; yet if one can simply eat the food provided, what is there worth conversing about?
On the day you stand before King Yama, he will not accept your verbal explanations.
Brothers, if you are those who have attained realization, you may spend your days living among the assembly as they do. But if you have not yet attained it, do not easily let the time pass by. Great!
You must be meticulous. The ancients had great complications in their ways of assisting one another. For instance, Xuefeng said, "The entire earth is your own self.
Jiashan said, "On the tips of the hundred grasses, recognize this old monk; in the midst of the bustling marketplace, recognize the Son of Heaven.
Luopu said, "When a single speck of dust arises, the entire earth is fully contained within it; on the tip of a single hair, there is the whole body of a lion."
"It is always you. Take hold of it and turn it over in your mind to contemplate it. As days pass and years deepen, there will naturally be a way of entry.
This matter admits of no substitute for you; it must reside within the sphere of each person themselves. Thus did the Old Monk appear in the world."
I am merely providing testimony for you. If you have even the slightest basis for your claim, I shall not fail to see through it.

If you have truly not yet attained the skillful means, it would be improper for me to dismiss you. Brothers, we are all equally those who have worn out our straw sandals and cast aside our teachers and parents to travel as pilgrims;
you must truly exert some measure of spirit before you can succeed. If you have not yet found a point of entry, [you must strive further].
In this situation, you must encounter your own kind—those who gnaw like dogs and pigs—who will not spare their own lives as they enter the mud and the water to assist you.
When there is something truly worth gnawing upon, even if you must raise your eyebrows, hang up your alms-bag, and break your staff, you must strive for ten or twenty years to reach the ultimate end;
do not worry that it will not be accomplished. Even if you fail to reach the ultimate end in this life, in a future life...
Furthermore, you will not lose your human form. Entering through this gate will also save you effort;
you will not have lived your life in vain, nor will you have failed your teachers, parents, or the donors of the ten directions. You must simply take heed;
do not wander aimlessly from prefecture to county, carrying your staff across a thousand or two thousand *li*, spending winter here and summer there.
Fine mountains and fine waters are suitable for taking up one's nature; there is much vegetarian offering, and it is easy to obtain robes and bowls.
How bitter, how bitter! To seek another’s single grain of rice, one loses half a year’s provisions. What benefit is there in traveling like this?
How can a faithful donor digest their vegetables and grains? You must look within yourself; no one can take your place. Time does not wait.
In dealing with others, one day you will suddenly find your vision falling to the ground. When that moment arrives, what will you have to rely upon?
Do not be like a crab falling into boiling water, your limbs flailing in confusion; there will be no room for you to engage in empty talk or boastful exaggerations.
Do not let this time pass in vain. Once a human body is lost, it is not regained for ten thousand kalpas; this is no small matter. Do not merely look at things as they appear for now.
[The Master] said: "In the past, even laypeople valued the Way. 'If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die in the evening.

How much more so for us śramaṇas—what matters must we practice? You must exert yourselves with great diligence. Take care. A monk asked Lingshu, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Lingshu remained silent.
After he passed away, his disciples were setting up a stele for his biography and wished to include this incident. They asked the Master [Xuefeng]: [Please explain this.]
[The Master asked: "When our late teacher remained silent, how could one erect a stele [for him]? The Master replied, "Teacher.
He ascended the hall and said, "The Buddha-dharma is indeed very much present; it is only that my tongue is too short. After a long pause, he said, "It is long now.

While everyone was working together to carry firewood, the Master took up a piece and threw it down, saying, "The entire Tripitaka speaks only of this. Seeing a monk measuring rice, he asked about the rice basket.
"How many Dharma-eyes are there inside? The monk had no reply. The Master spoke on his behalf, saying: "They cannot be exhausted even when measured with a bushel.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Each person has their own radiance; yet when looked for, it is not seen, shrouded in darkness.

What is this radiance of your own selves? He spoke on their behalf again, saying: "The kitchen, the storehouse, and the main gate. He further said: "A good thing is not as good as having none at all. Addressing the assembly, he said:
An ancient worthy said: "Medicine and disease treat one another; the entire earth is medicine. Which of these is your own self? He then said:
"When encountering the base, it is immediately noble. A monk asked: "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master clapped his hands once, took up his staff, and said: "Take this staff!
The monk took it and snapped it into two pieces. The Master said: "Even if you were to do so, I would still give you [a blow]."
"Thirty blows! [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "A single word is raised, and a thousand carts follow the same ruts;
it encompasses even the finest motes of dust—yet this is still but the teaching of transformation. If you are a patch-robed monk, what would you do?

If you attempt to deliberate here upon the meaning of the Buddhas and the meaning of the Patriarchs, the single path of Caoxi will sink into oblivion. Is there anyone who can speak? Come forward and speak! A monk asked:"
"What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? The Master said, "A sesame cake. [The monk] asked, "What connection is there here?
The Master said, "Truly, what connection is there? He then said, "All of you have reached a point where nothing more can be done."
Seeing that the man was attached to the "intent of the patriarchs," [the Master] asked: "Regarding talk that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs—what do you call a Buddha?
What do you call a patriarch? First, explain the principle of what transcends Buddhas and patriarchs.
He then asked about "exiting the three realms": "Bring forth the three realms for me to see. Is there anything of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing that obstructs or hinders you? There was none.
What sensory objects of sound and forms can you possibly comprehend? What kind of bowl are you trying to understand?
To take that as a basis for a view of differentiation—the ancient sages could not help it; they cast their bodies across to serve sentient beings, saying, "The whole body is entirely true.
Yet, in every single thing, the essence itself cannot be grasped. I tell you: right now, what business is there? It is already a case of burying yourself.
It is gone. If you truly have no point of entry, then for now, investigate and contemplate it alone.
Aside from dressing, eating, defecating, and urinating, what else is there? Why do you give rise to all these various delusive thoughts out of nowhere?
Furthermore, there is another type who, as if in a casual manner, gathers together to learn some ancient...
People talk about the Way, claiming that by using their cognitive nature to memorize and grasp through deluded thoughts and conjecture, they have "understood the Buddha-dharma.

They do nothing but talk nonsense all day long, passing their time at will; yet they remain dissatisfied with this, wandering thousands of miles away from their parents and teachers to pursue such a course.
What kind of urgency drives these men who merely "gather wild roots" to go on pilgrimage? Go! Go on pilgrimage!
He drove them out with his staff and ascended the hall. "Therefore, you must know that the times have grown turbid and we live in the dregs of the age.
Lately, monks go north claiming to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, or go south saying they are traveling to Mount Heng. To practice pilgrimage in such a manner is to be a monk in name only;
it is a waste of the faithful's offerings. Alas, alas! When questioned, they appear as dark as lacquer, doing nothing but indulging their own natures."

At that time, there may be three or two who, being wildly learned and merely able to memorize and retain teachings, travel everywhere seeking similar phrases to gain the seal of approval from elder masters.
They treat those of superior attainment with contempt and perform deeds of meager merit.
On the day when King Yama hammers his nails into them, do not say that no one told you so. If you are beginners or late learners, you must truly exert yourselves.
Spirit! Do not vainly record the words of others; much emptiness is not as good as a little reality. Later on, you will only find that you have deceived yourself.

What business is there? Come forward. The Master ascended the hall. When the assembly had gathered, he pointed his staff toward the space before him and said, "The great earth, heaven and earth, and all the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust—all are contained within this.
Who would dispute over the Buddha-dharma or seek victory and defeat? Is there anyone here who can offer a word of admonition?"
"Is that so? If no one dares to admonish you, wait until this old man admonishes you. The monk said, "I beg the Master to admonish me.
The Master said, "This wild fox spirit! He ascended the hall, took up his staff, and said, "The Bodhisattva Asaṅga has, for no reason, transformed himself into a single *zhilu* staff.
He then drew a line and said, "All the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are entirely caught within this tangle."
He then descended from his seat and ascended the hall, saying: "I look at you all; even within two or three turns of the teaching mechanism, you cannot grasp it.
What benefit is there in vainly donning the patched robe? Do you understand? I shall provide you with a commentary to break through this delusion.
In the future, when you travel to various quarters, if you see an elder and they raise a finger or hold up a whisk, saying, 'This is Chan; this is the Way,' drag your staff and smash it to pieces!"
He immediately departed. Had it not been so, you would all have fallen into the retinue of the celestial Māras and destroyed my lineage.
If you truly do not understand, then for now look within the thicket of entanglements. I have constantly told you:

the Buddhas of the three periods throughout all the lands as numerous as motes of dust, the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven, and the six patriarchs of the Tang land—all are present upon the tip of this staff.
He preaches the Dharma. His spiritual powers manifest transformations; his voice resonates throughout the ten directions, moving freely in every direction.
Do you understand? If you do not, do not merely engage in empty pretense. Even so, have you yet seen with true and authentic insight?
Even if you reach such a state, you have not yet dreamed of a monk or a novice. Not meeting a single person in a village of three households—suddenly!
Holding up his staff, he drew a line and said, "All is right here. He drew another line and said, "All depart from here as well. "Take care!
One day, the Master thrust his hand into the mouth of a wooden lion and cried out, "I am being bitten to death!
Save me! (Nanzong Rou offered this in his stead: "The Master’s hand went out too far. He ascended the hall and said: "Awakening to the Way through sound; clarifying the mind through form. Thereupon—
Raising his hand, he said: "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva buys a sesame cake with money. Lowering his hand, he said: "It turns out it was just a steamed bun.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a single treasure hidden within the mountain of form.
He took the lantern and placed it inside the Buddha Hall; he brought the triple gate and set it atop the lantern. "What is this? he asked himself.
He provided a substitute response, saying: "The mind shifts as it pursues external objects. He also said: "Clouds arise and thunder resounds. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"I will not ask you about the period before the fifteenth day; regarding the period after the fifteenth day, bring forth a single phrase! The assembly was speechless. He himself provided a substitute response, saying:
"Every day is a good day. Entering the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Ordinary people truly claim it exists; those of the Two Vehicles analyze it and claim..."
The Pratyekabuddha calls it illusory existence; the Bodhisattva regards its very substance as emptiness.
When a Zen monk sees a staff, he simply calls it a staff; when walking, he simply walks; when sitting, he simply sits—without disturbing anything.

A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "When spring comes, the grass grows green of itself. He questioned a newcomer, "Where are you from? The man replied, "Silla."

The Master said, "What will you take across the sea? The monk replied, "The grass bandit has been utterly defeated. The Master reached out his hand and said, "Why is it here with me? The monk replied, "Exactly so.
The Master said, "Feel free to leap about as you please. The monk was speechless. A monk asked, "How was it before Niu-tou saw the Fourth Patriarch?
The Master said, "Every household contemplates Avalokiteśvara. The monk asked, "And after he saw him? The Master said, "Fire."
The earthworm swallows the large insect. [A monk] asked, "What is the 'Single Song of Yunmen'? The Master said, "The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month.
[The monk] asked, "How about the one who sings it? The Master said, "Now, take it slowly. [A monk] asked, "What is the 'Mud Ox Bellowing on the Snowy Ridge'?"
The Master said, "Mountains and rivers run. [The monk] asked, "What is 'Yunmen’s wooden horse neighing'? The Master said, "Heaven and earth are dark.

[The monk] asked, "I request the Master to provide the essential framework for the matters that have come down from of old. The Master said, "In the morning look to the southeast; in the evening look to the northwest.

[The monk] asked, "If one understands it in this way, what then? The Master said, "When the eastern house lights its lamp, the western house sits in darkness. [The monk] asked, "Regarding the twelve hours of the day..."
"How can one avoid the fault of [falling into] non-emptiness? The Master said, "Where would you place this question?
The monk said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master to provide an example. The Master said, "Bring me pen and inkstone. The monk then brought the pen and inkstone. The Master composed a verse:
"If you look up without reflecting, you are already mistaken; If you attempt to deliberate, when will you ever awaken? What is the study? [The monk asked.]

"Your own self," the Master said. [The monk] asked, "I travel through mountains and enjoy the waters; what is the Master’s own self? The Master said, "Fortunately, the *vīnā* (chant leader) is not here.
[Another monk] asked, "What is it like when one swallows everything in a single gulp? The Master said, "I am inside your belly."
[The monk] asked, "Why is the Master inside this student's belly? The Master said, "Give me back the *huatou*. [The monk] asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Go.
[The monk] said, "I do not understand; please tell me. The Master said, "Your credentials as a *śrāmaṇera* are clear; why seek a further judgment?
[The monk] asked, "When birth and death arrive, how can they be dispelled? The Master extended his hand and said, "Return [it]."
"I have been in the cycle of birth and death for so long," he said, "but when I asked my parents, they would not permit me to leave the home-life.

How can I attain renunciation? The Master said, "Shallow. He said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Deep. He asked, "What is the student's own self? The Master said, "Afraid that I might not know.
He asked, "When all ten thousand functions have been exhausted, what then? The Master said, "Bring me the Buddha Hall here. The Master added, "Give it to me."
[The monk] deliberated and said, "How could this concern another's affairs? The Master shouted, "You empty-headed charlatan! A monk asked, "What is it like when the tree withers and the leaves fall?
The Master said, "The golden wind reveals its essence. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A dried-up dung pellet.
A monk asked, "Where do all Buddhas emerge from? The Master said, "Water flows uphill on the eastern mountain. A monk asked, "Regarding the ancients facing the wall..."

"What is the meaning? The Master said, "The seventh day. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Looking at the mountains in the daylight. The Master asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "From Mount Nanyue. The Master said, "I do not engage in such entanglements with others; come closer. When the monk approached, the Master said, "Go. A monk asked, "What is the house of the Master? The Master said, "The seventh day. There are two kinds of illness regarding the Dharmakāya. First, although one has attained the Dharmakāya, because attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not been forgotten and one's own views still persist, one remains seated within the Dharmakāya;

thus, there is no clarity in all places, and it is as if there were an object directly before one’s face—this is "one" [kind of illness]. Furthermore, even when one has penetrated the emptiness of all phenomena, there is still a lingering sense that something exists indistinctly;

this too is light that has not yet fully permeated through. Moreover, the Dharmakāya itself has two kinds of illness. Upon reaching the Dharmakāya, if attachment to phenomena is not forgotten and one's own views still remain, one sits within the Dharmakāya.
[The Master said: "It is one-sided. It is one. Even if you manage to penetrate through to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), you must not let it pass unexamined.

The Master said, "This is the realm of great beings such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. The monk cited Guankui’s ascent to the hall, where he said:

When the Master arrived at Jiangzhou, the Minister Chen invited him for a meal. As soon as he saw him, the Minister asked, "I shall not ask about the Confucian classics;
you have your own preceptors for the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. What is the meaning of being a patch-robed monk?"
Regarding the matter of a monk’s pilgrimage, the Master asked, "How many people have you questioned thus far? The monk replied, "I am questioning the Venerable One right now.
The Master said, "Set that aside for a moment; what is the meaning of the Teachings? The monk replied, "The yellow scrolls and red volumes.
The Master said, "This is merely written words and language; what is the meaning of the Teachings? The monk replied, "The mouth wishes to speak, yet words fail it; the mind..."
When the mind seeks to engage with objects, its reflections are forgotten. The Master said, "When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail; this is because it is confronted by speech.
When the mind wishes to engage with objects, its reflections are forgotten; this is because it is confronted by deluded thoughts. What is the intent of the teaching? Shu remained silent.
The Master said, "I have heard that you, Minister, study the *Lotus Sūtra*. Is this true? Shu replied, "It is. The Master said, "The sūtra says: 'All worldly livelihoods...'"

All these matters are entirely consistent with the true nature (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, tell me: how many people have fallen from their positions in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception?
The Minister was speechless. The Master said, "Minister, do not be so hasty. You have cast aside the Three Scriptures and Five Treatises."
Even those who have entered the monastic forests for ten or twenty years still find it difficult to master [the Way].

"Take care of yourselves. He ascended the hall and said: "All of you here have been carrying your alms-bags and traveling abroad.
Have you yet recognized your own nature? If you have recognized it, come forward and speak of it. If you have not recognized it, you are merely being deceived by others. Now I ask you all:
for how long have you been studying under a teacher and applying your minds to sweeping the floors and boiling tea?"
Tea. Wandering through mountains and playing by waters—pin it down for a moment! What do you call "self-nature"? Everyone, tell me:
that which is fundamentally unchanging and undifferentiated from beginning to end, neither high nor low, neither beautiful nor ugly, neither arising nor ceasing—where does it ultimately return?
Have you all yet realized its place of descent? If you can understand it here—
This is the dharma-gate of liberation of all Buddhas. To awaken to the Way and see one's nature, from beginning to end, there is neither doubt nor anxiety;
one may proceed freely in any direction, and no one can do anything to you. Every word spoken and every breath exhaled truly has its source.
It is like a person buying a field: they must obtain the original deed; if they do not obtain that original deed, in the end it remains [unsecured].
It is unstable. Even if you were to bring it before the authorities and have them issue a formal judgment, you still would not obtain it.
Alas, because you failed to secure the original deed, in the end, it was seized by others. You people who practice Chan and study the Way are just like this.
Is there anyone among you who has secured the original deed? Try bringing it forth and showing it to me. For now, what do you call the "original"?
This is the original pledge. Let everyone try to explain it. If you are truly sharp and discerning, as soon as you hear such words spoken, you will know where they lead.

If you do not know where they lead, then even if you study outwardly until you have acquired a thousand kinds of cleverness, memorization, and intellectual understanding—your mouth flowing like a river—it will never reach the ultimate point. It will remain worlds apart from your own true self. For now, go back to your robes.

The Master asked, “Who is the spectator? Dongshan said, “The one for whom the mechanism has been halted and the performance has ended. The Master said, “...”
"If that is so, then those who know the sound do not harmonize," [Zhaozhou] said. Shanshan asked, "What is the matter of one who knows the sound?
The Master said, "A great month has thirty days. Shanshan said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "I deserve to receive a severe blow from the Master's staff. Shanshan then desisted.
[Zhaozhou] asked, "Regarding the record of old at Vulture Peak, whom do you succeed this morning? The Master said, "Chushan."
"Stark and abrupt! The Han River flows eastward. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then you are a successor of Dongshan.
The Master said, "Not truly attending to the matter; calling a bell a jar."
A monk asked Chan Master Tong of Guangji Monastery in Dengzhou, “What is it like when all conditions have ceased?
The Master said, “A three-legged toad flies up into the sky. The monk asked, “What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharmakāya? The Master said, “The three peaks of Mount Hua are small.
The monk asked, “What is the meaning of this? The Master said, “The Yellow River flows with a rolling bottom.”
A monk asked Chan Master Hongjiao of Dongping Mountain in Shaoyou, "What is the barrier that points upward? The Master held up his whisk.
The monk said, "I, your disciple, have not yet spoken; I beg the Master to point it out again. The Master said, "This is not your realm.
The monk said, "Does the Master have no skillful means? The Master said, "A second offense will not be tolerated."
Chan Master Zongsheng of Ya Mountain in Qianzhou, successor to Chan Master Letan Qian, ascended the hall and said: "The sound of the bell is clear, the sound of the drum is resonant;
heard morning and evening, cease your deluded thoughts. If you can realize this, it is merely labor in vain to seek another path. Do not say that this mountain monk has no skill—*duh*!"
A monk asked Master Xiang, the Lotus Peak Hermit of Tiantai and dharma heir of Chan Master Fengxian Shen: "What is the bellowing of the snow-clad ridge’s clay ox? The Master said:
[The Master] listened. [A monk] asked, "What is the wooden horse of Yunmen neighing? The Master said, "An echo.
On the day he entered nirvana, he held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying, "When the ancients reached this point, why did they refuse to stay?

The assembly had no reply. The Master then said, "Because their journey lacked strength. He spoke again, asking, "Ultimately, how is it? Holding the staff across his shoulder, he said, "The staff is carried across."
Carrying his staff, he did not look back at anyone; he went straight into the thousands and tens of thousands of peaks. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
A monk asked Chan Master Chongsheng Yu of Jiangzhou, "What is the samādhi for a student to utilize? The Master said:
Carrying his staff slung across his shoulder, he asked, "What is the essential meaning? The Master said, "Step by step, tread upon reality.
Chan Master Deqing Yu of Dingzhou succeeded Chan Master Huiyuan of Dingshan.
Upon opening the hall for the assembly, he addressed the congregation, saying: "The immeasurable gates of the Dharma are all fully present."
It is sufficient. Nevertheless, although it is thus, you must first understand it thoroughly before you can attain it.
Regarding the skillful means for its removal, the sages of old appeared one after another and said: "The Lamp was transmitted; thereafter, the worthy ones stood shoulder to shoulder.
Thus it is called "succeeding the Patriarch. For this reason, mind transmits to mind and dharma seals dharma. But how is it transmitted? How is it sealed? Raising up his whisk, he said: "This..."
This is thus a testimony borne out by both humans and devas. If it is so, then they shall provide mutual proof. For those who have not yet understood, please feel free to ask questions.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The iron gate is a perilous path.

On the occasion of the end of the summer retreat, as the monks ascended the hall, a monk asked, "The ninety-day period of restraining the feet is now complete; what are the formalities for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony? The Master—
[The monk] said, “A monkey chasing a butterfly; it rests once every nine steps. [The monk] asked, “What is the meaning of this?
The Master presented a verse, saying: “Two children carry a wooden drum; The one on the left beats it, the one on the right dances.

In a single instant, they manifest hundreds of thousands of forms; I show them clearly to you—take heed and remember! [The monk] asked, “When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? The Master said:
The tortoise drills through the wall. Entering the hall: resting upon rocks and rinsing one's mouth with flowing water, one acts spontaneously according to the natural truth.
As the ancients said: "Pushing aside the mists and sweeping away the snow, they harmonize with the mica; digging into the stones and moving the pines, they obtain the *fuling* fungus.
At such a time, what more need be said? Do you all wish to understand? Listen to this verse: The long sky clears after the snowfall; wild geese fly across the vast plains.
Clouds drift in fragments, westward and eastward.
A monk asked Chan Master Bin of Hanzhu Mountain in Xiangzhou, "What is the Eye of the True Dharma? The Master said, "Blind. The monk asked, "What is the master’s pivot-pin?
The Master held up his whisk; the monk then shouted, and the Master struck him. [The monk] asked again.

"What is the teaching of the Three Vehicles? The Master said, "Shang Daren (The Superior Man). [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Hua Sanqian (Transforming the Three Thousand).
[This was the record of] Chan Master Piyun Ji, successor to [Master Xuefeng].
A monk asked Chan Master Zhao of Kaixian on Mount Lu, "I beg the Master to grant instruction regarding the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage.

The Master said, "When the white clouds part, one sees the bright moon. The monk said, "That is still a point of doubt for me. The Master said, "When the yellow leaves fall, one hears the sound of pounding clothes.
The monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "A single stream of cold mountain brook; its efficacy surpasses [all else]."
A disciple asked, "What about 'using' them? The Master said, "In a hundred pieces. He ascended the hall and said:

"The regulations of the monastic groves and the ancestral style of the Buddhas consist of one visit for instruction and one request, one bowl of congee and one meal. But tell me, what is it that you understand?
As for all of you, your minds do not rest and your thoughts do not abide. If you could rest where there is no resting, and have no thought where there is thought, then naturally—"
This accords with the principle of non-arising. To speak in such a manner is to laugh until one’s own mouth falls apart. *Chan*.
A monk asked Master Tianbao of Jinling, "What is it like when white clouds embrace a secluded rock?
The Master said, "Not your realm. The monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Divide five into three. The monk said, "I, your student, have not yet..."
At dawn, the Master said: "The nostrils and the needle-case.

Zen Master Xifeng Shao, the Dharma heir of [the previous master], was followed by Zen Master Xilang of Taoyuan Mountain in Cizhou. A monk asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said: [The nostrils and the needle-case].

[The Master] said, "If the One Who Came from the West had any intention [to harm me], he would have cut off this old monk's head. [The monk] asked, "Why then did he act like this? The Master replied, "Have you not heard it said:
'For the sake of the Dharma, one may lose one’s body'?"
A monk asked Chan Master Zhishan Fayun of Anzhou, "What is the Dharma site of the ancient Buddhas? The Master said, "The mountains are green and the waters are blue.
[He was] a successor of Chan Master Banyue Rou.
A monk asked Master Zhichen of Lantian County, “What is the gate of Great Samādhi? The Master said, “Gathering firewood and selecting vegetables. He ascended the hall and said:
“A mountain is formed by relying on the first basket of earth; a long journey is reached by depending on the first step.
Upādyāya, you have just now come from beside the hearth—is this the same as the first step or different? If you say it is the same, then you do not understand that there is no shifting. If...”
"Speaking of distinction, there is neither meeting nor shifting. Elder, how do you understand this? Do you understand yet? Here is not there;
there is not here. Now tell me: are they one place or two places? Is it shifting or non-shifting?
Is it coming and going, or is it not coming and going? If you can clarify this, then past and present will be as one, from beginning to end."
From that moment on, every thought-moment is impermanent; every mind is forever extinguished. Therefore it is said: "By observing the direction one knows where another has gone;
yet the one who went does not arrive at a destination. Venerable sir, you have just now come in such a manner; now, please depart in just such a manner. *Chan*.

Master Xuefeng Qingshan of Xichuan, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Miaoshengzhen, ascended the hall and said: "Yesterday was one; today is two. There is no need for deliberation—you must quickly have a sudden flash of realization.
If you do not have this flash of realization, you will miss your entire life; there will be no way out. *Duḥ!*"
Chan Master Xifeng Yunhuo of Jizhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Qingliang Ming.
He was the son of the Zeng family of that prefecture. Early in his career, he visited various masters; later, he met Qingliang.
He asked, "How is it before the Buddha appeared in the world? Qingliang replied, "Clouds obscure the trees at the gate of the sea. He asked, "And after he appeared in the world?"

"How is it? Liang asked. "It is like splitting open the Iron Ring Mountains," the Master replied. At these words, he attained great enlightenment. Liang certified his realization. He returned to reside at Baolong, where disciples gathered from all quarters.

Emperor Zhenzong sent an envoy to summon him for an audience regarding the essentials of the school. The Emperor kept him in the Imperial Garden for some time; there, he sat in silent meditation without eating.
The Emperor marveled at his extraordinary state and bestowed upon him the title Yuanjing (Perfect Purity). He took leave to return, receiving a great abundance of precious gifts.
Lung [the Emperor] declined both [offerings]. He composed a poem to honor the Master’s conduct and changed the name of Baolong Monastery to Xiangfu, thereby commemorating the Master’s residence.
Once, someone asked about the essential principles of the *Yi* (Book of Changes). The Master said: "The spirit arises from the formless and is perfected through the formed.
By proceeding from the existent back to the non-existent, one is then able to accord with the Way of the wondrous, perfect, and correct enlightenment. Therefore, from..."
Forty-nine. Extending this to eleven thousand five hundred and twenty, one exhausts the principles of the world and fully realizes human nature;
this is no different from the teaching of our Sage. On the day he entered parinirvāṇa, he said to the assembly: "Heaven is not high and earth is not thick;
it is simply that people of this age cannot see through it. Just look at the twenty years of my monastic life."
5. As before, he faced south and gazed at the Northern Dipper; then, with eyes closed, he passed away. Upon cremation, śarīra were obtained and a stupa was erected.
He was the Dharma successor of Chan Master Wenshu Zhen of the ninth generation under Nanyue.
When Chan Master Xiaocong of Dongshan in Ruizhou was traveling, he served as the head of the lamp-hall at Yunju.
There he heard a monk say that the Great Sage of Sizhou had recently appeared near Yangzhou. Someone asked: "If he is the Great Sage of Sizhou, why is he appearing in Yangzhou?"
"Why then did he appear in Yangzhou? The Master said, "The gentleman loves wealth, but he takes it by the right way.
Later, a monk reported this to Master Xiang of Lotus Peak. The Master was greatly astonished and said, "A descendant of Yunmen still remains!

In the middle of the night, he gazed toward Yunju and prostrated himself in his direction. After [the Master] took up residence there, a monk asked, "Before Bodhidharma transmitted the Seal of the Mind-ground, and before Śākyamuni..."
He untied the jewel from his topknot. At that time, if one were asked about the meaning of the Westward Journey, would there still be such a "meaning of the Westward Journey" or not?

The Master said, "In the sixth month, the rain falls incessantly; it broadens the hearts of the myriad people. The monk said, "If so, then clouds disperse and every house has its moon; spring comes and flowers bloom everywhere.
The Master said, "From the soles of your feet down to the Diamond Water’s edge, how much distance is there? The monk was speechless.
The Master said: "The Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing of this matter.
It is because you, Venerable One, have not realized it that those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure. To mistake the shadows for the head—is this not a great error?
Since the Patriarch came from the West specifically to sing of this matter, why need one further prattle on before the assembly? Take care. [Question: Regarding the rootless tree...

"Where was it planted? The Master said, "The permanent residence lasts for a thousand years; the monk is present for but a single day. A questioner asked, "What is the phrase that transcends sound and form?
The Master said, "Jambudvīpa in the south; Uttarakuru in the north. The questioner said, "If that is so, then this student knows how to acknowledge your kindness without confusion.
The Master said, "How deep are the four great oceans? A questioner asked, "How is it when the ancient mirror has not yet been polished? The Master said: [Silence].
"This is not far from Hanyang. [The monk] asked, "What is it like after the grinding? The Master said, "Before the Yellow Crane Tower is Parrot Isle.
[A monk] asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "When principle prevails, one follows it. He ascended the hall and said, "How can I, this mountain monk, say anything?
The ancient is the present; the present is the ancient. Therefore, the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* says: 'Pines are straight and thorns are crooked; cranes..."*

"The white crane is black; the crow is white. Do you still know this? Even so, it is not necessarily the case that pines are always straight and thorns are always curved, or that cranes are simply white and crows are simply black.

Dongshan said, "Here, there are also curved pines, there are also straight thorns, there are also black cranes, and there are also white crows. [He stood for a long time. He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "The student..."
"When one cannot advance and yet cannot retreat, what then? The Master said, "Clasping one's head, one weeps to the blue heavens. The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "Do you know where the bowl and the cooking pot fell? If you can know where they fell," [he continued].
"I have also come to ask you this. Thirty years from now, even if you were suddenly asked about it, it might not be certain. He ascended the hall and said: "Hanshan said:
'Red dust grows at the bottom of the well; white waves rise upon the high peaks. A stone woman gives birth to a stone child; tortoise-hair grows an inch at every joint.
If you wish to study Bodhi, simply look at these appearances. After a long silence, he said: 'Do you know where this lands?'"
If you do not know where it has fallen, look! Look! Bodhi has entered the Sangha hall. [He stands for a long time. Ascending the hall:
The spring cold is frozen and thick; last night there was fine snow. Do you see it? The great earth is covered in vast snow; the spring breeze remains as cold as ever.
To speak of Chan and speak of the Way is easy; to become a Buddha or a Patriarch is difficult. Be careful. Ascending the hall: The morning cock announces the dawn with its spirit.
After the gruel, the monk is wide awake; the lantern is still dozing, while the pillar is alert. He spoke again: "If it is alert, say it is alert;
if it is vividly clear, say it is vividly clear. Tomorrow and the day after, do not mistake the servant for the master. Take care."
On account of certain matters, he addressed the assembly: "The sky is clear, so the roof is covered; the weather is favorable, so the grain is harvested.
Having paid the royal taxes early, we beat our bellies and sing the *bā* songs. If one asks about Deshan’s “staff upon entering the gate,” it is still merely following a model and drawing a likeness.
If one asks about Linji’s “shout upon entering the gate,” it cannot avoid being like pressing one's eyes until flowers appear. Apart from these two paths, I wonder how Dongshan would have acted?

The Master said, "It has been a long time since the weather cleared and it rained; lately, clouds have begun to rise. He asked, "If someone were to ask you about the fundamental tenet of Dongshan in the future, how would you instruct the students to express it?
The Master replied, "The vegetables in the garden are extremely withered; I am carrying water to sprinkle on the spinach.
One day, feeling unwell, the Master ascended the hall to take his leave of the assembly and spoke this verse on the Dharmakāya: "Studying Chan..."
"The Way is not obscure. Ask through to the North Star hidden within the Dharma-body. "I am now old and decrepit, extremely frail;
seeing people, I have no strength to deliberate with them. Only my spade knows my intent: when planting pine trees, it ascends once more to Mount Kongara.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. He was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Kongara.
Chan Master Faguang of Gaoyang in Ruzhou, a successor of Chan Master Qin of Nantai, was asked by a monk: "What is the great compassion of the thousand hands and eyes? The Master said:
Falling into a pit or a ditch.
A monk asked Chan Master Jiecheng of Shishuang in Tanzhou: "The ancients said, 'Rolling up the curtain in broad daylight;
shifting the seat to face the green mountains. What is 'rolling up the curtain in broad daylight'? The Master said, "Bring me the pure pitcher. [The monk] asked, "What about..."
He moved his seat to face the green mountains. The Master said, "Put it back in its original place. Ascending the hall, he said: "There is no dharma outside the mind;
there is no mind outside the dharma. Flowing freely according to conditions, do not hesitate any longer. As soon as you all step onto the stairs and path, you should turn back.
Why must you wait for a second ladle of foul water to be poured upon you?"
A monk asked Chan Master Zhixian of Deshan in Dingzhou, a successor of Chan Master Deshan Yan, "What is it like when one sees form and thereby sees the mind? The Master said:

The horned bow bends like the moon; the precious sword is as sharp as frost. [The student] asked, "How should one understand this? The Master said, "The golden armor resembles fish scales; the vermilion banners are like flames.
[The student] asked, "I have come from afar to seek your guidance; I beg you, Master, to grant me an audience. The Master said, "I will not receive you.
[The student] said, "If that is so, then my question was offered in vain. The Master said, "Rarely do I meet a guest with pierced ears; often do I encounter those who mark the boat."
Question: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; why was he unable to attain the Way of Buddhahood? The Master said:
"Gazing greedily at the moon in the sky, he lost the pearl in his palm. Question: "What is it like when military orders are urgent?
The Master said: "Dust covers one's face in the middle of the crossroads. Question: "Why is it so? The Master said: "Knowing it yet deliberately committing it."
Question: What is the discourse on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? The Master said: "The stone rams and stone tigers chatter away. Question: What kind of teaching is this? The Master said:
"Long discourses cannot fully record it; short verses are beyond human hearing. Question: What is the meaning of "once calling upon the name of the Buddha"?
The Master said: "All thereby attain the Way of Buddhahood."

Master Yiqin of Emeishan, a successor of Master Jing of Heishui, ascended the hall. A monk came forward and bowed. The Master said, "The great earth shatters into a hundred fragments," and then descended from his seat.

Chan Master Hetan Huicheng of Hongzhou, a dharma successor of Chan Master Wuzu Keqin, was asked by a monk: "To see is form; to hear is sound. Apart from these two paths, I ask the Master to speak otherwise.
The Master said: "An old temple with a new plaque. [The monk] asked: "What is your companion among the myriad dharmas? The Master said: "Not being a companion to the myriad dharmas."
[The Master asked: "Who is this person? The Master said, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. One day, seeing a monk wearing his patched robe, the Master said, "How fine are these stitches!
The monk replied, "I simply want it to be sturdy. The Master said, "Why do you 'beat the grass to startle the snake'?
The monk said, "When a guest arrives, one must see to them. The Master said, "Is there only this, or is there something else? The monk replied, "Clouds arise upon the mountain peaks."
The Master said, "Not yet; speak further. [The monk] said, "Water dripping from the crevices of the rocks. He asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī himself; liberation is liberation itself."
Chan Master Zibo of Dongshan in Ruizhou ascended the hall and said: "Everyone is like this—calm winds and still waves. Where did they come from?
Suddenly encountering a vast expanse of surging waters with white waves lapping at the heavens—at such a time, it would be difficult even to find a single sailor.
Is there anyone among you who can take the helm? No one in the assembly responded. The Master said, "I have deceived the entire crew."
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Long waist and short legs.
Chan Master Siguang of Beitang in Fuzhou was asked by a monk, "What is the transformative and adaptive activity of a patch-robed monk?

The Master said, "Surging eastward and sinking westward. The monk asked, "After this transformation and adaptation, what is it like? The Master said, "The earth is fertile; the eggplants are tender. [Question: "As for such... [The text ends here.]
"What is the ancestral style of the Master's house? The Master said, "Writing the character on the right with the left hand. The student said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "The head is slanted and the legs are like willow branches."
The Dharma-body Verse of Chan Master Fourth Patriarch Duan of Qizhou says: "A lamp-wick pricks the foot of a stone man;
In haste, go and invite the learned physician Zhou. On the road, he meets Master Pang who asks him about it; In the sixth month, the sun dries his head as he hangs it out to bask."
A monk asked Zen Master Zhinyong of Yungai in Tanzhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The inscriptions on ancient temples are difficult to read. The monk asked, "What is the intent of this? The Master said, "Those who read them all knit their brows."
A monk asked Chan Master Tong of Haihui in Shu State, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "A persimmon bucket and a bamboo hat.
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "When walking, it is worn on the head; when sitting, it is hung on a high wall."
A monk asked Chan Master Miaoyuan of Dongshan in Ruizhou, “What is the Buddha? The Master said, “The head and brain are similar.
A monk asked Chan Master Zixiang of Yitai in Qizhou, “What is the realm of Yitai? The Master said, “On the roads, nothing is left behind.
The monk asked, “What is it like for one within that realm? The Master said, “The dog of Jie barks at Yao.”
A monk asked Zen Master Huaiqing of Tiantong in Mingzhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Dust does not settle in the eyes. The monk asked, "How should one understand this? The Master said, "Water does not remain in the ears.
The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall prostrate myself. The Master said, "When the eastern house lights its lamp, the western house sits in darkness."
A monk asked Chan Master Shuzhi of Baoyan in Yuezhou, “What is the Buddha? The Master said, “An earthen body and wooden bones.
The monk asked, “What is the underlying meaning? The Master said, “Adorned with five-colored gold. The monk said, “If that is so, I shall prostrate myself before you.
The Master said, “The *zhilu* staff of Tiantai.”

A monk asked Zen Master Xiu of Wuzushan in Qizhou, "It is said that 'there being no dharma to be preached, this is called preaching the Dharma. Since there is no dharma to be preached, with what will you preach?
The Master said, "The frost is cold and the ground is frozen. The monk said, "'Śūnyatā-born (Ākāśagarbha) did not understand sitting in the mountain cave;
he provoked the celestial flowers to come from the earth. The Master said, "The sun rises and the ice melts. As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "..."
"Why do you not advance a word? The monk remained silent. The Master said, "A cart should not be pushed sideways; principles must not be adjudicated with partiality.
Zen Master Bian of Baima in Xiangzhou was asked by a monk, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "When water comes, the river swells. The monk asked, "What is the Dharma?
The Master said, "When the wind comes, the trees move."
Chan Master Zhishu of Shuinan in Suizhou ascended the hall and said: "If you wish to know the Path of Liberation, the cock has crowed and the sky is already dawn.
The cypress tree in front of Zhaozhou’s courtyard knocks down the dates from Qingzhou. Tsk!"
Chan Master Qiyue of Shangfang in Anji County, successor of Chan Master Fuchang Shan. A monk asked, "What is bodhi? The Master said, "Brick heads and roof tiles.
The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Suffering. He ascended the hall and said: "Gathering up yellow leaves to burn into blue smoke, the bamboo..."

He slept through the night in his robes upon the couch. After the morning gruel, the signal drum struck three times for the end of the session. Who could speak further of the Ancestral Teacher’s Chan?
He then descended from the seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Changtan of Yuyang in Mingzhou, "What is existence within existence? The Master said, "The Golden River."

At the summit [of the mountain], he asked: "What is 'nothingness within nothingness'? The Master said: "In front of the Prajñā Hall. Ascending the hall, he said: "The thousand flowers compete in blooming;
the hundred birds sing out in spring—this is the phrase that points upward. The Buddhas appear in the world; the spiritual teachers give rise to compassion—this is the phrase that points downward.
What is the phrase that does not involve these two paths? If you can recognize it, you will breathe from the crown of your head. If you can recognize it..."
It is not permitted. It is like plowing a stony field with an earthen ox. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
Chan Master Rui Xin of Jinshan in Runzhou was asked by a monk: "The Buddha said, 'I have a great affliction, because I have a body.
Before my parents were born, I do not know where this body was located. The Master said: "Throughout vast kalpas, it has had no location. If..."

[The opponent] argues that [the concepts of] arising, ceasing, and extinction are proven to be non-existent. [The Master] says: "If that were so, then the mind that pervades the ten directions would not exist in any place whatsoever.
The Master said: "Shaking a stake in the mud. Ascending the hall, he said: "That which is valued in the mundane world are the Jade Disc of He Shi and the Pearl of Lord Sui.
[Yet] Jinshan calls them donkey dung and horse manure. That which is valued in the supramundane world are True Suchness and Liberation. Bodhi...
To speak of Nirvana is like calling a mountain of gold a "boiling bowl of pork fat" that makes a ringing sound. Tell me, where does such talk land?
It is not that the mind of grasping and rejecting is heavy, nor is it a matter of believing in heterodox and inverted views. Do you all wish to know?
A fierce tiger pays no heed to meat on a table; how could a roaring furnace cast the needle within one’s bag?
Chan Master Yishu of Yaoshan in Lizhou, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Qianmingxin, was asked by a monk: "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? The Master said:

"A great tree is wrapped in a large bark. The monk asked: "How was it after he appeared in the world? The Master said: "A small tree is entwined in a small bark. [The monk] asked: "How about now? (The Master remained silent.)
This is the Venerable Acala. The Master said: "The Four Heavenly Kings cannot lift him up.
Chan Master Zhimen Zu was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xuedou Chongxian of Mingzhou; he was the son of the Li family from Suining Prefecture and relied upon Renxian of Puan Monastery.
After the Superior Man left the household life and received full ordination, he took up his cross-staffed sūtra at the lecture hall to investigate principles and exhaust the profound mysteries.

His interrogations were as swift as charging blades, and his eloquence was unrivaled; all recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma, and everyone pointed him toward a journey south. He first visited Zhimen, where he immediately posed this question:
"If not even a single thought arises, how could there be any fault? Yunmen called for the Master to come forward. As soon as the Master drew near, Yunmen struck him across the mouth with his whisk.
When the Master prepared to open his mouth, Yunmen struck him again. At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and subsequently went to reside at Cuifeng.

Later, he moved to Xuedou. On the day he ascended the hall, standing before the Dharma seat, he looked out at the great assembly and said, "If we speak of seeing one another in the fundamental sense, there is no need to ascend this high Dharma seat.
