"Words wound people; they are like a thousand blades churning in one's belly. The monk drew a line with his hand and said, "What can be done about this?
The Master said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. A monk asked, "Do you receive those who come in such a manner? The Master said, "On a solitary peak, there are no guests to lodge.
The monk asked, "Do you receive those who do not come in such a manner? The Master said, "In steep rapids, no boat remains."
[The Master] said, "Setting aside for a moment 'thus' and 'not thus,' how is the phrase that pierces through the skull?
The Master replied, "It is laughable and it is also pitiable. Ascending the hall, he said, "You must grasp it while the black bean has not yet sprouted.
After a long silence, he called to the assembly, "The sword has gone far away!"
Chan Master Xiuhui Yuanzhao of Ciyun Monastery in Chuzhou ascended the hall and said: "A sliver of moon reflects in the cold pool; faint clouds fill the azure sky.
For one who has attained the Way, this is a truly excellent message. Is there anyone here who has attained the Way?
A faint cloud pierces through your skull; a sliver of moon strikes your nostrils. Be careful!"
A monk asked Zen Master Huītong of Guizong on Mount Lu, a successor of Zen Master Daomouyǒu: "What is the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth? The Master said:
"The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. [The student] asked, "What is the phrase that cuts off all streams? The Master said, "An iron mountain lies across the road.
[The student] asked, "What is the phrase of following the waves and riding the currents? The Master said, "The boatman sails down to Yangzhou.
[The student] asked, "What is the samādhi of every dust mote? The Master said, "Ashes fly and flames rage. [The student] asked, "What is the Great Dharma of the Buddha? The Master said...
[The student] asked, "The Yellow River water flows from the tip of Mount Kunlun. [The student] asked, "How does one practice throughout the twelve hours of the day?
The Master said, "An iron ox walks upon the spring grass. [The student] asked, "When returning to the West with a single shoe, what was the purpose?

The Master said, "Because one finds joy where conditions arise; it is not out of loathing for one's native land. [The student] asked, "What is the matter right before one's face? The Master said, "The bridge of the nose beneath the eyes."

Chui ascended the hall and said: "The mind arises following appearances; perception arises from the dust of the senses. To clearly perceive the fundamental mind is to know that the mind is without form.
Thus, the oceans of lands in the ten directions are perfectly luminous in every thought-moment, and the infinite Dharma gates encompass the heart in every instant. For one who acts thus,"
Why must one go to the eastern outskirts of the City of Borrowed Awareness to meet Mañjuśrī, only to find the gate of the pavilion opened to personally encounter Maitreya?
Therefore it is said: "The inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates converges within the single dharma-site. Raising his staff, he said:
"This is the One Dharma; that is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). This is the site of enlightenment; that is the One Dharma.
After a long silence, he said: "Look! Look! This staff pierces through the skulls of all of you; Mount Sumeru crushes the nostrils of all of you.
He struck the incense stand once and said: "For now, understand it right here. He ascended the hall and said: "From non-being, one enters..."
There is ease: it is difficult to enter non-existence from existence. At the place where both existence and non-existence are exhausted, do not be so coarse and negligent; look up and see!
Cold Mountain and Pick-up Boy pay homage to Fenggan.
Chan Master Hui-xian of Anxian Xingjiao Monastery at Anzhou ascended the hall and said: "I have a staff. With what can it be compared in ordinary times?
It was not gathered from the Southern Mountains, nor does it come from the western cliffs of Mount Kunlun. When lifted, it makes the eyes of all bright;
when set down, the dragon of the abyss retracts its neck. If you disciples would borrow it to look upon, it stands out as the most eminent among men."
[The Master] struck the incense stand and descended from his seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Jietibi of Furi Jinghui Temple in Lin’an, successor to Zen Master Liang of Yuwang: "What is the Vairocana Seal? The Master—
[The Master] said, "Striding through the snow in straw sandals. A student said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Every step leaves its trace.
Chan Master Shenhui of Tiantong in Fuzhou ascended the hall for the discourse: "The eighty-four thousand gates of the *pāramitās* are wide open at every door.
The Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms within the three-thousandfold world system, each preach the Dharma—neither speaking of existence nor speaking of non-existence."
I do not say it is neither existent nor non-existent; I do not say it is both existent and non-existent. Why? Because it transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
Meeting face-to-face, few recognize it when their eyes meet. Last night the frosty wind leaked a message: the plum blossoms remain as they were, adorning the cold branches.
Chan Master Yuanming Zhengtong of Lingyin in Lin’an, a successor of Chan Master Zhilin of Lingyin, was asked by a monk, “What is the Way?
The Master said, “When walking at night, do not step on white. The monk asked, “Who is the person on the Way? The Master said, “Huang Zhangsan and He Lisi.”

Chan Master Liyuan of Zhizhe Mountain in Wuzhou, successor to Chan Master Chengtian Jian, ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said: "When the Great Function manifests, no rules or regulations remain.
A single finger toward the east, and heaven and earth are hushed and still; a single finger toward the west, and all things crumble like ice melting away. South—"
A single finger toward the south: the Southern Dipper flees. A single finger toward the north: the Northern Dipper hides away. A single finger toward the zenith:
it strikes the nostrils of Śakra. A single finger toward the nadir: it pierces through the adamantine waters at the edge of the world.

As for this single finger before you all—what kind of matter does it accomplish? After a long silence, he struck the ground once and said: "On the road, a finger points to the fleeing deer; at the gate..."

*Daquan'er*. Chan Master Zujing Daming Faying of Da Mei, a successor of Chan Master Jiufeng Shao, was the son of the Zhang family of his native prefecture. He abandoned Confucian studies to undergo the scriptural examinations and attained [enlightenment].
Du Yi lectured at Yanqing. Whenever those studying the *Abhidharma* were stumped by questions from senior masters, they would invariably challenge the Master;

the Master would respond with such eloquence and discernment that he was revered by the assembly. Suddenly, he remarked, "Names and characteristics are circuitous and indirect; how could these be what I take as my primary principle?

He then went to consult Jiufeng. Upon meeting him, Jiufeng recognized his potential; they conversed as if he had long been a member of the monastic community, and Jiufeng subsequently gave him a rigorous, piercing instruction. The Master grasped the essential meaning. From then on...
"You have attained renown. Later, when he ascended the hall, it was the beginning of the thirty-six decades and the start of the seventy-two seasonal markers.
"Setting aside the final phrase for a moment, how would you speak the very first phrase? He then took up his staff and said:
Holding the brush at the turn of the year, may all matters be auspicious. Swiftly, as the decree commands! "Great assembly, when I, this mountain monk, chant and proclaim in this manner, tell me:
does it still contain the meaning of the Patriarchs? After a long silence, he said: "I remember Black Li Si from the eastern village."

Year after year, he personally wrote [this] at his gate. He stood upright with his staff and descended from the seat. At the beginning of the Xuanhe era, an imperial decree was issued for all monks and nuns to become "De-shi" (virtuous practitioners).

Although the masters of the Dharma deliberated together, not a single word was spoken to turn the Emperor's mind. The Master took up his brush and composed an exegesis on the *Laozi*, which he presented to the Emperor.
Upon reading it, the Emperor said to his close ministers, "Faying’s commentary on the *Daodejing* is concise in expression yet profound in principle."
"Such a work has never existed before. It should be granted entry into the Daoist Canon for circulation. Furthermore, please grant him the ceremonial cap, sash, altar, and edict.

Those who did not understand the Master’s intent often regarded this as sycophancy. In the autumn of the following year, an imperial decree was issued to restore the status of monks and nuns throughout the empire;

yet the Master alone remained unchanged in his resolve. By the beginning of the Shaoxing era, he would rise at dawn wearing a birch-bark cap, donning a crane-feather cloak, holding an ivory tablet, and [clad in]...

Wearing vermilion shoes, he struck the drum to assemble the multitude and ascended the seat. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Orchids flourish in the spring valley; chrysanthemums bloom by the autumn fence.
All things must inevitably experience their periods of flourishing and withering. In the past, monks and nuns were disparaged while the Way was exclusively served;

later, the Way was leveled and flatterers suppressed, and monks and nuns were restored. But tell me, what are the physical forms of these monks and nuns? He then took up a crown and showed it to the assembly, saying: "My head has always been..."
"Resembling the full moon, though one caps one's hair, one does not become an immortal. This morning, casting it down without hindrance, he releases divine light that pierces the azure sky.
He threw it to the ground, changed into monastic robes, and holding up a crane-feather cloak (*hegang*), said: "In days of yore, the Tathāgata traded for a fur robe;
for many years I have felt shame wearing this crane-feather cloak. Return to me the garments of a husband-man, the Subduer of Men; you must know this."
"The objects do not suit one another. I cast them down. He raised his ivory fan and said, "I suspected the meditation board was too groundless;
who would have thought it would be deceived by this ivory fan? For what reason today did you suddenly let go? An old immortal official retired from office throughout the heavens. He cast it down.
Pointing to his vermilion shoes, he said: "Dharma took one pair back with him; from this point on, his descendants have walked barefoot.

Borrowing these vermilion shoes to replace the hemp sandals—do not say that the times are difficult and hinder one's efforts. When seeking to transform into a Peng bird, failing to meet the right conditions, one remains no better than a Kun.
Trying to paint a tiger and ending up resembling a dog. He threw them down. Holding his staff crosswise, he said: "Today my staff has transformed into a dragon. He split it in two.
He shattered the myriad peaks of Mount Hua. Then, leaning his shoulder against it, he said: "Take care, O Buddha-mind, true and holy sovereign!
May you well employ the virtue of Yao to revitalize my school. He cast down his staff, closed his eyes, and passed away.
Chan Master Wenqing of Linxi Xingjiao in Yingzhou, successor to Chan Master Haoguang of Yuzquan, ascended the hall and said: "Six times six is thirty-six.
In the east, under the stems jia and yi, there is wood. The Great Statue of Jiazhou comes out of the pass; the Iron Ox of Shanfu enters Western Shu. *Chan*!"
A monk asked Chan Master Faxin of Fuchang in Jiangling, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Jiashan Zun: "The one flower opens into five petals; what is the first petal?"
The Master held up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The monk said, "Clouds arise in drifting flakes; raindrops fall in fine spray. The Master said, "Neither pained nor aware of injury.
The monk said, "This is still merely the wind rising and the intent for rain; what is the first leaf? The Master gave a snap with the sitting cloth.
The monk clapped his hands. The Master said, "Feel free to leap about as you please. He was asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master—

[The Master] said, "The young man from the eastern house and the Weaver Girl from the western house. A monk said, "I do not understand, Teacher. The Master said, "Casting aside the brush and tossing away the shuttle.
He ascended the hall, called to the assembly, and when the assembly looked up, the Master said, "The wind and weather at South Mountain are brisk," and then descended from his seat.
Chan Master Zongben Yuanzhao of Huilin Temple in Dongjing was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tianyi Huai. He was a native of the Guan family of Wuxi, Changzhou.
Of robust and imposing stature, he was simple and sincere in his character. At the age of nineteen, he left secular life under Chan Master Daosheng of Yong’an at Chengtian Temple in Gusu.
He served as an attendant in the master’s household for ten years. After receiving the tonsure and full ordination, he took his leave after another three years to travel to various regions.
Upon reaching Chiyang, he went to visit Zhenzong. Zhenzong raised the following topic:
"When humans have four hundred years, it constitutes one day and night in that heaven. Within a single such period, Maitreya brings five hundred billion devas to spiritual accomplishment."

The Master attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). He asked, "I do not yet understand what dharma you have preached. Tianqin replied, "I have preached only this very dharma.

[The Master asked,] "What is this dharma? After a long time, the Master attained awakening. One day, while in the meditation hall, Tianqin asked the Master, "When it is said that 'the mind itself is the Buddha,' what then?
The Master replied, "What difficulty is there in killing people and setting fires? Thereupon, his fame spread throughout the world. The Transport Commissioner...
When Imperial Commissioner Li Gongfu summoned the Master to inaugurate the Dharma at Rui Guang Temple, the assembly there flourished daily.

Chen Gongxiang, the Governor of Wulin, commissioned the Master to choose between the two monasteries of Cheng Tian and Xing Jiao to reside in; however, the people of Suzhou crowded the roads to block his departure and entreat him to stay.

Furthermore, due to the earnest requests of Jing Ci Temple, he issued a formal letter to inform the clergy and laity, saying: "I shall borrow the Master for three years to plant the seeds of merit for this region. It was not permitted [to leave].

I dare not detain you for long. The clergy and laity began to follow him. In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, Emperor Shenzong issued an edict to convert sixty-four courtyards of Xiangguosi into eight Chan and two Vinaya monasteries, and summoned the Master to serve as the first patriarch of Hui-lin Monastery.

Upon his arrival, the Emperor dispatched an envoy to inquire after his well-being; three days later, an imperial decree was transmitted ordering him to expound the Dharma at the three gates of the monastery for the sake of the officials and the common people.
The following day, he was summoned for an audience at the Yanhe Hall. When the Emperor asked about his practice and offered him a seat, the Master sat cross-legged.
The Emperor asked, "In which monastery did you receive your training? He replied, "Chengtian Yong'an in Suzhou. The Emperor was greatly pleased and offered him tea.

The Master immediately lifted the cup, drank deeply, and then swirled it while shaking it. The Emperor said, "The Chan school is just now flourishing; you should provide excellent guidance. The Master replied, "Your Majesty..."
"Knowing that this Way exists below [in the world] is like the sun shining down upon it. How could Your Servant dare to be indolent? Having spoken thus, he took his leave.

The Emperor watched him depart and said to those around him, "He is truly a monk of merit and wisdom. Later, when the Emperor passed away, [the new ruler] summoned him to enter the Funing Hall to preach the Dharma.

[The Master] requested to retire to the forests and valleys due to his old age; he was granted imperial permission to do as he pleased. He traveled extensively through various prefectures and counties, and no one was permitted to force him to remain in any one place.
He took up his drum and bid farewell to the assembly, reciting a verse: "Originally a guest with no home, how can one wander as one pleases?

With a favorable wind, I add oars and paddles; The boatman sets sail for Yangzhou. Once he had left the capital city, princes, dukes, and nobles who came to see him off followed in a continuous stream of carriages and horses.
As he was about to depart, the Master instructed them, saying: "Time and months cannot be toyed with; old age and sickness do not wait for anyone's appointment."
"Only practice with diligence and do not be indolent; this is the true manifestation of the Dharma. Those who heard this were moved to tears. Later, he resided at Lingyan.
His successors who transmitted the Dharma and the Way were beyond counting. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Han Xin facing the throne. The monk asked, "How should those of inferior capacity understand this? The Master said, "Ten thousand corpses prostrate for ten thousand li."

[The student] said, "Had I known of today's affairs earlier, I would have regretted not being more careful at the beginning. The Master said, "On the graves of the Three Sovereigns, the grass grows lushly.
I ask: above is heaven, below is earth; what is it that lies in between? The Master said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
[The student] said, "If that is so, then I thank the Master for his answer. The Master said, "The great earth, mountains, and rivers. [The student] said, "How could you, Master, [say such a thing]?"

[The Master] deceived [the monk]. The Master said, "Rather, it is my own fault. On the day of the Upper Yuan Festival, a monk asked, "When a thousand lamps illuminate one another and the sounds of strings and flutes mingle, at such a time as this, where is the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Thank you for your offering.
[The monk] asked, "Is this not your way of benefiting people, Master? The Master said, "It is very much like coming without having fasted. He ascended the hall and said, "In one..."
Within the tip of a single hair, the Jewel-King Buddha-land appears; sitting inside a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
Holding up his staff, he said: "This is the dust. How do you explain the principle of turning the Dharma Wheel?
Today, this mountain monk will not spare his eyebrows to reveal it for all of you. Pick it up! The waters of the sea surge with waves, and Mount Sumeru trembles. He let it go.

[The Master] descended from his seat. The four seas were tranquil and clear; heaven and earth were solemn and still. He addressed the assembly, saying: "I dare ask you all: tell me, is it when he picks up [the whisk], or is it when he puts it down?
To hesitate between cutting it off and not cutting it off—this is a double case. He struck the meditation platform and descended from his seat. He ascended the hall and said: "Look!
A brilliant, auspicious light shines, illuminating the great trichiliocosm—the ten billion lands as numerous as motes of dust, and the ten billion oceans of water."
"Billion Sumeru mountains, billion suns and moons, billion sets of four continents, and even lands as minute as motes of dust—all appear simultaneously within the light.
Do you all see them? If you can see them, I grant that you are personally present within the auspicious light.
If you do not see them, do not say that the auspicious light does not shine. *Chan* (Investigate!). [Ascending the hall: "The head is round..."
His head resembles the heavens; his square feet are like the earth. His ancient countenance is rugged and imposing, possessing the spirit of a great man.

He could kick over Mount Sumeru and trample the waters of the ocean until neither Śakra nor the Dragon Kings have a place to stand. Then, picking up his staff, he said: "Come back and try to evade me upon this staff!
*Du!* No matter what supernatural powers or transformations you may employ, in the end you must return to this very place. With this, he struck the ground with the staff.
[The Master’s] remains were interred in a stupa at Lingyan on Mount Su.
Chanyuan Chanshi Fayou of Fayun Temple in Dongjing was the son of the Xin family of Longcheng in Qinzhou. His mother dreamed...
An old monk sought lodging with her; she became pregnant upon waking from sleep. Previously, this old monk of Maiji Mountain had been on friendly terms with the Venerable Lu of Yingqian Temple.

He once wished to travel abroad under Lu’s guidance, but Lu declined him due to his advanced age. As he was departing, Lu spoke to him in passing, saying, "In the future, you should seek me out at the foot of Tiechang Ridge, before Zhupu Slope.
Later, when Lu heard that a child had suddenly been born to her, he realized it was the result of his own words.
He went there at once to see him. The boy gave a smile. At three years of age, he wished to follow Ru back home, and thus he took the surname Ru.

At nineteen, he sat for the scriptural examinations and received full ordination. He applied himself diligently to the lecture halls, studying the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, penetrating their subtle and essential meanings with mastery.
Upon hearing of the great renown of Master Huai’s dharma assembly at Tiexi Temple in Wuweijun, he went directly to pay his respects. Huai asked him, "Where do you sit?"
"What sutra do you lecture? he asked. The Master replied, "The Avataṃsaka. He asked, "What is the primary tenet of the Avataṃsaka? The Master replied, "The Dharma-realm is its tenet.
He asked, "What is the primary tenet of the Dharma-realm? The Master replied, "The mind is its tenet. He asked, "What is the primary tenet of the mind? The Master was unable to answer.
Huai said, "A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth. You must examine this for yourself; there must surely [be a way]."
Faming later heard a monk cite Baizhang’s question to Baoci: "What is it like before emotions arise? Baoci replied, "Separated.

At this, Faming suddenly attained great enlightenment. He went directly to the abbot’s quarters to present what he had realized. Baoci said, "You are truly a vessel for the Dharma; the future of our school rests with you.
Initially, he resided at Sifan in Longshu, and later, by imperial decree, he took up residence at Fayun in Changlu.

The Patriarchal Founder. When Emperor Shenzong passed away, [the Master] was summoned to preach the Dharma before the Imperial Spirit. He was bestowed with the title "Perfect Penetration" (Yuántōng). A monk asked:
"To attain nirvana without departing from birth and death, and to enter the Buddha-realm without leaving the realm of demons—how is this principle to be understood?
The Master said: "Red earth, tea, and cow's milk. The monk said: "Thank you for answering my question. The Master said: "What was the point of your question?"
"Ma! The monk hesitated, and the Master gave a shout. The monk asked, "In the second and third months of the spring, all things sprout.
I wonder, does the sprout of the Way also grow? The Master said, "Look for yourself. The monk asked, "Is this not the very point of instruction?
The Master said, "How tall is the banana tree? The monk said, "Wildfire cannot burn it; when the spring wind blows, it grows again. The Master [remained silent].

[The Master] said, "This belongs to Lord Bái. As for yours, what is it? [The monk] said, "Wait until another time. The Master said, "I see you cannot bring yourself to speak. He ascended the hall and said:
"Sailing according to the wind is precisely following the waves and drifting with the current; it is cutting off the flow of all streams."

It cannot be avoided; as before, there is leakage. When assigning office according to one's capacity, how can one transcend the constraints of length and shortness? Buying a hat to fit a head, it is difficult to find a perfect match.
Even if you were to reach a state where you see neither sky above nor earth below, and fail to distinguish east from west or north from south—[it would still not suffice].
"What use is there? Even if forged from pure steel or cast from raw iron, one must still break into a sweat on the brow.
Since none are like this, how can they be discussed? After a long silence, he said: "Who knows these pieces of sincere heart?
They make the 'Stone Child of Huangmei' laugh to death. He ascended the hall and said: "This mountain monk does not know how to speak with artifice; I simply respond to the occasion."
Calling out to one another to drink a bowl of tea—there is no secret instruction of the Patriarchs here either.

If you practitioners have not yet become intimately acquainted with this, you will step upon a scale-weight as hard as iron. [He] ascends the hall: Autumn clouds and autumn waters; green mountains fill the eyes. If you can realize it here—
"Thoroughly satisfied, utterly fulfilled. Should this not yet be so, the Daoist rides his ox backward. *Chan.* Entering the hall: "The cold rain falls fine;
the north wind blows high. It blows the sand and drives the stones; it uproots trees and makes the branches cry out. All of you know this well enough, but tell me: what color is the wind?
If you can recognize it, I grant that you possess the eye. If you do not recognize it, do not blame me for deceiving you. *Chan.* Entering the hall.
Sitting coldly at Shaolin for nine years, he was nonetheless seen through by Shen Guang. Now, jade and stone are difficult to distinguish; there is no choice but to wrap it in hemp and paper.
Do you understand? Those who laugh at me are many; those who smile at me are few. Entering the hall, [the Master said]:
"For a monk, to bow high to Śākyamuni and not prostrate before Maitreya is not considered extraordinary. Yet, as for sacrificing one's body for half a verse or [dying for] a single phrase—"
"Throwing fire! And what more would you have depicted? After a long silence, he said, "Each person dwells as a mountain man;

why need it be further explained? The Master manifested illness and addressed the assembly, saying: "I, this old monk, have presided over six monasteries, which has caused much trouble for the administrators, the head seat, and the great assembly.
Now that I have come here, the four elements are not firm; fire and wind are about to disperse. Each of you should find peace through the Way and do not violate my instructions."
He then said: "When coming there was nothing; when departing it is empty. The matter is the same in the south, north, east, and west. To dwell in the six sense bases provides no benefit.
After a long silence, the Chief Steward Huidang stepped forward and said: "Why does the Master not speak the final word?"
The Master said, "Take care, take care. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
Chan Master Ruochong Juehai of Huilinyuan in Xiangguo, Dongjing, was the son of the Zhong family of Jiangningfu.
He ascended the hall and said: "The azure void is still and cloudless; the autumn sky is bright with the moon. The long river is as clear as a silken ribbon; the pure wind comes forth."
Rest. The man of the Way beneath the forest trees is profound; looking at one another, our feelings are shared in joy.

O virtuous ones, what was just said—“clear breeze and bright moon”—is still a matter within the gate of provisional transformation (*jianhua*). What, then, is the matter from the standpoint of the man of the Way?

After a long silence, he said: “When at leisure, I gaze upon the flowing stream by the rock; wishing to wash my meditation robe, yet there is no dust. He ascended the hall [and said]: “Boundless meaning.”
The ocean is entirely encompassed within his gaze; the forms and appearances of the myriad phenomena are all contained within the scope of his illumination.
Why is it that you all, though bumping into and striking against him, remain unaware? After a long silence, he said: "Do not take offense at this mountain monk for being so intrusive."
Time passes as swiftly as a flying arrow; take heed.
Chan Master Guangzhao Yingfu of Changlu in Zhenzhou was the son of the Jiang family of Chuzhou. A monk asked: "The ancients said..."
"You may indeed understand the Tathāgata-dhyāna, brother, but you have not even dreamed of the Patriarchal-dhyāna.
"May I ask whether the Tathāgata-dhyāna and the Patriarchal-dhyāna are the same or different? The Master said, "A single arrow passes beyond Silla. The monk hesitated; the Master then gave a shout.
The monk asked, "What is it like when one recognizes the treasure within the robe? The Master said, "Try bringing it out and show me. The monk unfolded his hands.
[The Master] held up his hand. The Master said, "Do not point east and draw west; where is the treasure? The monk said, "How can it be that this student does not make use of it?
The Master said, "Try using it then. The monk gave a single stroke with his sitting mat. The Master said, "Everyone will laugh at you.

He entered the hall and addressed the assembly, saying, "The rivers and mountains wind around the railing, as if they were a screen of ink and water. The halls and pavilions soar into the void, as magnificent as..."
The grottoes of the immortals and sages: the myriad phenomena of the universe interpenetrate like the ocean-seal samādhi.

A single ray of divine light shines forth without any obstruction. Do you all understand? After a long silence, he said: "In the vast and empty expanse of heaven and earth, standing alone, toward what limit does one gaze?
*Chan*. Entering the hall, he looked at the assembly and said: "Why is it that this cannot be gathered together, nor scattered apart; the wind cannot blow through it?"
Water cannot wet it; fire cannot burn it; a blade cannot cut it through. What is this?
Among you in the assembly, is there any monk with a beak like a nail and a tongue of iron who can try to settle this for me? Is there anyone? After a long silence, he said:
"If there were not, this mountain monk would have lost face today. [He stood for a long time.
Chan Master Furi Zhicai of Lin’an Prefecture was a native of Taizhou. A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said:
Water cooled produces ice. [The student] asked, "What is it like to be one who walks the Way? The Master said, "Spring snow melts easily.
[The student] asked, "How does one discuss it? The Master snapped his fingers once. [The student] asked, "The East and West are transmitted in secret; why is it that everyone knows?"

The Master said, "In spring, there are not three days of clear weather. The monk said, "I have come specifically to request further instruction. The Master said, "Dragging through mud and carrying water.

Chan Master Chengxin Zong’s Dharma heir, Chan Master Yao of Huiji in Pengzhou, was asked by a monk: "The ancients said, 'I have a phrase;
wait for a tongueless person to understand speech, and then I will tell it to you. What is the meaning of this? The Master replied, "A fine discussion beneath a shadowless tree."
[The assembly] prostrates. The Master says: "The tiles shatter and the ice melts.
Chan Master Kezun of Zhongji in Fuzhou, a Dharma successor of Chan Master Baoben Lan, ascends the hall and says: "Pah! Pah! Pah! What thing is that chirping at the bottom of the well?"
"Even if one were to encompass the three thousandfold great chiliocosm, it would still be nothing but a ghost cave. *Duḥ!* (A shout). Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"Last night at the fourth watch, I arose and laughed loudly and incessantly. Fortunately, I had a good sleep; the frost-bell struck and broke into two pieces.
Ascending the hall again, [he said]: "Heoshan and Puhua suddenly went mad; beating drums and shaking bells, they put on a performance. The kalpa-fire blazes forth; it is appropriate..."
Boiling tea. A great mountain wind blows; it is good to ride the cool breeze. Four snakes in one basket—watch him play with them. Two rats gnawing at the wisteria, lacking self-awareness.
Where does the moon go when the ocean is bright? In the palace of Guanghan lies a bed of white silver. *Du!* [Heh! He ascended the hall.
The eighty-four thousand profound Dharma gates—each gate has a path that transcends heaven and earth. Why is it that each and every one fails to tread upon them?
It is simply because there are too many legs on the centipede. Not only are there many legs, there are also many mouths; iron-tongued, spike-beaked, they only serve to increase their own ugliness.
Brandishing mallets and raising fly-whisks is like washing mud with mud; raising eyebrows and blinking eyes is but the chicken in its coop. If you wish to know the Buddhas and Patriarchs...
"Where no path leads, the door is closed against falling blossoms as spring birds cry.
The *upādhyāya* Faming of Kaiyuan Monastery in Xingzhou had relied upon the Dharma for not long before he attained profound *dharmakṣānti*. Later, he returned to his native village.
His conduct was dissolute; he was a great lover of wine. Whenever he played *hulu*, he would invariably become heavily intoxicated, singing several stanzas of Liuchao lyrics as his daily routine.

The local villagers mocked him, refusing to invite him to vegetarian feasts but complying when invited for drink. This continued for over ten years, until everyone referred to him as the "Drunken Monk.
One day, he said to the assembly of the temple, "I shall depart tomorrow morning; you all must not go elsewhere."
The assembly laughed at him in secret. At dawn the next morning, he adjusted his robes, took his seat, and called out loudly, "I am departing!
Listen to one verse from me! When the assembly heard this, they rushed to see him. The Master then said, "Throughout my life I have stumbled and fallen while intoxicated;

yet even in intoxication, there was still discernment. Now tonight, when the wine has sobered, where is the willow-lined bank? Only the morning breeze and the waning moon. Having finished speaking, he became silent. They shook him, but he had already passed away.
[The Master] shed his skin.

Chan Master Chengxinming, the Dharma heir of [the previous master], Chan Master Guangji of Shanglan Monastery in Hongzhou, ascended the hall. Holding his staff crosswise, he called to the assembly, saying: "Do you still..."

"Do you recognize this old fellow from Shanglan? His eyes are like wooden stakes; his mouth is like a flat carrying pole. He makes no distinction between fine and coarse, nor does he know saltiness or blandness.
To preside over a monastery in such a manner is a hundred thousand transgressions. Do any of you, venerable practitioners of Chan, have anything to offer by way of repentance for this mountain monk?
After a long silence, he said, "This is driving me to my wit's end! He struck the ground with his staff and descended from the seat.

On the occasion of the Buddha’s birthday, Chan Master Miaofeng Ruchan of Fuzhou, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Guangyin Yao, ascended the hall and addressed the assembly: "Today is the anniversary of the Tathāgata’s birth.

Throughout the world, the monastic community without exception uses fragrant water to bathe him, collectively repaying his immense kindness. Why is it that, according to the teachings, [it is said]..."
"The Way. As for the Tathāgata, he comes from nowhere. Since he comes from nowhere, one does not know who it is that has descended to be born.

Please try to speak on this. If you can speak it, your debt of gratitude will be repaid; if you cannot speak it, on the eighth day of the fourth month next year, I shall still pour [water] directly upon your head."
A monk asked Chan Master Jingwu of Qingshan Monastery at Baiyang in Lin’an, successor to Chan Master Yuan of Yunju: “What is the Buddha? The Master said:
He asked, "Who? The monk replied, "I am specifically asking the Master. The Master said, "A hawk flies over Silla. He ascended the hall and said, "To speak is to move the lips;
to act is to move the feet. Even if one neither speaks nor acts—mistake, mistake! He struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall.
Chan Master Huitai of Shanguan in Changzhou ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas appeared in the world to extensively expound the Three Vehicles;
Bodhidharma came from the West to secretly transmit the Great Matter. Those of superior capacity transcend immediately upon hearing a single word;

those of middling and inferior capacity must proceed through gradual stages to illuminate the ground of the mind. Whether by singing the Way in a single phrase, or unfolding it through three sentences, or responding with skillful means,"

The pivot [of the teaching] thus becomes manifold in meaning; yet if one grasps its essential core, it is all but empty flowers. To exhaustively investigate the source with a single phrase is to bury the ancestral Way.
I dare ask you all: what is the phrase that accords with the time and the season? After a long silence, he said: "Faint clouds hang over the Milky Way;
sparse raindrops fall upon the catalpa trees. *Chán*.

Chan Master Deqi of Chongfu Monastery in Raoyou ascended the hall and said: "If you can understand it here, you will be able to enter the realm of a Buddha and sit within a single site of enlightenment (*dōjō*).
There, the waterfowl and trees will together discourse upon this essential point, and the pavilions and halls will jointly expound the True Vehicle.
You shall continue the lamp of the thousand sages that never ends, illuminating with impartial flames in all eight directions. Therefore it is said: 'In..."
In heaven it is the same as heaven; among humans it is the same as humans. Is there anyone who understands this? After a long silence, he said:
"The golden bird at the bottom of the water, the sun in the sky; the pupils in one's eyes, the person before one."
Chan Master Huaiji Zhenjue of Baolin Monastery in Wuzhou ascended the hall and said: "The legacy of Shanhui remains for five hundred years;
the clouds and the colors of Mount Huang remain as they were. Now the Patriarchal Command is being put into practice once more: a single phrase circulates throughout the great thousandfold world."
The great assembly, tell me: what kind of phrase is this? Is it the one that "covers heaven and earth," "cuts off all streams," and "follows the waves"?
*Hūṃ*. What connection could there be? Since the time of the Buddhas and patriarchs, it has never been moved.
"Today, the true mechanism must not be leaked," he said, looking over the assembly. "If you go to other places, do not misrepresent this.
Master Zongyou of Rizhao in Hongzhou ascended the hall and said, "Today at Longquan, I shall speak a bit of 'ge' (nonsense) for you all."
Teng remained silent for a long while and said, "Branches and vines grow further upon branches and vines.

Regarding the Dharma successor of Chan Master Zhikai Yi, Chan Master Zhiyin of Huangbo in Ruizhou: A monk asked, "What is the phrase that provides strength? The Master replied, "The feet. The monk said:
The student did not understand. The Master said, "With every step, one moves forward. Ascending the hall, he said: "For forty-nine years he preached, his grace and moisture benefiting birds and fish;

having traveled a hundred thousand leagues, he has awakened humans and devas. As for these two old fellows—one speaking of the long and the short, the other babbling in gibberish—I should give each of them thirty blows of the staff.
Why? Because one speaks of the long and the short, while the other speaks in a jumble of words. Nevertheless, even so..."
Let this one move pass for now.
Chan Master Daizhong Delong Haiyin of Fuzhou ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma is not a different Dharma; the Way is not a separate Way.
At every moment one encounters Śākyamuni; in every place one runs into Bodhidharma. A step taken brings shoulders touching; a word spoken—"
Biting through it; not biting through it. Great, great! [The Master] ascends the hall. "Those who wish to achieve intellectual transcendence must first master the movement of stillness.
He strikes the meditation staff and says: *Oṃ sūru-siri svāhā*. Return to the hall for tea. He ascends the hall again.
"Why can one whose contact with objects is unimpeded not lift their head? Why can one whose ground is secure and firm find no place to set foot?"
It is like when a heavenly king bestows a magnificent mansion. Though one has obtained a great residence, one must enter through a gate;

thus it is called a "gate. Fan Kui trampled it open and the True Lord emerged; the Great Spirit raised his hand and the brocade-scaled dragon sprayed forth. *Cān*. [He] ascended the hall. At dawn, it is the hour of Yin.
Who is it that awakens? Everywhere is Amitābha Buddha; in every house is Avalokiteśvara. A qilin gazes at the Northern Dipper within the moon;
a *bi* plum facing the sun is green on one side.
The lay official Liu Jingchen, whose courtesy name was Xingchao, entered the ranks of the bureaucracy in his youth due to his exceptional talent.
At first, he did not place faith in the Buddha-dharma. When he reached the age of thirty-two, he encountered Chan Master Zhaojue of Donglin, who instructed and enlightened him;

he subsequently became deeply respectful and submissive. Thereupon, he devoted himself heart and soul to the Way of the Patriarchs. Later, he traveled to the capital to pay his respects to Chan Master Chong of Huiyin. At...
A monk asked Xuedou, "What is the source of all Buddhas? Xuedou replied, "The cold hues of a thousand peaks. Upon hearing these words, the monk attained realization.

Over a year later, while serving as an official in the Luoyang administration, he went to visit Chan Master Gaofeng Yuanmiao at Shaoshan. As he was about to depart for his post, he took leave of Shaoshan, who instructed him, saying:
"With such dedication as you apply yourself, why worry about not attaining awakening? Hereafter, should there be extraordinary states of experience," [he continued,] "do not..."
"Rejoice! You should quickly gather [your faculties]. If you can gather them, you will become a vessel for the Dharma;
if you cannot gather them, you will suffer from the illness of unrest and incur the calamity of losing your mind.

Not long after, he returned to the capital and went to Zhihai to rely upon Chan Master Zhengjue Yi, inquiring about the causes and conditions [of his illness]. Zhihai said, "The ancients said: 'The ordinary mind...'"
This is the Way. Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, you emit light and shake the earth, yet you do not realize it yourself;

instead, you rush outward in search of it, becoming increasingly estranged and distant. Your doubts grow ever deeper and remain unresolved. One evening, upon entering the room, Hai cited from the *Chuan Deng Lu*:
When King Xiangzhi asked Venerable Pratītya, "What is the Buddha? the Venerable replied, "To see one's own nature is to see the Buddha."
He spoke and questioned him, but the Master was unable to respond. His doubts grew profound, and he returned home to go to bed. He slept soundly until the fifth watch;

upon waking, while he was still reflecting on the matter, he beheld various extraordinary signs. His inner and outer being were completely permeated, his six sense organs vibrated, and heaven and earth seemed to spin.
It was as if clouds had parted to reveal the moon, and his joy was beyond measure. Suddenly, he recalled the words with which Shao Shan had charged him at their parting.

The Master [Zhaozhou] temporarily suppressed him. At dawn, he went to Zhihai and reported everything he had attained. Zhihai acted as his witness and said, "Furthermore, you must be able to put it into practice before you have truly attained it.
Zhaozhou asked, "Is it not necessary to practice it? Zhihai replied in a stern voice, "What kind of matter is this? How can you speak of 'practice'?
Zhaozhou attained a silent realization and subsequently composed eight verses on "Illuminating the Mind-Ground" (*Xindi song*), as well as...
An Exhortation to Confucianism to Enlighten the World. The words say: "The enlightenment of the Way lies in seeing one's nature.
That which I have realized is nothing other than seeing one's nature. Mencius said:

"The mouth’s desire for flavors, the eyes’ desire for colors, the ears’ desire for sounds, the nose’s desire for odors, and the four limbs’ desire for ease and comfort—these are the nature. Yangzi said:
Seeing, hearing, speaking, acting, and thinking are the attributes of one's nature. To perceive this is to be able to clarify the Way.
One should know that the Way is not distant; for every person, the relationship to the Way is like that of fish to water—they have never been separated from it for even a moment.

It is only because one is deluded regarding oneself and pursues external objects that one follows this path throughout one’s life without realizing it. The Buddha calls this "Great Awakening" (Mahābodhi), and Confucius calls it being "Awakened First";
it is simply the awakening to this. An ancient said: "Throughout past and present, there has never been a fall; it is clearly before one's eyes. He also said:
"The Great Way is right before one's eyes, yet for all its importance, it is difficult to see while looking at it. If you wish to know the true nature of the Great Way—
The essence does not depart from sound, form, or speech. It is further said: "Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning, one rises together with him.
Rising and falling, we are always相随 (ever-accompanying); speaking and remaining silent, we dwell together. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this very voice.
These words of the Buddha are the most intimate of paths. When standing, one sees him present before oneself; when in a carriage, one [sees him]...
"To see it leaning against the crossbar; to look for it as being in front, and suddenly find it behind;
to seek it to the left or right, and encounter its source"—these are the words of the Confucianists regarding the Way that is most near. Yet how can this Way be so?

It can only be transmitted through the mind and does not rely on written words. Thus, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, the wondrous mind was transmitted to Kāśyapa; and when Bodhidharma faced [the wall]...
The wall was broken through, and the essential meaning was entrusted to Shen Guang. Once the six petals had unfolded, a thousand flowers vied in their splendor.
As the school split into branches and sects, each established its own tradition. Thus, some signaled with a blink of an eye or a raised eyebrow, or by clenching a fist or pointing a finger;

others administered blows or shouts, or brandished fly-whisks and struck gongs; some held tridents or drew bows, or rolled balls and danced with ritual tablets; others dragged stones or moved earth, and beat drums or blew horns.
Whether through silence or speech, a sigh or a smile, or even through various other skillful means, all are intended to benefit others intimately.

Yet, precisely because they are so intimate, people are often at a loss for what to do. Those who catch a glimpse of them, however, find no separation between themselves and the truth, not even by a hair’s breadth.

Should one hesitate or remain in doubt, even across ten thousand miles, those who wish to clarify the Way ought not to neglect this. Transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, it continues unbroken to this day;
it truly embodies what our Confucian tradition calls "restraining anger without venting it" and "opening [the mind] without opposition."
That I have attained anything at all is truly due to this gate. Reflecting upon our own Confucian tradition, it possesses its own path. How excellent are the words of Confucius:
"He silently comprehends them and retains them; he unifies them with a single thread. Thus, the Way exists within the very act of beholding, and the meaning is conveyed by pointing at the palm.
All such instances accord with the subtle purport of the School of the Lineage and capture the true mechanism beyond formal teaching. Nevertheless...
The Way of Confucius was transmitted to Zisi; Zisi transmitted it to Mencius.
After Mencius passed away, its transmission was lost, and what has been handed down to the world is merely the written word. Therefore, my studies must seek self-realization before they may cease.
Fortunately, one night I attained awakening; regarding everything seen by my eyes and heard by my ears, my mind—
Whatever is conceived by the mind, whatever is spoken by the mouth, and whatever is moved by the hands and feet—all are nothing other than the wondrous.
Having attained this for a long time, it increasingly manifests before one; yet whenever one attempts to impart it to others, they are unable to receive it.

Only then does one realize that this wondrous Way truly cannot be transmitted through written words. Alas! This Way is transmitted when there is a person worthy of it; if there is no such person, it remains untransmitted.
Thus it was cut off. I have now recovered it. Who might resemble him? Whether such a person will exist during my remaining years or not is something that cannot be known.
Therefore, I have composed records, eulogies, songs, and prose to disseminate this matter, and have further written this treatise to instruct my disciples.
The layman Qingxian Gong Zhao Bian,
courtesy name Yuedao, was the dharma heir of Chan Master Quan of Jiangshan,
the twelfth generation descendant of Nanyue. At over forty years of age, he cast aside sensory pleasures and focused his mind.
Dingjiao came from Hui’er’s school and resided at Nanzen Temple in Quzhou. Master Gong visited him daily, yet Hui never permitted him to utter a single word.

Later, while serving as the governor of Qingzhou, he often sat in meditation during his leisure time from official affairs. Suddenly, a great thunderclap struck with such force that he attained immediate enlightenment.
He composed a verse, saying: "Sitting silently in the public hall, leaning back against the empty rest; The source of the mind is unmoving, profound and still like water. A single sound—"
"The thunderbolt strikes and the crown of the head opens; awaken that which belongs to yourself from of old. When Huiwen heard this, he said with a smile, "Zhao Yuedao has merely struck lucky.
When Duke Zheng Fu was initially not yet inclined toward the School of the Lineage (Zongmen), the Duke exhorted him with a letter, saying: "I humbly submit..."

Your stewardship is thus at its ultimate height of wealth and honor; your virtue and character are thus at their most flourishing peak; your fortune, longevity, and well-being are thus fully provided;
and your retirement in leisure and ease are thus at such a lofty state. Yet, that which you have not yet given much heed to is the Tathāgata’s single great cause and condition.
If you can seek with single-minded sincerity that which is to be realized and awakened, then on another day, I shall offer congratulations to you, sir.

The Master was seventy-two years old when he retired from office as Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince and returned home. His relatives, elders, and village residents treated him exactly as they had before.
He built the Gaozhai (High Chamber) for his own enjoyment. In a verse inscribed there to express his intent, he wrote:

"Golden girdle fastened at the waist, now retired and hidden away; The message within this state is but ordinary. If worldly people wish to know the old man of Gaozhai, He is simply the one from Kecheng Village."
Zhao Silang spoke again, saying, "Be most careful not to mistake [the truth]. On the verge of death, he left a letter to Fohui, which said:

"Had it not been for your daily admonitions and instructions, I would certainly have failed to gain strength at this point. Fohui lamented him with a verse: "In office, you were an auspicious omen for the state;

returning home, you serve as a model for the world. Now that the Golden Grain has departed from the human realm, the Jade Tower is completed in heaven. Your sword of wisdom is without the slightest flaw; like ice..."
The jar is utterly pure; the spring breeze flows through the waterway. A solitary moon shines brightly upon the clouds.
Chan Master Shuben Dadao of Fayun Monastery in Dongjing was a successor of Chan Master Helin Ben. His clan was the Dong family, descendants of Han Zhongshu. Great...

His father Qi and his father Wen both served as officials in Ying, and thus he became a native of Ying. His mother had no sons; she prayed to the Great Being in White Robes (Pītavāsas) and subsequently conceived him.

When the Master grew up, he read extensively across all branches of literature, yet he maintained a life of pure cultivation and had no intention of pursuing an official career. In the eighth year of the Jiayou era, [he entered the monastic order].
Together with his younger brother Shansi, he went to the Capital’s Dizangyuan Temple. There he selected the scriptures for ordination and studied the *Vinaya*.
Traveling eastward, he reached Gusu, where he paid homage to Yuanzhao at Ruiwang Temple. Yuanzhao took a special interest in him, and thus they attained accord regarding the essential meaning.

After five years, he ascended further into the subtle and profound depths. Yuanzhao then instructed him to rely upon the teachings of Yuantong Xiu; the Master went there and again mastered its essentials. In the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era, he crossed [the river].
Huishou served as the Governor of Taizhou. After a long time, he left that post to reside at Shuanglin, later moving to Jingci. Subsequently, by imperial decree, he was transferred to Fayun.
A monk asked, "The precious stupa is fundamentally without seams; how can you point this out to people? The Master said, "Mist and clouds arise upon its front and back;
stars and moon circle its rafters and beams. The monk asked, "Who is the person within the stupa? The Master said, "Throughout the day, they know nothing of the affairs of the mundane world."
"For many years I have occupied this land of white clouds. He asked, "Is there anything further above this? The Master said, "You are truly insatiable.
[The monk] asked, "If one were to discuss this matter, it is like two families playing Go. When a student comes forward, I request a move from the Master."
The Master said, "I have already seen the wheel. The monk said, "Wrong. The Master said, "Right. The monk said, "There is no path to advance upon.
The Master struck his staff once and said, "What can be done about this? The monk asked, "As for the time before black and white were yet distinguished, how was it then?
The Master said, "For now, let me grant you one move. [The monk] asked, "How does one progress from atop a hundred-foot pole?"
The Master said, "Perilous. [The monk] asked, "If one proceeds in this very way, what then? The Master said, "A hundredfold fragments.

[The monk] asked, "I do not ask about the reward for labor during the three summer months; as for matters from now on, how should they be handled? The Master said, "Shave the head clean; wash the bowl clean."

[The monk] said, "I thank the Master for your instruction. The Master said, "A drop of water is hard to digest. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Above, one sees no heaven; below, one sees no earth.
It fills and obstructs all of space, leaving no place to take refuge. To explain it clearly for you would be ineffective; instead, look toward the South Mountain at the turtle-nosed snake.
He threw down his staff and descended from the seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Shenning Fayin of Mount Jinshan in Zhenjiang Prefecture, "Emperor Tianhuang spoke thus;
Longtan spoke thus. I wonder, how would you speak, Master? The Master replied, "Holding a white jade whip in his hand."
The donkey’s pearls were all smashed to pieces. [The Master] said, "There is a portion for withdrawing. The Master said, "One who recognizes their error must surely reform it.
He ascended the hall, looked at the assembly, and said, "The ancients said: 'In the eye, it is called seeing; in the ear, it is called hearing; in the nose, smelling fragrance;
in the tongue, engaging in discourse; in the body, perceiving touch; in the mind, grasping at conditions. Although this is so, one sees only the sharpness of the tip of the awl, but not..."
Observe that the chisel-head is square. If it were a mountain of gold, it would not be so;

there are eyes that cannot see, ears that cannot hear, a nose that does not know fragrance, a tongue that does not discourse, a body that does not perceive touch, and a mind that has severed all攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to conditions).
In a single thought-moment of resonance, the six sense-faculties are liberated. I venture to ask, O virtuous practitioners of Chan: tell me, how is this different from what came before?
The same is distinct; let there be no monk with the eye of complete penetration who comes forward to deliver a message.
If there is none, I shall once again break it open for you all layer by layer: when released, it allows private passage for carriages and horses; when clenched, not even a hair’s breadth remains.
If one is a veteran of the battle of realization, one may freely withstand the slanders and denigrations of right and wrong.
A monk asked Chan Master Yuan Chengyan of Zishou Monastery in Shouzhou, "Is there anything extraordinary within the Great Canon?
The Master said, "I only fear that you will not believe it. The monk asked, "How is this so? The Master said, "That which is black is it."

[The painting is] black; the yellow background is paper. [The master] says: "This is the response to the teacher’s question. The Master said: "Receive the meaning of the hook, but do not fixate on the zero point of the scale.
He ascended the hall and said: "Clouds arise at the mouth of the valley; the moon fills the long river. The woodcutter chops deep into the clouds; the fisherman casts his line from the sandbar.
Arriving here, even if you were Wu Daozi or Zhang Sengyou, there would be no place for you to apply your hand. After a long silence...

He said: "Go to the hall and ask the Holy Monk. [The monk] entered for the formal discourse. The heavens and earth are solemn and still; the seas are calm and the rivers clear. The wind does not rustle the branches;
the rain does not break the clods of earth. Spring brings forth life and summer fosters growth; autumn gathers the harvest and winter stores it away. This is the Dharma of the world.
"What is the Buddha-dharma? After a long silence, he said: "If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma.
Chan Master Shouyi Fazhen of Benjue Temple in Xiuzhou was the son of the Shen family of Jiangyin. A monk asked: "How is it..."
"This is the mystery within the phrase. The Master said, "A man from Kunlun riding an elephant, pulled by a lotus fiber.
[The monk] asked, "What is the mystery within the essence? The Master said, "A shadow; the moon in the sky soaking into the cold pond. [The monk] asked, "What is the mystery within the mystery?

The Master said, "Sleeping with a sword on one's person upon the long meditation couch. [The monk] asked, "Is there anything further beyond this? The Master said, "Put it down. He then ascended the hall for formal instruction.

He raised his whisk and said, "The Buddhas of the three periods and the six generations of patriarchs are all right here. Do you see them? Since you do not see them, it is because you are not equal to the task.
He then spoke a Dharma for them, saying, "There is no duality, nor is there a division; there is no distinction, nor is there any interruption. Do you hear this? You are still not alert.
Now, they have all gone at once to the world of Fragrant Accumulation in the upper direction. (He shook the whisk.)
The whisk-bearer said, "Step back, step back! You are poking right in my eyes. He ascended the hall. "Half-folded, arranged in threes—everyone can say this.
Removing one and picking up seven also requires deliberation. On this very day, what is it that Yunmen spoke?
Do not seek it elsewhere. How will you reveal this message? After a long silence, he said, "The sun and moon flow on ever-changing."
Chan Master Xiuyong of Touzi in Shu Prefecture was asked by a monk: "The Dharma is equal; there is no high or low. Why is it that Zhaozhou received people according to three grades?
The Master said, "Entering the water, one sees the tall man. The monk said, "I cannot yet understand this, Master.

fortunately, the former sages have provided a "second gate," which is sufficient for us all to speak here and there together. Thus it is said: "Spring gives birth, summer..."
"Long. Autumn falls, winter withers; the four seasons shift and change as they revolve upon the long road.

the Buddha of Jiazhou hides within a lotus fiber. He then ascended the hall. "Majestic Mount Shaoshi forever anchors the myriad peaks; sometimes it emerges cradled from amidst the clouds, and sometimes..."

thus people call him the "Wall-Gazing Barbarian Monk. O virtuous ones, how can you avoid this reproach? Enough, enough! It would be better to simply maintain your recitations.

Chan Master Shou'en of Dizang in Fuzhou was the son of the Qiu family of that same prefecture. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Sleeping during the day is of no benefit.
