Chan Master Xiangyan Yisong Rubi of Dengzhou, a dharma heir of Chan Master Xiangyan Yue of Fuzhou, was the son of the Rao family. He ascended the hall [to preach]. "The transformations are subtle..."
Why such haste to move? In a single breath, in every thought-moment, there are eighty-four thousand gates of expedient means.
Tell me, which gate is it that cannot be entered? Whether you enter or do not enter—when dawn comes, the rain beats upon the banana leaves until they are wet.
Let us respectfully ask the person within: standing grandly face-to-face outside the gate, one hears the woodpecker cry. He speaks a verse: *Pock! Pock! Pock!*
There are worms within while they peck from without; how many are these people, drifting in a daze! A single thrust behind the crown of the head, and yet they remain unawakened.
If you do not awaken, listen further to this mountain monk’s *pe-lo-p'o-lo*.
Chan Master Jishi Huiguang of Lingyin Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Shenchu of Huelin. He was born into the Xiaothou family of Qiántáng. A monk asked:
"The colors of the Flying Mountain manifest the Dharma-body of purity; the sounds of the merging streams and ravines expound the broad and long tongue-mark. Precisely at such a time as this—"
At that time, [a monk] asked, "What is Yunmen’s One Song? The Master said, "The rain on the leaves of the banana tree at the third watch.

The monk said, "A single phrase fully presented transcends Buddhas and patriarchs; all those in crimson and purple at the banquet are connoisseurs of this. The Master said, "When meeting people, do not misquote it."
Ascending the hall, he said: "There is no need to seek the Truth; why must you cease your views? Riding a cow backward into the Buddha Hall, a single sound of the flute leaves heaven and earth empty.
Who knows who can recognize the face of Gautama?"
Chan Master Miaoyin Yugou of Guoqing Temple in Taizhou ascended the hall and said: "Why is it that those who can speak with their whole mouths do not know what truly 'is'?
And why is it that those who fully know what 'is' cannot speak with their whole mouths? Tell me, where does the crux lie?
If you can understand this, I grant you that illumination and function are simultaneous, and clarity and obscurity are both resolved. However, were it otherwise..."
"Not so. To speak it, or not to speak it; to know its existence, or not to know its existence. The Great Tiger of the Southern Mountain knows how to let out a lion’s roar.
Master Chuchi Puzhao of Guoqing Temple in Taizhou ascended the hall and said: "Lingyun awakened through the peach blossoms; Xuansha [stood by]..."
They refuse to accept it—how many deluded Chan practitioners there are! They shoulder snow to fill the well. This spring the flowers bloom once more;
who can grasp this meaning? Truly, few know it: when the flowers fall, the spring breeze is still.

Chan Master Jiuzuo Huisui of Quanzhou ascended the hall. "Today at Jiuzuo, atop a solitary peak and the highest summit, I shall launch a single iron boat and cut off the vital passages for all people in the world.
I will cause them to ply their oars and move their paddles, yet not allow them to have a single silken prize.
Tell me, in whose hands does it lie? He took up his staff and said, "Look! Look! I told you so."
This dragon was stubbornly incredulous; it was only when he casually snatched it away that people were startled.

Regarding the Dharma heir of Chan Master Rannan, Chan Master Yuanzu of Zisheng Monastery in Xiuzhou, a monk asked: "The purple-gold lotus supports feet with a thousand wheels; the white jade *ūrṇā*..."
[The questioner asked: "How is it that the body of myriad virtues shines? What is the Buddha? The Master said: "Dragging a spear and wearing armor. [The questioner said:
"A thousand verses strung like flowers differ in their categories, yet the moon they point to returns to a single principle. "What is the Dharma? The Master said: "The statutes of Yuanyong;
the ordinances of Shaosheng. [The questioner said: "In the groves, you are a refined guest beyond the world; in the human realm, you are a lotus amidst the fire. "What is the Sangha?"
The Master said: "Spreading the mat and grasping the bowl.
This was Chan Master Shoujian of Wanshan on Mount Lu, a successor of Chan Master Huilenghai.
He was a native of Xiangzhou. On the first day of the year, he ascended the hall and said: "There is one person who does not bow."
He does not welcome the arrival of the new year; cold and heat cannot invade his body, and the holy and the profane cannot blur his traces.
From the beginning, his nostrils have pointed toward the heavens—who cares for the many years on the calendar? "Assembly, tell me: where is this man now?
He strikes the meditation staff and says, "Ho! Ho! Ho! Nowhere to go."

Chan Master Weichu of Huangbo in Ruizhou, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Kaixian Zong, was the son of the Cai family of Changzhou. He ascended the hall and said: "I see Elder Brother Zong."
Throughout my life, I have sat in silent stillness like withered wood—a mere physical shell.

I have never clamored with my lips, nor have I used the words and teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as a mere facade for my own school. My sole aim is that you may bring yourself to a state of complete rest;
then, naturally, you will not fall into error upon this leaking shell of a body. A monk asked: "If one does not fall into error upon this leaking shell of a body, then—"
[The student] asked, "How exactly does one maintain this? The Master said, "There is no place for you to apply your mind. [The student] said, "Does the Master have no expedient means?
The Master said, "If there is no sauce for the pan-cake, how can pressing sand produce oil?"
A monk asked Chan Master Hai of Mount Lu at Tanzhou, "What is it like when one takes three steps forward? The Master said, "One bumps one's head and strikes one's forehead.
The monk asked, "What is it like when one takes three steps backward? The Master said, "One falls into a pit and drops into a ditch.
The monk asked, "What is it like when one neither advances nor retreats? The Master said, "A corpse standing on its feet."

Zen Master Xiqing Huiyun’s Dharma heir, Zen Master Huishun of Xichan in Fuzhou, was a native of Zhending Prefecture. He ascended the hall and said: "Once every five days there is a formal session; on the eighth, fourteenth, and twenty-third days there is a general discourse.
Though I may speak a thousand times or ten thousand times—speaking horizontally or vertically—if suddenly a man comes forward and says, 'As for speaking, I do not care...'"
"No. But what can one do? At the three gates, two of them refused to consent. I then said to them, "Blind fellows!
Had it not been for those two, Xichan would have been like one who never met a true知音 (one who understands)."
The Dharma Successor of Chan Master Ming of Xuedou, the fifteenth generation under Nanyue,
Chan Master Ning of Qishan in Muzhou, ascended the hall and said: "Sometimes, atop a solitary peak, one whistles to the moon and sleeps amidst the clouds."
At that time, the great ocean surges with tossing waves and rushing billows; sometimes, at the crossroads, there are holes here and there in every direction.
Do you all understand this thoroughly? When the camphor tree flowers in full bloom, the plantain leaves are most numerous.
Chan Master Wuyun Wu of Lin’anfu, a dharma successor of Chan Master Chang of Jingci, was a native of the Tiexi region. He ascended the hall and said: "The old fellow Yuetao said:
'When walking, one does not see walking—what is this? When sitting, one does not see sitting—what is this? When putting on clothes, one does not see..."
When putting on clothes, what is this? When eating a meal, one does not see the eating; what is this?
Although this mountain monk sleeps in the same bed as others, we nevertheless each dream our own dreams. Why is this? When walking, one sees walking; when sitting, one sees sitting.
When putting on clothes, he sees himself putting on clothes; when eating rice, he sees himself eating rice.
There is nothing he does not see, yet there is no underlying principle [to be found]. What is this? Everyone, tell me: is it the old fellow’s? Is it Wuyun’s?
[He] takes up his staff, strikes once, and says: "Peaches red, plums white, and roses purple— When asked about the spring breeze, none know it at all."

Chan Master Yuanmiao Chichan of Zhongzhu in Lin’an, a successor of Chan Master Yunyanguang, was a member of the Wang family of Wuzhou. A monk asked, "What is the phrase that cuts off the flow of all streams?
The Master said, "Even Buddhas and Patriarchs have no opening for their mouths. The monk asked, "What is the phrase of the box and its lid fitting perfectly? [The Master replied: "..."
The *Kun* verse. The Master said: "It encompasses the earth and pervades the heavens. [A monk] asked: "What is the phrase of 'following the waves and riding the currents'?
The Master said: "Sometimes one enters the wild weeds; sometimes one ascends a solitary peak. Ascending the hall, he said: "At dusk the cock crows for dawn; at midnight the sun shines bright.
It startles the snow-lion, who opens wide its red eyes. Ascending the hall, he said: "Last year’s plum blossoms, this year’s willows—their countenances..."
"The fragrance of the form. He lets out a shout. After a long silence, he says: "If you had not received this one shout, I would have almost said that it remains as it was.
But tell me: after saying it, what then? The eyes pop out!"
Chan Master Lingyan Yuanri of Fuzhou, successor to Chan Master Yuantong Tan, ascended the hall and said: "There is nothing not realized in awakening; there is nothing not attained in realization.
For nine years he faced the wall in vain labor; a three-legged donkey leaps up into the sky. A clay ox enters the sea leaving no trace. Thus it is.
It is indeed so. Nine times nine is eighty-one.
A monk asked Chan Master Si-da of Yuquan in Jingmen, successor to Chan Master Hai of Yue-lu: "What is the single seal that seals the void? The Master said:

The myriad phenomena dissolve back into the ancient mirror. [The student] asked, "What is 'one seal impressing water'? The Master said, "The reflection of the autumn moon falls into a thousand rivers.
[The student] asked, "What is 'one seal impressing mud'? The Master said, "Observe closely before the patterns have yet arisen."

Chan Master Yisan Shen of Guangxiao Temple in Wenzhou, a successor in the sixteenth generation under the lineage of Chan Master Miaozhu of Nanyue, was a native of that same prefecture. He ascended the hall and said: "A dragon gives birth to dragons and phoenixes."

A phoenix is born; a rat raises its young along the ridgepole of the house. Great Master Bodhidharma did not understand Zen; traveling through the Wei and Liang courts, he engaged in nothing but empty clamor.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "One nine, two nines—when we meet, we do not take our hands out. Three nines make twenty-seven; at the fence-top, the *bīlù* flute is blown.
I recall little Śākyamuni, with both hands cradling his bent knees. Do you know? Do you not know? Is it real? Is it not real?"
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Ascending the hall: Vimalakīrti remained silent; Samantabhadra spoke at length.
The sages of successive generations have each displayed their own strengths and weaknesses. Do you not see? When the flowers fall in the third month, the cuckoo cries;

every single cry is a drop of blood. Ascending the hall: The wind whistles, the leaves flutter, the clouds drift in fragments, and the waters stretch vast and boundless. Standing alone on the riverbank.
To whom was it said? "A flight of two or three wild geese soaring beyond the heavens.
It is not yet clear who the Dharma heir is;
the Master Shixing arrived together with his fellow practitioner, Chan Master Rongxun. He ascended the hall and, holding up his staff with his right hand, said:
He leaned his staff against his left side and, after a long silence, said: "If this matter had not been entrusted to my elder brother, Fuyong, it would have been very difficult to fully comprehend.

He then descended from his seat. (Huanglong Nan commented: "When the true nature cannot be employed, one simply stops; yet he instead used the Buddha-dharma as a favor for others, causing people for a thousand years to regard it as a source of ridicule.")

Furthermore, tell me: where does the point of profit and harm lie? Jingshan Rong said: "Master Xing may truly be said to have distinguished the soil by its sprouts and recognized a person by their speech. Once one has arrived at the gate, one is immediately stripped bare; beyond the colors of black and yellow, one discerns the horse."

Yuelin Chenxianwei said, "Huanglong Nan says that when the real nature and its function cannot be attained, one simply stops; yet he instead treats the Buddha-dharma as mere social courtesy, causing it to become a laughingstock for a thousand years. To critique in such a manner is to blind the eyes of an entire city.
The Chan Master Yushan of Chaling had never traveled on pilgrimage. Once, when an itinerant monk from Mount Lu arrived, they discussed matters concerning the School of the Lineage (Zongmen).
The guest instructed him to contemplate the question: "When one is atop a hundred-foot pole, how does one advance further? Fandeng replied, "Ugh! (Ao).

This lasted for three years. One day, while riding a donkey across a bridge, he stepped on a plank and fell; at that moment, he attained sudden great enlightenment. He then composed a verse which said:
"I possess a divine pearl within my brow, Long confined by the locks of worldly toil. Today, the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, Illuminating ten thousand peaks of mountains and rivers.
From this point on, he no longer traveled to seek teachers elsewhere. This master was the Venerable Yuanwen of Baima.

Upon attaining the realization of his Master, Yun composed this eulogy: "Having advanced further from the top of a hundred-foot pole, A single step upon the mountain stream bridge submerged mountains and rivers.
From this moment forth, he never leaves the banks of Tea Creek; His every chant and song is nothing but 'Ra-li-ra'."

Dharma Master Sengzhao encountered the persecution of the Qin Emperor. As he was about to undergo execution, he spoke this verse: "The four elements originally have no master; The five aggregates are fundamentally empty.
To bring my head before the white blade Is like cutting through the spring breeze. [Xuansha said: "How great is Dharma Master Zhao! Even at the moment of death, he still speaks in his sleep."]
The Chan Master Guanhui of Chan-yue composed a poem that says: "When Chan practitioners meet, they merely snap their fingers;
How many people can truly know this mind? Master Daisui raised this as a question, asking: "What is this mind? The Master had no reply.
(Gui-zong Rou offered this on his behalf: "How many people can truly know it?")
First, Chan Master Jingzhao asked National Teacher Lengyan: "The sutra says that if one can turn things over, one is identical to the Tathāgata;
if one is turned by things, one is called an ordinary person. Now, regarding the Shengyuan Tower, how would you turn it?
Lengyan had no reply. (Fenyang spoke on his behalf, saying: "Both are already old.")
Master Gōngqī was on his way to Luóhàn when he encountered a young gentleman riding an ox.
The Master asked, "Which way does the road to Luóhàn go? The gentleman slapped the ox and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master shouted, "You beast!
The gentleman replied, "Which way does the road to Luóhàn go? The Master then slapped the ox and said, "Speak! Speak! The gentleman said, "Even if it were as you say..."
There were still some hooves and horns remaining. The Master struck him, whereupon the official slapped the ox and ran off.
During the Tang Dynasty, when Chan Master Yin was young, while he was once using a mallet to strike at the earth, he saw a large clod of soil;

he playfully struck it violently with the mallet, and as it shattered, he attained great enlightenment (later, an old master heard this and said: "The entire mountain and river world was reduced to a hundred fragments by a single blow from Chan Master Yin").

Chan Master Yunding of Mount Dongshan in Fuzhou was a native of Quanzhou (his clan name is lost). Having failed the imperial examinations for the second time, he went to Yuntai Dahou Temple to shave his head and receive full ordination.
He then visited Dayu Zhi and Shending Yin; later, upon meeting venerable elders under Luohan, he finally attained thorough realization of his own nature.
His reputation for the study of the Way spread widely, and the monastic community referred to him as "Ding Sanjiao" (the Third Patriarch of the Three Teachings). A monk asked:
"What is the Master’s daily activity? The Master said, "I eat; you suffer hunger.
[The monk] asked, "If every dharma does not reach another, how is this so? The Master said, "When you commit a transgression, I know it all.
He asked, "What is the Master’s single fly-whisk? The Master said, "It shatters the den of cultivation. [The monk] said, "In that case, there is originally nothing at all."
The Master said, "Who is it that knows there is nothing? He replied, "It is my fault, O Master. The Master said, "It would have been better had you reflected further.

The Layman asked, "Dongshan said, 'There is one thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth. I wonder what kind of thing this is? The Master said, "Carrying an iron cangue and receiving an iron staff.
He said, "Heaven and earth turn dark; mountains and rivers flee. The Master said, "Before the Hall of Lord Yama."
"Add one ghost; it lies beneath Mount Beimang for a thousand years. The scholar cries out, 'How joyful! How joyful! The Master said, "This too is a wild fox swallowing a mouse.
Invited by the Daoist of Jiulong Guan and three scholars, he ascended the hall and said:

"The Confucian school draws the Eight Trigrams and composes contracts, yet they do not save one from the cycle of rebirth in the six realms. The Daoist school pays homage to the Nine Sovereigns and refines the true qi, yet they do not..."

He has mastered the calculations of the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Our Śākyamuni World-Honored One penetrates the calculations of the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and rescues those in the saṃsāra of the six realms.

With great vows, he gathers in humans and devas, like the wind-circle supporting the sun and moon; with great wisdom, he shatters birth and death, as if the kalpa-fire were consuming the finest autumn hair.
Those who enter my gate naturally transform heaven and earth and perceive the hidden spirits and ghosts, enabling them to...
Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, the great earth, and the vast oceans enter into a single pore; yet all sentient beings neither perceive nor know this.
I speak of this Dharma-gate as being like space, which contains all myriad phenomena: the one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes the one.
If a person attains this one, then all matters are completed. Be careful.
Chan Master Chongyun of Yunyou in Wuzhou (now known as Fayun) first visited Xuefeng and subsequently relied upon Shishuang, whereupon he attained enlightenment.

He returned to his hometown to live in seclusion, covering his body with nothing but a single robe. Later, while presiding over the assembly in the Dharma Hall, he said: "The single arrow of Yunyou: empty space has no front or back;
shot forth it pervades the ten directions, yet for all intents and purposes, no one sees it. At that time, a monk asked: "How is it?"
"This is the Master’s single arrow. The Master said: "Throughout the entire world, there are no skulls.

Shuangxi Buna, the Chan Master Ru, was mourned with a poem by Chan Master Song, which read: "To succeed to the Patriarchate in our generation, His life’s conditions and conduct are worthy of emulation.
Throughout his life he remained ever on the Way; Recognizing his illness, he was too weary to seek a physician. His appearance is ancient..."
Difficult to write! His spirit was so lofty that the world knew it not; where could the clouds of compassion be spread? The solitary moon is naturally suited to him alone.
Having finished reading, the Master raised his brush and replied: "Who else has a path that accords with my lifelong aspirations? You, Idler, know my heart best.
Had I not intended to part from you at first, I feared I might have missed this one poem for my fellow practitioner. He dropped his brush and passed away while seated, at the age of sixty.
Later, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord, and his true countenance remained solemnly present.
Chan Master Tong of Touzi in Shuzhou was asked by a monk: "What is it like before Bodhidharma came? The Master said: "Fishermen’s songs resound on both banks. [The monk] asked:
"What is it like after he came? The Master said: "The great ocean surges with wind and waves. [The monk] asked: "What is the solitary [peak]?"
Atop the peak are long pines of steadfast character. The Master said, "They can serve as lords of the myriad phenomena, yet they do not wither with the changing of the four seasons.
[The monk] asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma here at your place, Master? The Master said, "Striking the west wall from the east wall."
When the imperial court issued an edict to convert Fahai Monastery in Chuzhou into a Shenxiao Palace, Master Chan Master Li ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:
"It is precisely because one has not yet attained thorough penetration that one speaks of right and wrong; it is because one lacks true realization that one distinguishes between 'this' and 'that.
Since even my own body does not exist, what need is there to speak of anything external to the body? View it with the correct eye."
Come! What a laughingstock this has been. Now that the Sage Ruler has issued his decree to convert monasteries into Shenshao Palaces, it is like placing a crown atop the Buddha’s head;
when one calculates it, what could be wrong with it? Today, this mountain monk cannot help but carry my staff across my shoulder.
Suspend your alms-bag high and take up residence within the seamless stupa; beneath the rootless tree, you shall whistle at the moon and chant with the wind.
Leave it to those immortal guests who ride the clouds and the lofty recluses who drive their cranes to come here to incantate water, write talismans, and perform rites by clacking their teeth.
In years to come, when you have attained the Way and ascended on a white cloud during the day, you will be able to repay the unrequitable debt of gratitude and assist in the Unconditioned.
This transformation—fear not that it is not jade; if it is jade, how marvelous! Yet, even so, tell me:
how shall this mountain monk express his turning-over-the-body phrase? Do you understand? He cast down his whisk and immediately passed into stillness.
The Prefect submitted a memorial regarding these matters. By imperial decree, the name of the temple was changed to "Zhenshen" (True Body).

On the day Chan Master Ming of Tianning in Ruizhou was ordained as a monk from a layman’s status, the Master ascended the seat; after concluding his expression of gratitude for the imperial favor, he said:
"The wooden tally is grasped at hand; the sitting mat is cast down in the moment. Clouds disperse and waters flow away; heaven and earth are silent and still."
"Empty! he said, and immediately closed his eyes and passed away.
Later, a monk asked Zen Master Renwang Qin of Shu, "What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "Hearing the name is not as good as seeing the face.

The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master replied, "A monkey performing in a bustling marketplace. The monk asked, "What about... [The text breaks off here.]
"What is the Way? He replied, "A tiger looking at a water mill.
(The surname of the Iron Chain Mountain Master of Jinling is lost. A monk asked, "I have long heard of the Iron Chain; I wonder what its face and appearance are like?"

The Master struck a pillar. A monk said, "Thank you for showing me. The Master asked, "On what basis do you say such a thing? The monk then struck the pillar. The Master said, "Tell me, where does the search lie?

The monk made a gesture of measuring. The Master said: *Note: This passage is a classic encounter dialogue (kōan) from the *Wumenguan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 49, concerning the interaction between Master Fenyang Shanzhao and a monk regarding the nature of reality and the limits of conceptualization.*
Today I have met a fellow practitioner.
As for Master Louzi, it is unknown where he was from, and even his name and lineage have not been handed down.

One day, while wandering through the streets and markets, he happened to adjust his socks and belt beneath a wine tower. Thereupon, he heard someone on the upper floor singing a song that went: "Since you have no..."
He thought, "I shall now cease my mental activity," and suddenly attained great enlightenment; consequently, he was styled Louzi.
Later, when the Dharma Master Shenzhao Benru requested instruction on the *Sūtra-king* from the Venerable Ziming, the Venerable called out in a thunderous voice:
"Your name is Benru (Inherently Thus). The Master immediately attained realization and composed a verse, saying: "Everywhere I encounter the path back home; At every turn, I reach my native land.
This matter has been manifest from the beginning; Why must I wait for deliberation?"
Dharma Master Yuanzhi Zhengwu of Shangzhushan in Lin’an was the son of the Lin family of Tāizhōu.

He relied upon Dharma Master Xiān of the White Lotus Society and inquired about the Way of the Total Transformation. Xiān pointed to a walking lamp and said: "A lamp such as this is devoid of intrinsic nature and transcends all negation."

Fundamentally empty and quiescent, the principle is fully present. Yet, because the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones perceive it differently, transformation is involved therein.
As the Master did not yet accord with this, he later recited the *Lotus Sūtra* while sweeping the floor. Upon reaching the passage, "Know that dharmas are eternally without nature;

the Buddha-seed arises from conditions," he finally understood the essential meaning. He informed Huiliang, who approved. Since the Master had led his disciples, he had long been concerned about the studies of his own school.
Such people are confined by names and forms and bound by written records; they even treat the transmission of the Tiantai school as a mere study of texts.
The Southern School looked down upon them, so [the Master] went to visit Chan Master Ciyun Yuan of Huguo Temple.
During a conversation at night, the Master cited the verse by Dongpo on staying at Donglin and said, "It is not easy to reach such a state. Ciyun replied, "You have not yet seen the path."
"What do you mean by 'arriving'? he asked. The Master said, "It is simply as they say: 'The sound of the mountain brook is itself the broad and long tongue;
the color of the mountains—is this not the pure body? If one has not reached this state, how could there be such a message? The monk said, "You are merely an outsider.
The Master said, "If you will not be stingy, you may explain it for me. The Master said, "Then you must simply exert yourself right here."
He watched intently for a chance to seize him. If he could catch him and break him, he would also know where his own *benming yuanchen* (the primary seat of life) was located.
The Master did not sleep the entire night. When the dawn bell rang, he removed his secret provisions and spoke another verse, saying:

"Master Dongpo is far too talkative; he wishes to penetrate the barriers of sound and form. If the stream were sound and the mountain were form, then without mountain or water, one would be a person of great sorrow. He specifically told this hermitage master, who said, "I have already told you that you are a man from outside the gate. The Master bowed in thanks. Shortly thereafter, there was someone soliciting funds to repair the roof tiles of Mazu’s Hall, seeking words to promote the project. The Master wrote: The Master’s words were inscribed upon the tiles. When the tiles were completed, the donor asked for a verse to commemorate them. The Master wrote: *The tiles are finished, the work is done;* *The old Buddha’s hall is restored anew.* *If you wish to see the ancient traces,* *Look at the tiles beneath your feet.* When the donor saw this, he was deeply moved and offered a large sum of money as a gift.

The Master refused it, saying, "This is merely a small matter; I do not need such wealth. The donor insisted, saying, "Please accept it to show your gratitude. The Master then composed a verse: *The donor’s heart is vast and deep;* *The Master’s virtue is profound and subtle.* *Though the offering is large, it is not accepted;* *The merit gained is immeasurable.* The donor was even more moved by these words and presented him with a further gift. The Master again declined, saying, "I am already full. The donor pressed him once more, saying, "Please accept it to show your compassion. The Master then wrote another verse: *The donor’s heart is vast and deep;* *The Master’s virtue is profound and subtle.* *Though the offering is large, it is not accepted;* *The merit gained is immeasurable.* The donor was so profoundly moved that he wept. The Master then accepted the gift. Later, when the donor passed away, the Master sent a messenger to his home to inquire after his family. Upon learning that the son had inherited his father’s estate, the Master sent a letter to the son, saying: *Your father’s heart was vast and deep;* *His virtue was profound and subtle.* *He gave generously and received nothing;* *His merit is truly immeasurable.* The son read the letter and was deeply moved, bowing in gratitude. This is the story of how the Master used his words to guide and transform others. It is recorded here to serve as an example for future generations. May all who encounter this teaching attain liberation. Thus ends the record.
He said, "Send word to the old master of Jiangxi: let him be scorched by the sun and fanned by the wind. It is not that his descendants lack the means to manage it;
they simply wish to see the moment when the ice melts and the structure crumbles. Chan Master Ciana saw this and laughed, saying, "One must indeed be this very *śramaṇa* to achieve such a thing."
Chan Master Chenggu of Jianfu in Raoyou was of lofty and pure conduct, and his nature was empty and luminous.
He visited Chan Master Jingxuan of Daguang, who remarked, "He is merely a fellow from within the weeds. Thereupon, he went to visit Master Ya of Fuyan, who likewise said:
He was simply a liberated monk. Consequently, he remained silent all day long, deeply investigating the grand regulations of the former masters.

One day, upon reading the words of Yunmen, he suddenly attained awakening. From then on, he concealed his talents and sought no fame, dwelling at the site of the stupa of Chan Master Hongjue at Yunju.
Scholars from the four quarters flocked to him, and for this reason he was called "The Ancient Stupa Master" (Guta Zhu). Jing...

In the fourth year of the Yuanshou era, Lord Fan Zhongyan was appointed as the governor of Poyang. Having heard of the Master’s virtue and realization, he invited him to reside at Jianfu Temple to propagate the ancestral teachings.
A monk asked, “Great Teacher of Virtue, with what do you instruct people? The Master said, “Do not. The monk said, “If that is so, then there is questioning and answering.
The Master said, “Do not question. The lush green bamboo is entirely True Suchness; the dense... [the trees]...”
"The yellow flowers are none other than *prajñā*. What is *prajñā*? The Master said, "In the Yellow Springs (the underworld), there is no distinction between old and young.

The monk said, "When spring comes, the grass turns green of itself. The Master said, "One's reputation shall be imperishable. The monk said, "If that is so, even the blue-eyed barbarian monk would frown.
The Master said, "Step back three paces. The monk said, "How bitter! The Master then uttered "Hūṃ, hūṃ. [The monk] asked Linji about raising the whisk. The student...
A monk raised his fist. "Is this the same or different? The Master said, "False words confuse the multitude. The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall act according to your command.

The Master said, "To the ends of the earth and the corners of the sea. The monk asked, "Regarding 'a single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function operate simultaneously'—what is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Dry firewood and damp reeds. The monk then shouted. The Master said, "Blazing red flames fill the sky. He ascended the hall for formal instruction.
Now, those who have left the household life are for the sake of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Within the unconditioned dharma, there is neither benefit nor merit.

Lately, those who have left the household life have been greedily attached to blessings and wisdom, which is entirely contrary to the Way. If one seeks blessings and wisdom, one must first clarify the mind;
yet if one wishes to reach the Way, there is no place for you to apply the mind. Therefore, I constantly advise all people: do not study the Buddha-dharma; simply [be yourself].
Rest your mind. Those of sharp faculties will attain liberation at the moment of hearing; those of dull faculties may take three or five years, but not more than ten.
If you do not awaken, I, this old monk, shall send you to the Hell of Plucked-out Tongues. *Chan*.
Zen Master Jōkai Shūmitsu of Wazhou (heir to Jianfu Gu) was asked by a monk, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Bowing my head, bowing my head.
The monk asked, "Does the student have a share in this? The Master said, "Touching my forehead, touching my forehead. The monk performed a dance and departed.
The Master said, "It resembles it, yet it is not yet it.
Regarding the question posed by the layman Yang Jie of Wubei concerning the essential nature of the *vinaya* as expounded by Vinaya Master Xuán, Master [Fàn]zǔ replied with this verse:
"How could emotion and wisdom ever differ? The dog barks while the snake moves on its own. Zhōngnán is indeed..."
This is the meaning. "Striking the third watch at noon.
Long ago, there was an elder who did not speak with the monks for an entire summer retreat. A monk sighed and said, "I have spent this entire summer in vain;
I did not dare hope that the Master would preach the Buddha-dharma, yet I hoped at least to hear two characters of the True Cause."
He attained it. When an elder heard of this, he said, "Dharma brother, do not speak so hastily. If one speaks of the true cause, there is not even a single word.
Having finished speaking, he tapped his teeth and said, "Just now, I spoke without reason; I should not have spoken like that. An elder next door heard this and said, "What a fine pot of soup!
A single mouse-dung has ruined it. (Yunmen and Xuedou added: "In whose house is there not an ounce or two of mouse-dung in the pot?")
Once there was a monk who did not read the sutras while in the scripture hall, but sat in meditation every day.
The Librarian asked, "Why do you not read the sutras? The monk replied, "I am illiterate. The Librarian said, "Why do you not ask others?
The monk stepped forward, joined his palms, and bowed, asking, "What character is this? The Librarian had no reply. (The Dàtōng edition adds: "Or again, he said he did not recognize it.")

Once there was an elderly master living in a hermitage. He wrote the character for "mind" (心) above his door, he wrote the character for "mind" on his window, and he wrote the character for "mind" on his wall.
(Fayan said: "Above the door, one should simply write 'door'; on the window, one should simply write 'window'; on the wall, one should simply write 'wall'.

Xuangjue said: "One need not write 'door' above the door; one need not write 'window' on the window; one need not write 'wall' on the wall. Why? Because the meaning of the characters is already manifest.")

In the past, there were two hermits living in separate huts. They had not seen one another for ten days, and when they suddenly met, the senior hermit asked the junior hermit, "I have not seen you for a long time; where have you been?
The junior hermit replied, "I have been in my hut building a seamless stupa. The senior hermit said, "I also wish to build one. May I borrow your stupa from you?"
[The Master] made the likeness. The abbot below said, "Why did you not say so sooner? It has just been borrowed by someone else. (Fayan said:
"Now tell me, was it his likeness that was borrowed, or was it not his likeness?")
Once there was a hermit who, seeing a monk approach, held up his fire-tube and asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not.
The hermit said, "This is something that has not been exhausted in thirty years. The monk then asked, "What did you use before those thirty years?
The hermit had no reply. (Nanquan Ruyi spoke on his behalf, saying: "One must know this as well.")
Once there was an old master who, when asked by the Prince of Jiangnan, "I have a water buffalo that has not a single blade of grass for ten thousand miles;
I do not know where to let it loose," remained speechless. (Gui-zong Rou offered this on his behalf: "Let it loose in a good place.")
Once there was an elderly master who asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "I have come from Niu-tou Mountain to pay homage to the Patriarch.
The master asked, "Did you see the Patriarch? The monk had no reply. (Gui-zong Rou offered this substitute response: "It is very much like not believing him.")
Once there was an elder who spoke in verse: "A single void atop the mountain of the five aggregates; Entering and exiting through the same gate, yet we do not meet.
For immeasurable kalpas we have rented this dwelling; Yet until the end, we fail to recognize the true Master. [Another elder said:
"If you do not know him, whom did you ask when you first rented? ]
A monk asked an old master, "What is it like to be one among those within the secret chamber? The old master said, "When there is a guest, I do not answer.
(Xuansha said, "When was it ever secret? Niu-tou Rouru addressed the old master differently, saying, "Why did you allow him to see?")
Once there was an elderly master. When a monk asked him, "The soul returns, come back; eat the mulberries of my home garden," [the monk] asked, "What are the mulberries of the home garden?
(Xuanguo answered on his behalf: "Even so, they cannot be eaten. Fadeng said: "They will defile your mouth.")
Once, an elder said, "The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years to seek someone of like mind.
If you understand it in this way, there will come a day when you eat iron rods. Another elder said, "The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years;
how can he not feel ashamed? If you understand it in this way, you must buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty more years. (Langye Huijue said: Since it is not so, then...)

"What was the meaning of the Founding Patriarch facing the wall? After a long silence, he said: "If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata."
Once there was an elder master. When a monk asked him, "A lion uses its full strength to seize a rabbit and its full strength to seize an elephant;
I wonder, what kind of strength does it fully employ? The elder replied, "The strength of non-deception" (Fayan commented elsewhere: "He did not understand the words of the ancients").
Once there was an elder who said: "This plot of land has been entrusted to me for a long time;

I shall remain standing here and wait for you to grasp its meaning. (Fayan said: "I, this mountain monk, shall now sit here and wait for you to grasp it. Is there any principle in this? Which is close and which is distant? Try to judge for me.")

In the past, there was an elderly master who kept a young attendant, yet neither of them knew the proper rules of conduct. One day, a traveling monk arrived and instructed the boy in the rituals of etiquette.
Later that evening, seeing the elderly master returning from outside, the boy went forward to offer his greetings. The master was surprised and perplexed.
He then asked the boy, "Who taught you this? The boy replied, "A certain senior monk (shangzuo) in the hall.
The old master summoned that monk and questioned him: "Senior monk, you travel among other houses; what kind of mental conduct is this?
This boy has been raised by me for two or three years and is naturally quite pitiable. Who taught you to corrupt him? Pack your things quickly and leave at once!"
Drenched by the rain at twilight, he was driven out. (Fayan said: "The ancients were so manifest; how strange is this little bit of their 'house style. But tell me, what was their intention?")
Once, there was a monk who arrived at Caoxi. At that time, the monk in charge of the robes and bowl held up the robe and said, "This is what could not be lifted at the head of Mount Dayu.
The visiting monk asked, "Why is it in your hands, Venerable? The monk in charge had no reply.
(Yunmen said, "Neither of them has reached a resolution," and he also said, "I thought this was a lion cub.")
Long ago, there was a monk who, while studying the *Lotus Sūtra*, reached the passage: "All dharmas, from their very origin, are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction.
Suddenly, he was seized by doubt that he could not resolve. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he constantly investigated this for himself, yet gained nothing at all.

One spring day, hearing the song of a warbler, he attained sudden enlightenment. He then continued the preceding verse, saying: "All dharmas, from their very origin, Are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction."
When spring arrives, the hundred flowers bloom; the yellow oriole sings atop the willows.

Long ago, there was an elder who asked a presiding master (zhuozu): "Regarding the commentaries and sub-commentaries (*shuchao*), how do their explanations of the meaning differ in breadth or brevity?
The master replied, "The commentary explains the sub-commentary; the sub-commentary explains the sūtra. The elder asked, "What does the sūtra explain? The master was speechless.
Formerly, when people from the kingdom of Koguryo came to Qiantang, they carved a sacred image of Avalokiteśvara. When they attempted to lift it onto their ship, it would not budge at all.
Consequently, they invited it to be enshrined for veneration at Kaiyuan Temple in Mingzhou. Later, someone posed this question: "It is said that there is no land where he does not manifest his body;

why then did the sacred image not go to the kingdom of Koguryo? Changqing Ling said, "Though his manifestations are universal, the forms perceived are partial. Fayan Ze said, "Have you not yet recognized Avalokiteśvara?"
Before the pagoda at Sizhou, a monk was prostrating. Someone asked him, "Venerable Sir, you prostrate every day; do you actually see the Great Sage?
(Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying: "Tell me, what is the meaning of your prostration?")
A *shishi* (attendant) at Sizhou Ta Tou locked the gate at the appointed hour. Someone asked, "Since you are the Great Master of the Three Realms, why are you being locked up by your disciple?
The attendant had no reply. (Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying: "The disciple locks it; the Great Master locks it. Fadeng spoke on his behalf, saying: "Give me back the key!
An old master also spoke on his behalf, saying: "Jizhou locks it; Qianzhou locks it.")
A statue of a holy monk was being dripped upon by leaking roof water. Someone asked the monk, "Since you are a holy monk, why do you have leaks?
The monk had no reply. (National Teacher Shao spoke on his behalf, saying: "Being leakless does not make one a holy monk.")
Someone asked a monk, "What kind of lamp do you light? The monk replied, "A perpetually burning lamp. [The man] asked, "When was it lit? [The monk] said, "It was lit last year.

[The man] asked, "Where is the perpetual light? The monk was speechless. (Changqing Ling, acting on his behalf, said: "If he had not done so, you would have known that you were being deceived by him. Fayan spoke differently: "He was moved by profit.")
There was a presiding master (zuozhu) who, while reciting the name of Amitābha, was called by a junior monk.
When he turned his head to look back, the junior monk did not respond. This happened three or four times. The master rebuked him, saying, "I have called you three or four times; what is the matter?

The junior monk replied, "For how many years have you been calling him [Amitābha] and yet succeeded? As soon as I call him, he immediately creates karma" (Fadeng spoke on his behalf, saying, "Shoo! Rebuke him!").
There was a monk who, having finished reciting the sutra with a young boy, told him to place the sutra inside the case.
The boy said, "Where shall I put what I have recited? (Fadeng spoke on his behalf, saying: "What sutra did you recite?")

A monk was annotating the *Daode jing*. Someone asked him, "I have long heard that the Great Virtuous One has annotated the *Daode jing*. The monk replied, "I do not dare. [The questioner] asked, "How is it?
[Fadeng spoke on behalf of the monk, saying: "It is [the work of] Your Disciple (the Emperor Minghuang)."

There was a monk who entered the underworld and saw Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva asked him, "What practice have you cultivated throughout your life? The monk replied, "I recite the Lotus Sūtra.
[Kṣitigarbha] said, "'Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. Is this speaking, or is it not speaking?"
The monk had no reply (Gui-zong Rou spoke on his behalf, saying: "This one returns; I dare to circulate this").
Under the assembly of Master Yan-guan, there was a chief administrative monk who suddenly saw a ghost messenger come to pursue him.
The monk said to him, "I am the chief administrator and have not yet had the leisure to practice. May I beg for seven days' grace? The messenger said, "I shall wait and report it."
"O King, if you grant permission, I shall come in seven days; otherwise, I will arrive in an instant. Having spoken, he vanished.
When the seven days had passed, the king came again to seek the monk, but he was nowhere to be found. Later, someone questioned a monk:
"If you were to be sought out and found, how would you handle him? (Dongshan spoke on his behalf: "He has already been found by him.")
A monk from Liutong Monastery in Taizhou wished to cross by boat. Someone asked him, "Since you possess the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), why do you rely on a boat?
The monk had no reply. (National Teacher Shao of Tiantai spoke on his behalf, saying: "I did not wish to startle the assembly.")
One day, the monk of Dajian Temple requested that the Second Seat be invited to open the hall for a formal discourse before Song Linggong, the Governor of Hongzhou.
The Governor said, "Why not invite the First Seat? The assembly was speechless. (Fayan spoke on their behalf: "There is no need to go to such lengths.")

The Chancellor of Jiangnan, Feng Yanshi, was traveling with several monks to Mount Zhong. Upon reaching the "One-Man Spring," he asked, "At a spring for only one person, how can so many people find it sufficient?
A monk replied, "We do not allow it to be lacking. Yanshi did not accept this answer and instead said, "Who is it that lacks?
(Fayan provided an alternative reading: "Who is it that is insufficient?")
The official asked the monk, "What is your name? The monk replied, "No selection. The official said, "If someone were suddenly to give you a bowl of sand, what then?
The monk replied, "I thank the official for his offering. (Fayan commented elsewhere: "This is still a matter of selection.")
There was a monk living in a hermitage in Guangnan. When the sovereign went out hunting, his attendants informed the master of the hermitage, saying, "The Great King is coming; please rise.
The master replied, "Not only would I not rise for the Great King, I would not even rise for the Buddha. The King asked, "Is it not the case that the Buddha is your teacher?"
The Master said, "Yes. The King asked, "Why do you not rise when seeing the Master? (Fayan spoke on his behalf: "Not yet sufficient to repay your kindness.
On Hongtang Bridge in Fuzhou, there were monks sitting in a row. An official asked, "Is there a Buddha here? The monks had no reply.
(Fayan spoke on their behalf: "Who are you?")
In the past, there was an official who entered the Tianwang Temple in Zhenzhou. Upon seeing the divine image, he asked the temple master, "What meritorious function does this represent?
The master replied, "It is the Guardian King of the State. The official asked, "Does it protect only this country, or does it protect all other countries as well?

The master replied, "When in Qin, it protects Qin; when in Chu, it protects Chu. The official then said, "On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month, smash down the city walls of Zhenzhou! At that, the sky...
"Where has the King gone? The master had no reply.

Formerly, there was an official who composed a "Treatise on the Non-existence of Ghosts. One night at midnight, while he was wielding his brush, he suddenly saw a ghost appear and say, "You claim there are no ghosts;
what about me? (Wuzu Yan said: "If I, this old monk, had seen him back then, I would have simply made my hand into the beak of a magpie and said to him, 'Gu-gua! [a cry of protest].)
Once there was a practitioner of the Way who sat with his back turned toward the Buddha in front of the Buddha Hall. A monk said, "Practitioner of the Way, do not sit with your back to the Buddha.
The practitioner replied, "In the fundamental teaching of the Great Virtuous One, it is said that 'the Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm. Where, then, could one possibly sit?
The monk had no reply. (Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying: "I recognize you.")

There was a practitioner who followed a Dharma Master into the Buddha Hall. The practitioner spat toward the Buddha, and the Master said, "Practitioner, you lack propriety. Why do you spit at the Buddha?
The practitioner replied, "I have come from a place where there is no Buddha to spit upon someone like me.

The Master had no response. [Master] Guishan said: "The benevolent one, however, is not benevolent; the non-benevolent one, however, is benevolent. [Yangshan] spoke on behalf of the Dharma Master, saying: "Simply spit at the practitioner. He further said: "If the practitioner has something to say, then tell him: 'Return it to me!'"
[He came from a place where there are no practitioners].
A dead fish was floating on the surface of the water. Someone asked a monk, "Is it not the case that this fish takes water as its life? The monk said:
"Yes. [The Master asked: "Why, then, did he die in the water? The monk was unable to answer. (Master Tianlong Ji of Hangzhou spoke on his behalf:
"It is because he chose not to die on the bank.")
A hawk pursues a pigeon, which flies onto the railing of the Buddha Hall and trembles.
Someone asks a monk, "All sentient beings dwell in constant peace and joy within the shadow of the Buddha. Why does this pigeon tremble upon seeing the Buddha?
The monk has no reply. (Fadeng speaks on his behalf: "He is afraid of the Buddha.")
Once there was a monk who, while traveling along the road to Fushan, encountered an old salt seller.
The monk asked, "Where does the road to Fushan lead? The old man remained silent for a long time. The monk asked again, and the old man said, "Are you deaf?
The monk replied, "What did you say to me? The old man said, "I told you where the road to Fushan leads. The monk asked, "Do you understand Zen? The old man said, [silently].
"Do not say you understand Chan; even the Buddha-dharma will eventually be exhausted. The monk said, "Try to explain it for me. The old man lifted up his salt basket. The monk said, "Difficult.
The old man asked, "What do you call this? The monk said, "Salt. The old man asked, "What connection does that have [to the Dharma]?
The monk asked, "And what do you call it? The old man replied, "I cannot tell you again that it is salt. (Jingshan Rong’s *Niàn*)

[The Master] said: "Look at this peddler of private salt! How did he come to possess such a total, penetrating hand-eye? Having encountered [the monk], he immediately revealed his style; turning his back, he cast out his hook and deployed his snare. Releasing and gathering, he sought only for people to know that he existed. What a pity—this monk was much like one who bumps into a pillar. You blind fellow!

Had you seen him at that moment, if you had stirred up the matter in such a way as to overturn the salt basket and depart, it would have left this salt-seller in doubt. What kind of eyes does this monk possess?"
Long ago, there was an old woman who supported a hermit for twenty years. She regularly sent a young girl of eighteen to serve him with meals.
One day, she ordered the girl to hold the hermit firmly and asked, "At this very moment, what is it like? The hermit replied:
"A withered tree leaning against a cold cliff; for three winters there has been no warmth.

The woman brought this up to the old lady, who said, "For twenty years I have provided offerings only to a worldly fellow. She then sent him away and burned down his hut. Miam Jie commented: "This koan is rarely taken up or discussed within the monastic community.

I, Master Jie, cannot help but strip my face bare and suffer a defeat, yet I wish for those everywhere to examine it. He then called to the assembly, saying: 'This old woman’s inner chamber is secure and private, impenetrable as a watertight seal. Yet she biased herself toward...'"

Flowers are scattered upon withered trees; flames burst forth from within cold crags. This monk stands solitary and remote, accustomed to plunging into surging waves. He casually cuts off the tide that rises to the heavens, yet in the end, his body remains without so much as a drop of water. If one examines this closely, there is no doubt that these two men have been shackled and bound;

yet, as for the Buddha-dharma, they have not even dreamed of it. When Wujou handled the matter in such a manner, where did his intent ultimately lie? After a long silence, he said: "A tangle of willow threads cannot be gathered up; together with the mist, they rest upon the jade railing."

**The Railing.** Jingshan Rong held up his staff and said: "This old woman spent twenty years piling up dust and earth around a eggplant tree. After such a long time, she caused someone to go specifically to investigate it, thinking, 'I shall plant this as a weed for my own household.

Yet, it turns out to be a sprout growing in a different soil. Consequently, he sent her away and burned down her hut. "If I, this mountain monk, had waited for her to embrace me and asked, 'At this very moment, what is it? I would simply have held up my whisk and said, 'I have given you proof. Had she hesitated even further, I would have pushed her away.

Not only would her hut have been spared from burning, but her eyes would have been made clear for a thousand ages. How could she have fallen into the pit of the 'withered tree and cold cliff' where there is no warmth?"
Once, there was a monk who went to visit Mihu. On the road, he encountered an old woman living in a hermitage.
The monk asked, "Do you have any kinsmen? She replied, "I do. The monk asked, "Where are they? She said, "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth; whether grass or trees—all are my kinsmen.
The monk said, "Are you not coming as a nun (śramaṇī)? She replied, "What do you see in me? The monk said:
The laywoman said, "You cannot be a monk. The monk said, "Old woman, do not cause confusion within the Buddha-dharma.
The laywoman said, "I am not causing confusion within the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "If you act in this way, is that not causing confusion within the Buddha-dharma? The laywoman said:
"You are a man; I am a woman. How could we ever have been confused? (Jingshan Rong’s commentary says: "I laugh at this monk for traveling on pilgrimage and casually running into this old woman.")

To be confronted face-to-face yet fail to turn the pivot and bring forth function, but instead merely block and resist as if facing a gale, wandering about in a different direction—this is why one was struck three times and knocked four times by the old woman, appearing much like one standing downwind with no freedom of action.

This woman did not know what kind of person she had encountered; meeting him so unexpectedly, she was nonetheless able to reveal the true standard of the Way, seeing that his eyes were clear and bright.

Had it been this mountain monk, when the woman said, "Mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, and trees are all my kinsmen," I would have simply held up my staff and shown it to her, saying, "Why does he not bow to you? If she had attempted to respond, I would have struck her right on the head, ensuring that the old woman could never turn back and leave.
The laywoman Pangxing entered Lukmen Temple to offer a vegetarian feast. The rector requested her intention for the dedication of merit.

The laywoman took up a comb, stuck it behind her hair-knot, and said, "I have dedicated the merit. She then departed. (Jingshan Rong’s commentary: This extraordinary matter belongs to an extraordinary person; she carries out a meaning that transcends the ordinary.)

This must be revealed by an extraordinary person. When Dame Pang acted in this way, she was truly startling to the multitude and difficult to describe; it was not merely something extraordinary or marvelous. However, because the *vina* (chant leader) could not produce a single stroke of skillful means, he greatly failed the mountain monk.

Had he been the *vina*, he would have given her a punch on the back to ensure that rewards and punishments were clearly distinguished, thereby further demonstrating that there are people within the Dharma Garden.

The nun Chen Dao-po of Wenzhou once traveled extensively to seek instruction from renowned masters throughout the various regions. Later, she attained enlightenment under the guidance of Master Jing at Changlao Mountain.
She composed a verse which says: Upon the level summit of the high ridge, There are but woodcutters everywhere.
Everyone harbors the intent of axe and hatchet, Yet they do not see the mountain flowers reflecting red in the water.
Once, there was a laywoman who entered the monastery to distribute money to the assembly of monks according to their seniority. A monk said, "Place one portion before the Holy Monks.
The woman asked, "How old are the Holy Monks? The monk had no reply. (Fayan Daoyuan spoke on his behalf: "One knows it when the heart's intention is fulfilled. Baoning Yong spoke on his behalf:
"I only fear that the donor’s power does not reach that far.")
Chan Master Fojue of Qingzhou composed a verse on the story of Master Yangshan’s lion, saying: "A single color surpasses all indications to people;
Within a world of white silver, he yawns and stretches. Transcendently, he topples it down and then raises it up again; How can this compare to the spring breeze warming the new day?"
Yuantong Shanguo (who succeeded Fojue): When Furi came from Jiangyou to Yanjing, he stayed at Dasheng'an Temple.
One day, he was conversing with Fojue at night; the Master [Shanguo] was then twelve years old and stood in attendance by his seat.
Furi said, "Since I came from the south, I have not yet encountered a single person who has grasped the Buddha-dharma with the tip of my staff. The Master joined his palms and stepped forward.
Yunju said, "From now on, Master, your staff will be short. Yunju was greatly startled and said, "I must request this man to continue the lineage of my own Linji school.
Yunju replied, "How could there be two schools—Yunmen and Linji? Yunju praised him incessantly.

Later, when Emperor Jin Sejong visited the Shrine of the Auspicious Image at Sungan Temple, he asked the Master, "Is it right to prostrate? Or is it right not to prostrate? The Master replied, "If one prostrates..."

They respected one another; had they not bowed, each would have claimed superiority for themselves. The Emperor was greatly pleased. Later, while residing at Yansheng Monastery, the Master addressed the assembly by citing the story of Guanyin and the sesame cake.
The Master said, "The Elder of Shaoyang could truly be described as one whose song grows ever loftier while those who join in the harmony grow ever fewer.
Now, however, we are here at Yansheng, entering the Fangwang Samādhi upon the tip of a whisk, entering meditative concentration in the East."

Arising from the west... even to the case where one enters meditative absorption in a male body and arises in a female body. Do you understand? The wild landscape is no longer interrupted by mountains;
the moonlight flows directly through to the water. Long ago, there were two monks traveling together; the one of impatient temperament was in front.
The Master called out to the one behind him, saying, "Time passes swiftly; hurry up and come forward! The monk behind replied, "The Great Way is vast and wide;
why such haste? The Master composed a verse, saying: "Time passes swiftly; hurry up and come forward.
Tread upon the path’s end, and the *utpala* flower blooms. The Great Way is vast and wide; why such haste? Relax your belly, and all is encompassed at once. The Master.
Seeing that Xuanwu’s words were frivolous and sarcastic, Yuxiang reprimanded him, saying: "If everyone were like you, how could the Buddha-dharma have reached its present state?
Emperor Xianzong of the Jin dynasty commanded a palace messenger to bring a sheet of paper for Chan Master Xuanwu Yuxiang (who was a successor of Yuantong) at Qingshou Monastery in Yanjing.

Zhang wrote the two characters "Mind" (xin) and "Buddha" (fo) and asked the Master, "What kind of characters are these? At that time, Yuan Tong was seated nearby and replied immediately, "Neither mind, nor Buddha.
This pleased Zhang's mind. The following day, he issued an imperial decree bestowing upon him a long-short poem (changduanju) which said: [The poem follows.]
If you can simply understand that all phenomena arise through causes and conditions, what need is there to ask about the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) in daily life?

Do not harbor further doubts throughout the twelve periods of the day; you must always recognize it with sovereign ease. From the beginning, there has been no obstruction—buddha after buddha, mind after mind.
If the mind relies upon the Buddha, it is still a defilement. The Master replied in thanks: "Unconditioned and effortless. To identify with the unconditioned is itself a bondage. [He] illuminated.

To act at this very moment is already too late—like lightning flashing or a shooting star streaking away. It is neither mind nor Buddha; yet even to call it "not mind" is still to treat it as a thing.
When both person and environment are empty, the myriad phenomena are reflected within a single mirror.
The lay practitioner Zhao Wenyu (Sishuanyuantong) of Mount Huang once composed this verse: "Deluded thoughts are originally and fundamentally true;
To try to eliminate them is to raise another layer of dust. In speech, thought, movement, and stillness—who provides the power? If you examine closely, there is no one other than yourself."
Master Ding of Gaoyou (a successor of Xuangu) went to attend upon Xuangu. In the meditation hall, Xuangu raised a kōan: A monk asked Xuansha, “What is the pure *dharmakāya*?
Xuansha replied, “Dripping pus. Master Ding suddenly attained realization. Later, when a monk asked him, “What does the golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net eat?
the Master said, “A dry piece of excrement.”
Chan Master Bao of Puzhao in Zhengzhou was the son of the Wu family from Cizhou. While he was building Yangshan Temple in Fuyang, someone suddenly inscribed a poem upon a pillar that read:
"People say the turtledove is clumsy; I say the turtledove is clever. With one piece of wood and two pieces of wood, One’s household needs are fully provided.
The Master attained great enlightenment and immediately retired to the Western Mountains to dwell in a thatched hut. He then traveled extensively...
Zhushan went to Baoyan Temple in Hongyu. One night, a great wind shook the earth, and he passed away while sitting in meditative equipoise.
Chan Master Yun’an Qing of Jingshan in Hangzhou was a native of Jianyang. Regarding the koan of Yangqi’s “Three-Legged Donkey,” he offered this verse:
Yangqi had a donkey, Its eyes flashing like lightning; It trampled all people underfoot— What need is there to speak of three?
Jiao. Chan Master Juchuan Hai of Zhulin composed a verse on wind bells: Copper lips and iron tongues, too sharp and new;
Hung at the corner of the tower, they do not reckon the passing spring. The hundreds of thousands of *samādhi* dharmas beyond words— Through the wind, they are spoken to those who truly know.
Chan Master Xuming Jiaoheng of Qingshou Temple in Yanjing was the son of the Wang family of Rencheng in Jizhou.

Previously, there was a monk named Fuan of Ciji Temple who had lived in mountain retreats for many years; while resting against a tree in Mangshan Village, he passed away and dreamed that he sought lodging, whereupon the Master was born.
At the age of seven, he left home to become a monk; at fifteen, he began traveling to visit various teachers. Upon hearing of the Dharma of Zhengzhou Puzhao...
The Master went to visit Xizheng and attended upon him morning and evening, yet he did not attain any realization.

Later, while traveling to Suizhou on business, he suddenly had an awakening while on horseback as he recalled the circumstances of the wooden board. Although his doubts were not yet entirely dispelled, as they neared the river crossing, his companion Jing said, "This is the river crossing.
The Master dismounted, filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy. Upon returning, he told Bao about it, and Bao said:
This man lying stiffly on his back seemed as though he wished to move. [The Master] showed him the kōan of Nitchū Butsu (Sun-Face Buddha).

One day, upon hearing the sound of the wooden board signaling the meal, he attained direct realization and presented this verse: "Sun-face, Moon-face, stars streaming, lightning flashing— If you hesitate even longer, an arrow will strike your face!
*Du!* Ba said, "I cannot deceive you. Autumn, the seventh month, the tenth day, of the *Jǐmǎo* year of the Xīngdìng era.
On that day, he wrote a verse and passed away while sitting upright.
Chan Master Laishan of Zhenfu asked, "Where is the abbot Iron Ox’s stupa? The Master pointed his finger toward it.
[The monk] suddenly attained realization and then presented this verse: "O Iron Ox, O Iron Ox! Seek nothing else. If someone asks..."

Hemp. Now tell me: who is it that remains at ease?
Grand Master Huihong of the Yeli Yuan on Mount Wutai, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, reached the passage: "When one person gives rise to the true [mind]..."
The ten directions were extinguished. Suddenly he attained awakening and went to see Chan Master Wen of Heshuo to recount what he had realized.

Wen approved of him. His verse at the time of death said: "Sixty years of springtime, plus eight more; the floating clouds have cleared away, revealing the blue sky. As I depart, I kick over Mount Sumeru;
in the night that follows, the moon atop the mountain is perfectly full. He changed his robes and passed away while sitting upright.
Chan Master Yuanmo Huikong of Jianning Prefecture was the son of the Su family of Gutian.

One day, while in meditative absorption, he traveled to Mount Jiang and arrived at the site where Chan Master Xuanjiang had practiced. An old man came forward to greet him, saying, "I have guarded this mountain for five hundred years.
Having finished speaking, he transformed into a black dragon and departed. Upon awakening from his trance, the Master said, "I must return [to this place]."
Ben returned to Yuan and subsequently established a hermitage on this mountain. One day he said to the assembly, "In the presence of the Buddha, I was known as Bodhisattva Huikong.
Now that my karmic conditions for transformation have been fulfilled, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. He then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the assembly.
Again, he spoke in verse: "For over forty years I dwelt amidst the dust of the mundane world, And now I have revealed the Honored One within this very midst.
One night a spring wind arose from the eastern cliffs, Blowing the flowers open until the trees were full of spring.
An iron boat, without rudder nor sail, Is steered into the ocean of the nature-lotus. The final pivot of the mechanism is now explained: White clouds have never been separate from the vast sky."
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth leave no trace when sought; the void is struck through without cause.
Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon one's crown, the original nature’s perfect luminosity is never lost. He further said:

At that time, clouds and mist arose on all sides, and thunder and rain broke forth violently. Subsequently, he manifested fire to cremate himself.
The assembly collected his sacred remains and enshrined them in a stupa to the west of the hermitage.
Chan Master Foguang Daowu of Puzhao Temple in Zhengzhou was the son of the Guan family from Lanzhou.

While staying overnight at a shop in Wanzi, he heard the neighing of a horse and attained a sudden, great enlightenment. He spoke a verse, saying: "Jian ye lo, jian ye lo; throughout the void, it is only this.
Returning home, he told his mother, "I have picked up an object on the road. His mother asked, "What object? The Master replied: [The verse].
"Since beginningless time, I have not seen [this]. The mother said, "What joy is there in that? Thereupon, he took his leave to travel to various quarters.
His mother asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "Water flowing must reach the sea; a crane emerges from atop the white clouds. He went to attend upon Chan Master Baizhang Hai.
He then received the seal of transmission. In the twenty-fourth year of the Taiding era, he presided over Puzhao Temple.

Clad in white robes, riding a yellow calf, and blowing a short flute, he wandered through Luoyang. He once said: "If you say I am an ordinary person, I have previously come from the rank of the sages.
If you say I am a sage, I am now going back to the rank of the ordinary. If you say I am neither ordinary nor sage, I shall instead go to Vairocana."
He had a separate place of practice at Ding-shang. He entered nirvana in the fifth year of the Taihe era.
In the fifth year of the Jiayou era, Chan Master Pujue Chunpeng of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou received an imperial decree returning the Jiuliso area to the Jiqing Prefecture.
He ascended the hall and said: "A single plot of idle land before the mountain; from vast kalpas past, it has had no boundaries."
This morning, having been restored, I have returned once more. Sitting, I cut off both the head and the tail of my feet; east is thus, west is thus—north, south, east, and west are not otherwise.
But how, ultimately, does one repay this kindness? Ten *li* of lotus flowers, nine *li* of pine trees—a single incense stick before the Hall of Direct Pointing.
Zen Master Wujin Zudeng of Yunfeng on Mount Tiantai was the son of the Wang family of Siming.
He studied under Rixi Yong at Tianning Monastery and asked: "The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift; I beg for your instruction.
Rixi said, "In the twelve periods of the day, investigate this closely and secretly. When you suddenly strike upon it, come back and ask again. The Master raised his voice and said, "Impermanence!"
"Swift! The matter of birth and death is great. Before he had finished speaking, Xī gave a shout. The Master prostrated. Xī asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate?
The Master replied, "To open one's mouth is already an error. Xī nodded in approval. Later, he planted his staff at Yunfeng and did not emerge from the mountain for fifty years.
On the eighth day of the second month in the second year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness. The assembly requested—
The verse reads: "Arising and ceasing, coming and going, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. Having toppled the five Sumerus, all is vast and open, without front or back.

Chan Master Xueting of Xianlin Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Gui family of Renhe. Having left home life, he went to visit Xiuxiu at Xianlin; upon seeing him, they reached a mutual accord.
Later, hearing the sound of a bell, he attained great enlightenment and spoke this verse: "The perfect resonance is not heard by the mind; The great trichiliocosm is illuminated as one.
Having brushed past the ultimate barrier, No further mysteries or subtleties remain. Xiuxiu certified his realization and instructed the assembly.
He cites the anecdote of Baizhang’s tending of the fire and Huangbo’s (Tiaoshan) subsequent enlightenment, commenting: "Whether the family is poor or rich, only father and son know;

Hehe! The old man did not cease his efforts, and the youth did not fail to exert himself."
