"It is said that all Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas emerge from this sutra. What is this sutra? The Master replied: "Recite it constantly."

"It does not cease; it is neither meaning nor sound. [The student] asked, "How then should one receive and uphold it? The Master said, "If you wish to receive and uphold it, you must listen with your eyes."
The abbot of Huiri Hermitage in Yongfeng, Xinzhou, was the son of the Qiu family of that same prefecture. He left home at the age of seven and received full ordination at Mingxin Temple.
Having attained spiritual resonance with Yunju, he traveled extensively through the regions of Xiang and Han before returning to Yongfeng, where he sometimes dwelt among the crags and valleys.
He lived in a marketplace, where the local people called him Master Qiu Shibo. Whenever anyone questioned him, he would answer with "I do not know.
One day, he suddenly said to the villagers, "I am going on a pilgrimage tomorrow; you all should come to see me off.

Thereupon, those who wished to provide offerings for the journey gathered in full. The Master laughed incessantly. When the crowd asked him the reason, he immediately wrote this verse: "Master Qiu Shibo does not know."
"Dawn! Silent and still, bright and clear. At midday, three watches are struck. Who can strike them all? Having said this, he threw down his brush and passed away.
Chan Master Yongcheng of Nanfeng in Quanzhou addressed the assembly: "From Mount Jiji, the flame was continued; from Shaoshi, the fragrance flowed."
He spreads the great clouds of compassion and widely opens the sun of wisdom. The teachings are divided into the Three Piṭakas, yet they point directly to the One Mind.
Sometimes he fully raises [the teaching] while simultaneously applying the staff and the shout; sometimes he employs granting and revoking while establishing the roles of host and guest.

Whether it be the Vajra pressing its sword or the Lion turning over, whether it be illumination and function crashing like thunder or the sharp edge of the wit flashing like lightning—all these are nothing other than the excision of delusion and the opening up of the vast expanse.

Profound and subtle! Directly beneath, clarify the fundamental principle and reach the ground of reality. O worthy ones, only when you have reached this point may I allow even a single thread of a path to be discussed with you.
If it is otherwise, all will be mere interpretations based on the teacher; such a state is not the way.
Chan Master Zuquan of Daomiao in Tanzhou was a successor of Chan Master Daomiao Xiu. He was a native of the Wu clan of Fuzhou. A monk asked, "What is the house style of Daomiao?
The Master said, "The bamboo has joints above and below; the pine is green now as it was of old. The monk asked, "I do not know what is drunk therein."
"What are you eating? The Master said, "When hungry, I eat the jade-grained rice of the Excellency; when thirsty, I drink the tea from before the Shen-yun Granary.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Way has no fixed disorder; the Dharma is free from seeing and knowing. When words and phrases coincide, they have no fixed definition at all.

Since of old, there have been no overnight guests at the Dragon Gate; until now, the Bird Path has been cut off of all tracks. If you wish to understand the ultimate meaning within this, [look] into the fire..."
The cicada swallows the large insect. *Du!* [He] ascends the hall. "Rain falls, the steps are damp; when dry and sunny, the water does not flow.
A bird's nest is at the bottom of the vast sea; a fish leaps atop a rocky mountain. Among the assembly, there is much deliberation: "The first two lines are words of plain reality;
the latter two lines are talk beyond the ordinary. If you understand it thus, you will see only the jagged rocks. Not...
Seeing the jade scattered and fallen; if one sees the jade scattered and fallen, only then will one know the path is vast and expansive.
Heh! When a monk asked Chan Master Wenyuan of Nanyue Fuyan, "What is the Buddha? the Master spat directly in his face.
On the day Master Yungong of Nantai on Mount Nanyue ascended the hall for his inaugural sermon, he said: "Rarely encountered and difficult to meet—this is precisely the time.
Why is this so? Śākyamuni has already passed away, and Maitreya is not yet born. [He held up his whisk and] said:
'Right now, at this very moment, the Buddha-dharma is entirely contained within this whisk. Whether letting go or holding fast, everything depends on the occasion. Letting go..."
As the wind blows, the grass bends; even rubble and debris gleam with light. Shide and Hanshan nod their heads and clap their hands.
Held fast, there is no leakage of water; even refined gold loses its luster. Deshan and Linji swallow their breath and silence their voices.
At such a time, is it letting go? Is it holding fast? After a long silence, he said: "Look after five days."

Chan Master Shaojue Chunbai of Zhaojue Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture, successor to Chan Master Huangbo Xing, ascended the hall and said: "When cold, one turns toward the fire; when hot, one fans oneself;
when hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps. Therefore, there is the cypress tree before Zhaozhou’s courtyard and the bamboo grove behind Xiangyan’s ridge."
The pine tree. Since it was planted, it has had no other use than to draw in the pure breeze. But tell me: what is the ultimate reality?
Jiazi and Yichou are the metal within the sea; Bingyin and Dingmao are the fire within the furnace.
Chan Master Daoying of Jianfu Temple in Raoyou, successor to Chan Master Kaiyuan Qi, was asked by a monk: "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world?

The Master said: "A crystal vase holding flowers. The monk asked: "How was it after he appeared in the world? The Master said: "An agate bowl filled with fruit. The monk asked: "I do not yet understand..."
"Is the Master today the same as before, or is he different? The Master said, "He kicks over the vase and drags down the bowl. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Speaking in terms of the Way, speech is not permitted, nor is silence permitted. Even if one forgets both speech and silence, there is still no connection to it."
Why is this? There is no path within the phrase; the meaning resides within the phrase. It is neither intention nor non-intention, and it is beyond the reach of conceptual calculation.
If one is struck directly on the head with a single point and the eye opens wide at the crown of the skull, there is indeed a sense of swift realization here.
If, however, one lowers the head and seeks it within the root of intention, one will ultimately fail to grasp it. Thus one knows that all phenomena...

There is no root; those who seek its exhaustion err. The single source has cut off all traces; those who wish to return are lost. Behold the radiance of the ancient Buddhas and the majestic bearing of the former masters:
each and every one was manifested from within a state of desirelessness and non-reliance. At times, they were solitary, lofty, and sharply transcendent.
Ultimately, it cannot be grasped. At times, it is harmoniously fused and integrated, such that nothing at all can be perceived.
It never remains fixed in one place, nor is it bound to two ends. There is neither "is" nor "is not"; there is neither "non-is" nor "non-is-not.
To gain is to gain nothing; to lose is to lose nothing. It has never been separated by even a hair’s breadth, nor has it ever shifted by so much as a strand of silk. It is luminously clear.

The ancient road does not belong to the realm of the profound and subtle. Brought forth face-to-face, it passes by in a mere flash. It does not abide in the position of correctness; how could it fall into the path of deviation?
It does not tread upon the Great Way; how could it hasten toward a narrow trail? Drifting and wandering, what dwells there and what acts?

Turning back, nothing is encountered; looking before one, there is no counterpart. To contemplate universally with a single thought, all is vast, empty, and still. This is the essential core of the teaching, [transmitted by] the thousand sages.
It is not transmitted; it is directly and thoroughly understood. One transcends right where one is. Thus, in the state of bare, unadorned clarity, it is easy;
yet in the state of vivid, distinct awareness, it is difficult. Without being stained or defiled, one must simply strip away and cast off all attachments.

If one is the original hands and feet, letting go without grasping, that which does not return emits light and manifests auspicious signs in every instance, while in every instance all traces are erased and all footprints cut off.
Upon the pivot of the spiritual mechanism, there is no lingering; within words, there is nothing to reveal. Stirring it to the very bottom, it remains undisturbed.
The entire body strikes it, yet it does not shatter. Tell me, after all, what is this? How can it be so spiritually penetrating?
How can it be so extraordinary? How can it be so firm and certain? Friends, do not try to recognize its face;
there is no need to assign it a name, nor should you seek its location. Why? It has no location; it has no name; it is...
It has no face. As soon as a single thought of seeking arises, even if it be as small as a mote of dust, one is immediately separated by ten or five lifetimes.
If you further attempt to manage or contemplate it, you will only see it become increasingly chaotic and cluttered. It is better to let it remain free and at ease for a long time.
When it wishes to arise, it arises; when it wishes to abide, it abides. This is both the natural and the non-natural; this is both suchness and the non-such.
Suchness is itself profound stillness, yet it is not profound stillness; it is itself decay, yet it is not decay. There is no attachment to birth and no fear of death;
there is no seeking of Buddhas and no dread of Māras. One does not meet with Bodhi, nor does one dwell with afflictions. One does not accept a single dharma, nor does one reject a single dharma.
There is neither being-present nor not-being-present; it is neither separate nor not-separate. If one can see and realize it in this way, one is liberated.
"Kāśyapa is Kāśyapa; Dharma is Dharma. What does it have to do with me?

To speak in such a manner—when scrutinized within the school of the patch-robed monks, even one wearing a coarse skirt and straw sandals cannot avoid getting a bit of mud and water on oneself, let alone you all who further claim, 'This is a statement of plain reality,' or 'This is a gate of differentiation.'"
This is the pivotal mechanism; this is the root of the Way’s faculties and objects.
They teach and practice one another like people in a village of seven households passing along a secret code—what connection does it have to the truth? There is nothing to do; take care.

Lecturer Zunseng Youpeng of Quanzhou was the son of the Jiang family of that prefecture. Having been selected for his mastery of the scriptures at the age of seven, he shaved his head and studied extensively at various monastic academies.

He once composed commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which scholars revered. Yet, he always harbored doubts regarding the path of direct pointing by the Patriarchs;
thus, he frequently associated with Chan practitioners. One day, he went to visit Kaiyuan; before his foot had even crossed the threshold, [he experienced realization].
His mind suddenly attained realization. Yuanchu then asked, "Master, what have you come for? The Master replied, "I dare not treat my ears as noble and my eyes as base.
Yuanchu said, "Though you are old and venerable, why must you be like this? The Master said, "He who considers himself self-sufficient does not grow.
Yuanchu said, "I do not ask about your morning study of the *Avataṃsaka* and your night reading of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. What is the single phrase for the present moment? The Master—
[The Master] said, "The sun is exactly at noon. Yuan said, "Idle talk—say something more. The Master said, "Throughout my life I have relied on loyalty and trust;
today I leave myself to the wind and waves. Although it is so, as for the Master speaking thus, what connection does it have?
One must have the new precept-holder’s straw sandals worn. Yuan said, "I will let you pass here for now. But should you suddenly encounter Bodhidharma..."
The questioner asked, "How would you say it? The Master then gave a shout. Yuan said, "This lecturer, meeting the old monk today, has his qi surging up to the Ox and Dipper constellations.
The Master said, "A second offense will not be tolerated. Yuan clapped his hands and laughed loudly.
A monk asked Chan Master Shansui of Longwang Mountain in Tanzhou, a successor of Chan Master Weiyang Wei: "What is the realm of the Dragon King? The Master said, "The crystal palace.
The monk asked, "What is the Dragon King’s wish-fulfilling jewel? The Master said, "In the topknot upon his head. The monk... [continued].
[The monk] prostrated. The Master said, "Do not say that things are not as you wish.
A monk asked Zen Master Yongtai of Zhiyuan on Mount Huangbo in Ruizhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Cast in iron. The monk hesitated. The Master said, "Do you understand? The monk prostrated. The Master said, "Why [do you not...]"
It has always been thus.
Zen Master Huiri of Mount Lu ascended the hall and said: "There is no need to seek the mind; one must only cease [dualistic] views.
Although the Great Master of the Third Patriarch avoided the golden hook, he was unaware that he had already swallowed the red line. Huiri, however, is not like this.
There is no need to seek the Truth nor to cease all views; riding a bull backward, one enters the Buddha Hall. With a single blast from the herdsman’s flute, heaven and earth are vast and wide.
I bow my head to Gautama, the true Yellow-Faced One.
Chan Master Fayuan Ganshi’s Dharma heir, Chan Master Fada Baopian of Yuyang Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture, was a native of the Yu clan of Ruzhou.

A monk asked, "Please speak, Master, regarding the place where one does not fall into stages. The Master said, "A wax figure facing the fire. The monk asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "Thin."
At Chuchu, he first attained penetration.

Chan Master Yungai Zhi’s dharma successor was Chan Master Dafaru of Daochang Monastery in Anji Prefecture, a native of the Xu family of Quzhou. Having studied under Yungai, he attained enlightenment through the teachings of Fenyang.
The "Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality" (Shi zhi tong zhen). Commonly, it is said that the "Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality" is frequently discussed;
thus, the monastic communities refer to it as the "Ten Identicals. Both Shuian and Yuanji relied upon this teaching. Yuanji once praised it, saying: "A face of raw iron is difficult to approach;
in an ordinary step, he moves heaven and earth. Playfully grasping the 'Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality,' he does not fail Huanglong."
The Legitimate Bone-Descendant. Entering the hall, [the Master] said: "When cognitive vision establishes cognition, that is the root of ignorance.
When cognitive vision is without seeing, this is nirvana—taintless, truly pure. How could anything else be admitted within it? The Old Śākyamuni has laid himself down completely;
how shall his descendants of later generations receive and continue him? Do you wish to understand? The Way of Penetrating the Profound is not of the human world. Full.
"Look at the green mountains—where are they? and so forth.
Chan Master Baoshou Zuile of Fuzhou was a native of Gutian. He ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas are not real; they preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
The Bodhisattvas possess wisdom, yet their vision of nature is not clear. The white clouds have no intentionality, yet they... (He sprinkled [the water]).
It rains for the world; though the great earth has no sentient beings, it can cause all grasses and trees to grow. If you understand this, you still remain within the realm of conceptual cognition;
if you do not understand it, you fall into the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). How can one be identical to that which transcends these two paths?
The sea is so vast it cannot hide the moon; the mountains are so deep they are exceptionally cold.
A monk asked Chan Master Hui-ming Jie-kong of Shifo Monastery in Xiangzhou, “What is the realm of the Precious Marks?
The Master said, “Carved out over three lifetimes. The monk asked, “Who is within that realm? The Master said, “One Buddha and two Bodhisattvas.”

Chan Master Guanghui Da’ao of Fuzhou, successor to Chan Master Wenzhu of Xuansha, ascended the hall and said: "The Buddha awakens through a mind free of intention; it is because of the Buddha that the mind is deluded.
In the place where the Buddha-mind is pure and clear, a wild monkey cries beyond the clouds."
One day, Chan Master Yongyuan of Sizhou in Pingjiang Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Jianlong, asked Jianlong:

"When Linji was at Huangbo, he asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times and was struck three times. What was the intent behind this? Before he had even finished speaking, he was...

[The Master] struck his whisk once. The Master immediately grasped the essential meaning of the school. On the day he opened the hall for teaching, a monk asked: "The fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds;

we pray that the Master will preach the Dharma. The Master said: "Having eyes but no ears, sitting by the fire in the sixth month. [The monk] said: "A single phrase cuts off the current; ten thousand functions are suddenly stilled. The Master said:
"Listening to matters without clarity, one calls a bell a jar. [The monk] asked: "Morning attendance and evening requests—what is accomplished thereby?"
"What kind of peripheral matter is this? the Master said. "I only want you to come to rest. [The monk] said, "Had I known earlier that the lamp was fire, the rice would have been cooked long ago.
The Master said, "Why are your nostrils pierced by this staff? [The monk] said, "How could one possibly twist the crooked to make it straight?
The Master said, "Let him first get out his breath. He ascended the hall and said: "One, two, three, four, five—crickets in the fire."
The cicada swallows the tiger; six, seven, eight, nine, ten. A clay ox on the bottom of the water stands upon the waves.

Day and night the rain falls in torrents. An unperforated iron hammer cannot be soaked through. It cannot be soaked through—how urgent is the matter at hand! The hundred rivers surge and Mount Sumeru trembles.
Eight-armed Nātha comes crashing out, prostrating and praising it as something beyond reach. *Ei!* [He] ascended the hall.
Holding his staff horizontally, he looked at the assembly and said, "Today, we have met with a fall on level ground. He then descended from the seat.

Chan Master Yuanzheng Chuan deng of Chengtian Yong’an in Pingjiang Prefecture—a successor to Chan Master Baoben Yuan—was born into the Zheng family of Yanzhou. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
The multitudes of devas and humans all rely upon the power of this grace. Great assembly, there is one person who says: "I do not rely on the power of the Buddha's grace;
I do not dwell within the three realms, nor am I subject to the five elements. The Patriarchs dare not define me, and the Buddhas of the past dare not bestow a name upon me.
Tell me, who is this person? After a long silence, he said: "Leaning against a stone cliff, he burns his iron bowl."
A copper pitcher was propped against a pine branch.

Chan Master Wen Yi of Qin-ning in An-hua, Tanzhou, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Longqing Xian, ascended the hall and said: "Plucking the flower and smiling—this was a vain exertion of effort. He stood.
"Snow reaching the waist is a labor spent in vain. How does it compare to Old Lu, who had no use for such things? Yet he transmitted the robe and bowl to stir up the true wind.
"Great assembly, tell me: which is the robe and bowl transmitted by Old Lu? Is it that which could not be lifted at the head of Mount Dayu?
Do not mistakenly fixate on the zero point of the scale. [He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat.]

Zen Master Weishuang of Kuangxiao Temple in Ningguo Prefecture, a Dharma heir of the Third Patriarch Zongcan, ascended the hall and said: "Today is the first day of the sixth month; half the year has already passed.
I inform you seekers of the profound mystery: recognize your mother’s face. Whether you can realize your mother’s face or not—look! A heron flies by."
Entering the azure waves, he shakes out a ball of silver-embroidered thread.
Zen Master Qitian, successor to Zen Master Ying of Lestam, was asked by a monk: "I, a student, have come before you; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said:
“Did you just hear the sound of the drum? The monk replied, “I heard it. The Master said, “Give me back the head of this dialogue.
The monk bowed. The Master said, “This will leave people in doubt. He ascended the hall, let out a shout, and said, “The lion’s roar! Then he let out another shout and said:
The Elephant King let out a yawn and then gave a roar, saying, "A mad dog chasing a clod of earth. He roared again, saying, "A shrimp cannot leap out of its basket.
Then he said, "Of these four roars, there is one that is fit to be the teacher of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Let those with clear eyes, you monks, try to discern which it is.
If you cannot discern it, you are much like one who has lost his way in broad daylight. He ascended the hall and, after a long silence, said:

His nature was tranquil and his spirit carefree. He then let out a shout, saying, "The mind is stirred and the spirit grows weary. He then looked to his left and right and said, "Guarding the truth, one’s will is fulfilled.

Picking up his staff, he said, "Chasing after objects, the intention shifts. Suddenly calling to the assembly, he said, "If you do not find strange things strange, the strangeness will vanish of its own accord.
Leaning on his staff, he descended from the seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Yun of Huiming in Quanzhou, "Within the ocean of Prajñā, how do you act for the sake of others?
The Master said, "The clouds part and the Milky Way stretches far. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master said, "Seeing blood at the tip of the staff.

Another asked, "Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon it long ago, yet until this very day he has not attained the wondrous. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "It is so ugly and clumsy it is unbearable."
At that time,
Chan Master Wujie Jingtan of Yuyang Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Baoning Ji. He was a native of Jiahe and later returned to Qiantang.
On one day, Fahui ascended the hall and said: "By nature I have long lain amidst the white clouds in the deep mountains;
by chance I have come here to lodge my idle body. Do not come to ask me about Chan or the Way; I am but a man who eats rice and voids excrement.

In the summer of the Bingyin year of the Xiangxing era, he took leave of the court nobility and returned to hand over the affairs of the monastery. The fourfold assembly crowded around to watch him as he waved his fan for a long time, then wrote this verse: "This fellow from..."

Coming and going, there is no seam or fissure. For fifty-six years he has established his reputation as a master. Today he dies and meets King Yama; the Sword-Trees and Knife-Mountains strike fear into all.
He then drew a circle and said, "Ha! Let the various quarters do as they please—drilling tortoises and beating tiles."
He passed away with his legs drawn up; after the cremation, his *śarīra* were like falling sleet. His disciples took the bones and returned to Mount Aśoka to erect a stūpa.
Chan Master Jiexiang of Zhenru Temple in Taizhou, a native of the Lin clan of Xinghua, ascended the hall and said: "The dawn of early winter has changed."
The weather is cold; leaves fall and return to their roots, revealing distant mountains. This is not a phenomenon of seeing, hearing, arising, or ceasing;
do not look upon it as seeing and hearing.
—A Dharma Successor of Chan Master Wuzu Fanchen.
A monk asked Chan Master Chushi Qing of Nanyuaya Shousheng in Qizhou, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go?
The Master said, "The waters at Lingfeng are swift. The monk said, "In that case, he is not reborn? The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven!"
Chan Master Weigu of Baizhang in Ruizhou, successor to Chan Master Huanglong Su, ascended the hall. Once the assembly had gathered and settled, he held up his staff and showed it to them, saying:
"Much emptiness is not as good as a little reality.
*He struck once and immediately rose.* The monks of the Chan Master Yuezhu Zu Jian of Jiading Prefecture requested the master’s essential words for their records. The master said:

"When Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted the mind-seal alone. The Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi did not recognize a single character. Today, the words used by those appearing in the world in various quarters—"
The words are like mountains; they further increase the binding ropes. Then, striking the meditation seat, he said: "If you can realize it here, you are still of dull faculties.
If you have not yet attained this, then sleep as you please in the depths of the white clouds—just do not let the cold monkeys howl at midnight."
A monk asked Master Shi, the Abbot of Jingzhao Hermitage, a dharma successor of Chan Master Shilang Lin: "Who is the master of this hermitage? The Master said:

"I have never permitted this from the beginning. When the monk hesitated, the Master said, "If you understand, then you understand; that which is original cannot be established through names or characters.
As the monk was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him out. In his quarters, the Master would constantly hold up his whisk for the assembly, saying:
"If you call it a whisk, it is still not it. If you do not call it a whisk, you are willfully ignorant. What do you call it?"
"What are you doing? [The Master asked] because a monk had requested instruction. The Master answered him with a verse: "I have a single fly-whisk;
in its use, there is no other contrivance. Sometimes it hangs from a pine branch, letting its head dangle in the dew."
Chan Master Nian of Wanshou Monastery in Chenzhou, successor to Chan Master Huaguang Gong, was asked by a monk: "The peerless assembly of the Dragon Flower has just begun this morning.
I wonder, in what place does the World-Honored One Maitreya currently reside? The Master replied, "At the head of the pork stall. The monk said, "If that is the World-Honored One Maitreya..."
"Why are you at the pork stall? The Master said, "If you are not one who plays in the tide, do not enter the great waves.
[The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what then is the matter? The Master said, "The barbarian does not tie his sash. On New Year's Day, he ascended the hall.
Coming and going are boundless; movement and stillness share a single source. It contains virtue yet returns to emptiness; it transcends selflessness and stands far apart.
The sun of yesterday and the sun of today shine with no duality of light; the wind of yesterday and the wind of today blow with no duality of motion.
It rained yesterday and it rains today; the moisture does not double its wetness. Within this interval, one seeks the marks of coming and going but cannot find them.
Why? When the minds of self and other arise, there is no trace at the place of their arising. When the mind of self is forgotten, there is no mark of extinction in that forgetting.
If the great assembly can understand it here, you will share the same root as heaven and earth and be one body with all things.
If you have not yet attained clarity, this mountain monk shall expound it for you verse by verse. First Verse on the First Day of the New Year:

The ancient Buddha’s家风 (family style) emerges from this; No need to labor toward the ultimate. Throughout kalpas, how has it ever been different from today? Second Verse on the First Day of the New Year: Silent...
Desolate and cold, devoid of flavor. Zhaozhou calls out, "Come, let us drink tea. Raising your eyebrows, you must have a sudden flash of insight.
On the third day of the New Year, I prostrate and offer greetings to all who have come. If you ask about the affairs within Mount Xiangshan, the stream of Lingyuan flows as blue as indigo.
(He gives a shout and descends from his seat.)

The lay practitioner Su Che, style name Ziyou, was a successor of Chan Master Shun of Shanglan. In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, while serving as an official in Suizhou, he was demoted to the post of salt and liquor tax collector in Ruizhou.
At that time, Chan Master Shun of Shanglan in Hongzhou was [the teacher] of his father, Wen’an.

The Master had a karmic affinity with him, so he went to visit him. They found great joy in meeting one another. The Master consulted him regarding the Dharma of the mind, and [Zhaozhou] accordingly showed him the karmic conditions of "pinching the nose.
Thereupon, he attained realization and presented this verse: "In middle age I heard the Way and realized my former errors; By chance I have met the Elder Master Shun.
Pinching the nose, I directly penetrated the true countenance; Shaking my head, I will not accept any other tongs or hammers. [He then left for] Kū... (text fragmentary)
Master Tōhabunaru, what is your business? White wine and green salt—who am I? With shame before the waning moon over the eastern eaves, I drink a cup of nectar as smooth as molasses.

The Dharma successor of Chan Master Huanglong Xin of the fourteenth generation under Nanyue, Chan Master Chaozong Huifang of Heshan in Jizhou, ascended the hall and held up his whisk, saying: "Look, look! It is just this."
This "One" (箇): in Linji, illumination and function proceed together; in Yunmen, principle and phenomenon are both complete;
in Caodong, the biased and the correct harmonize and penetrate; in Guishan, the hidden mechanism is perfectly integrated; and in Fayan, how could it be merely "mind-only"?
Nevertheless, while the formal arrangements and pedagogical devices of these five houses are not without their distinctions, even if one were able to discern them with such boldness and clarity—
"Understanding departure is still a matter of shadows and light. If you wish to resist birth and death, there is a world of difference between them.
Now, as for the single phrase 'transcending birth and death,' how would you say it? After a long silence, he said, "I have nearly provided a mistaken commentary."
Chan Master Chongjue Kong of Lin’an Prefecture was a native of Gushu. He ascended the hall and said: "The ten directions have no walls; the four sides have no gates.
Pure and naked, bright and clear—there is nothing to grasp. He then raised his whisk and said:
"The old fellow Guǎngxī used to flaunt his elegance on the crossroads, selling his cleverness by saying, 'I know how to thread pearls.'"
Jade tablets; tangled silk from the Huai River rolled upon bamboo tubes; brothels and wine shops; commoners and servants gathered like broken tiles;
tiger dens and demon palaces; Nanda and Kāla-Kumbhaka in their wrath. Encountering King Wen, they promoted rites and music; meeting Jie and Zhou, they displayed arms and shields.
Today, having been spotted by Chongjue, they are left utterly humiliated. The Master composed a verse on the "Wild Fox" kōan, saying: "Spitting blood at others first soils one's own mouth."
Mouth. Baizhang’s wild fox lost its head and ran madly; suddenly called back, it performed a somersault.
Chan Master Zu Xiuzhen of Shangfeng in Tanzhou, a native of the He family of Changde Prefecture, ascended the hall and said:
"Before the cliff of the withered tree, the night-blooming flower opens; the iron ox still lies in the misty sands. I bring forth once more the shadow of the whip. [He struck his whisk.]
He said, "A single thought of turning the mind is arriving home. He then gave a shout and descended from his seat.
A monk asked Zen Master Jixing Huiquan of Jiuding in Jiading Prefecture, "When the mind is deluded, the *Lotus Sūtra* revolves;

when the mind awakens, one revolves the *Lotus Sūtra*. I do not know what the meaning of this is. The Master said, "The wind is warm and the birds' songs shatter; the sun is high and the flower shadows shift."

[The Master] ascends the hall and says: "In the past, Yunmen had three phrases: the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth, the phrase that cuts off all streams, and the phrase that follows the waves and rides the currents.
Today, Jiuding also has three phrases: namely, the phrase 'when hungry, eat';
the phrase 'when cold, turn toward the fire'; and the phrase 'when weary, lie down to sleep. If one discusses this in terms of the Buddha-dharma, then Jiuding—"
"Yunmen faces Jiuding directly and stands downwind. If one were to discuss this according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), then Yunmen faces Jiuding directly and stands downwind;
these two statements are contradictory. Furthermore, what is the point at which Jiuding acts for others?

The Chan Master Xingkong Miaopu of Huating, Jiaxing Prefecture, was a native of Hanzhou. Having long relied upon Siji (Sicong) to attain realization, he traveled to Xiushui to follow the legacy of Chuanshi (Zhaozhou).
He built a thatched hut in the wilds of Qinglong and amused himself by blowing an iron flute;
those who obtained his many poetic compositions would invariably treasure them. One of his mountain retreat poems says: "When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, one is still separated..."
"Delusion! When the single dust of form does not exist, what remains of the other sense-objects? A hundred birds do not come, and spring passes away again;

one does not know who is the person dwelling in the hermitage. He further admonished the assembly, saying: "Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city: by day, defend against the six thieves; by night, remain alert."
The commander of the central army can carry out his orders; without moving a blade of grass or a drop of blood, he brings about Great Peace. It is also said:

"Eating without plowing and wearing clothes without sericulture—tranquil and at ease beyond the mundane world during this sagely age. Yet, if you have not yet passed through the master’s pivotal gate, you must still maintain your intent and act with expedient skill.
It is further said: "In the twelve hours of the day, do not cease your work; exhaust it, exhaust it until there is nothing left to exhaust."
One must penetrate thoroughly to the bottomless depths; one must trample down the first peak of Mount Sumeru.
At the beginning of the Jianyan era, Xu Ming rebelled and passed through Wuzhen, carrying out widespread slaughter. Many of the local people fled, but the Master alone went forth carrying his staff.

When the rebels saw his imposing and extraordinary appearance, they suspected he was a hidden partisan and asked him where he was going. The Master replied, "I am a Chan practitioner; I wish to go to Mijin Temple."
The bandits were enraged and intended to execute him. The Master said, "If a great man desires his head, simply chop it off; why resort to anger? My death is certain.
I wish only for a single meal as a parting gift. The bandits served him meat and rice. The Master ate as he normally would during a vegetarian fast.
After finishing the meal, he asked, "Who shall compose a literary inscription for my sacrifice? The bandits laughed but did not answer. The Master then requested a brush.
He wrote in large characters: "Alas! That the numinous spirit exhausts me with life is the fault of the Great Mass; that it employs me with longevity is the error of Yin and Yang;
that it deprives me of wealth is due to the irregularity of the Five Elements; that it afflicts me with destiny is because the timing of the days was not auspicious.
How lamentable! How ultimate! Fortunately, there is the Way that transcends the mundane, which allows me to awaken to my own nature and its wondrousness."

As for the mind—how could its wondrous mind have anything with which to neighbor? Above, it accords with the true transformation of all Buddhas; below, it merges with the ignorance of ordinary beings.
Not a speck of dust moves; it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. How wondrous! How wondrous! The sun and moon are not sufficient to be called luminous;
heaven and earth are not sufficient to be called great. It is vast and unimpeded, without obstruction or hindrance. Six.
For over ten years he harmonized with the light and mingled with the mundane; at forty-two *lǎ* (years since ordination), he roamed at ease and lived in freedom.
He greeted people with joy, yet did not bow before the Buddha. "How joyful! How joyful! Alas for this young man, his elegance was so radiant.

Returning with composure, he entrusted himself to the spring breeze; his body, like empty space, shall ultimately never decay. "May you enjoy this! Having said this, he raised his chopsticks and ate heartily.
The bandits laughed aloud. After they had finished eating, he said again, "Since we have encountered this era of calamity and chaos, I am a man of joyous vigor.
Now is precisely the time to act; I pray you, let me cut you in two with a single stroke. He then shouted, "Strike! Strike! Only then did the bandits realize his extraordinary nature;
they bowed their heads in repentance for their transgression and ordered guards to escort him out. Thus, the houses of Wuzhen were spared from burning; this was truly the Master’s kindness.

When both the clergy and the laity heard this, their reverence for him increased all the more. There was a monk who saw the Master seeing the Buddha and not bowing; he sang out in protest and asked, "Since you have seen the Buddha, why do you not bow?
The Master struck him with his palm and said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master struck him again with his palm and said: [The story concludes here].
"A household has no two masters. In the winter of the Gengshen year of the Xiangshi era, he hollowed out a large basin and plugged it up.
He wrote a letter to Chan Master Chi of Xuedou, saying: "I shall undergo water burial. When Chi arrived in the Renxu year, he saw that [the basin] still remained.
He composed a verse to mock him, saying: "Alas, Old Xingkong! You insist on feeding the fish and turtles. If you will not go with a resolute heart, then..."
He told this to others. When the Master read the verse, he laughed and said, "Wait until your elder brother returns to verify it next year; then have him announce it to the fourfold assembly.
When the assembly had gathered, the Master preached the essentials of the Dharma for them, and further spoke this verse: "To die while sitting or standing is not as good as water burial.
First, it saves the need for firewood; second, it saves the digging of a grave. To cast off one's hands and go forth—how unimpeded and exhilarating! Who is the one who knows this? A boat."
Master Zi’s lofty spirit is difficult to emulate after a thousand years; few now sing his single verse of fisherman’s song.
He then sat cross-legged within a basin and drifted downstream with the tide. The assembly followed him all the way to the seashore, their gaze following him until it was lost.

The Master took a piece of *xi* rhinoceros horn to plug the opening and returned; the crowd crowded around to watch, yet no water entered. He then resumed his drift with the current, singing: "The boatman..."

He returned to his hometown in the year [blank]. His traces vanished, and his wondrousness was difficult to measure. The true wind of his teaching spread far and wide among those who could appreciate it;

he played his iron flute crosswise as a finale to his performance. The sound of that flute was mournful and choked. Shortly thereafter, amidst the vast expanse, he was seen throwing his flute into the air and vanishing.
The multitude sighed with longing and worshipped an image of him. Three days later, he appeared on the sand, sitting in the lotus posture as if alive. Thus ends the account of Dao.

The laity vied with one another to go and welcome him back, and he remained for five days. He was cremated, and the *śarīra* relics were as numerous as they could not be counted, each as large as a bean.
Two cranes circled in the air and only departed when the fire had gone out. The assembly enshrined the *śarīra* and sacred bones, constructing a stupa at Qinglong.
The Head Seat Daolong of Zhongshan in Yanzhou was the son of the Dong family of Tonglu. He received full ordination at Zhongshan Temple.

Having traveled widely, he was esteemed and held in high regard by the venerable monks wherever he went. In his later years, he arrived at Huanglong, where Sijian Huiyuan (Sixin) invited him to serve as the Head of the Assembly (*zuoyuan*).
After Huiyuan passed away, Daolong returned to seclusion at Zhongshan. Admiring the world-transcending character of the Venerable Master Chen, he bolted his door and withdrew from worldly affairs.
He would sell his yarn several times a day for his own amusement, and no one recognized him. He always wore a single sock on one hand.
Whenever a Chan practitioner arrived, he would hold it up and show it to them, saying, "I have been wearing this sock for thirty years. A monk from a local temple asked him jokingly:
"What is the samādhi of non-contention? The Master then struck him with his palm.
The head seat Qi Mi of Yangzhou was a native of that very prefecture; Sijian (Dead Heart) called him a "thorough practitioner.
Several scholars repeatedly invited him to a famous mountain, but he would not go. Later, he manifested his passing at Gushan in Tan. His miraculous traces were numerous. His disciples...
Once, he had his portrait painted and requested a eulogy. I wrote for him: "This fellow, with his ash-grey head and mud-stained face, usually does not wish to reveal himself.
Now that he has been brought before people by means of a painting, it is much like shooting an arrow into empty space. How vexing! What a pity—that three feet of silk from the human world."
The practitioner of the Empty Chamber, Zhītōng, was the daughter of Fàn Xūn, a Grand Marshal of the Dragon Diagram (Lóngtú).

From childhood she was intelligent and wise; as she grew up, she married Tí, the grandson of Chancellor Sū Sòng. Before long, she grew weary of worldly phenomena and returned home to seek ordination. Her father opposed this, so she instead pursued pure cultivation.

Upon contemplating the *Fǎjiè Guān* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm), she suddenly attained realization and composed two successive verses to express her insight. The first says: Vast and boundless is the dust of the world...

The central essence is one suchness; vertically and horizontally, they interpenetrate and seal Vairocana. The entire wave is water, yet the wave is not water; the entire water becomes waves, yet the water remains distinct.
It is further said: "Objects and self are fundamentally non-different; the myriad phenomena are like reflections in a mirror.

Clearly manifest, they transcend the roles of principal and attendant; perfectly realized, they penetrate the true void. A single entity contains manifold dharmas, interlacing within the net of Indra, layer upon layer without end."

At the point of ultimate exhaustion, both movement and stillness are entirely pervasive and unobstructed. Later, when his parents had both passed away, his elder brother Jüan took up a post as the Commandant of Féníng.
Tōng accompanied him there. Having heard of the name of Sīxīn, he went once more to pay his respects. Upon meeting him, Sīxīn perceived what Tōng had attained and immediately asked:
"When the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita sold his heart and liver, whom did he teach to study Prajñā? Tōng replied: "If you have no mind, then I shall also rest. Furthermore—
Question: "When moistened by the same rain, the roots and sprouts differ. Upon a ground where there is neither yin nor yang, what grows?
Tong said: "One flower with five petals. He asked again: "Throughout the twelve hours of the day, in what place do you establish yourself and sustain your life? Tong said:
"Preceptor, you had better cherish your eyebrows," he said. Xinghua struck him, saying, "This woman is creating disorder out of sequence.
She then performed a full prostration, and Xinghua approved. Thereupon, his reputation spread far and wide. During the Zhenghe era, he resided in Jinling.

Once, while providing a communal bath at Baoning Temple, he posted a notice on the gate that read: "If there is not a single thing, what is there to wash? If even a speck of dust exists, it arises from..."
"Where have you come from? You must first grasp a single phrase of the profound mystery; only then can everyone enter the bath together. Guling only knew how to rub backs;
the Bodhisattva has never yet clarified his mind. When one wishes to realize the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, it is necessary for sweat to break out over the entire body. Thus they all say.
Water can wash away filth; how could one know that water itself is also dust? Even if the filth and the water were suddenly removed, even reaching this state, one must still wash it away.
Later, she became a *bhikṣuṇī* named Wéijiu. She hung up her staff at Xizhú in Gūsū. Among those who received instruction from her day and night, there were many who attained the Way.
Suddenly, manifesting illness, she wrote a verse and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. There is a record titled the *Míngxīn Lù*.

Chan Master Focin Cai of Shangfeng in Tanzhou was a successor of Chan Master Huanglong Qing.
He was the son of the Yao family of Fuzhou; he received the tonsure in his youth and later received full ordination before traveling abroad.
Later, while staying with Chan Master Haiyin Long during the Dazhong era, Fang encountered the elder practitioner Yuan Daozhe. As the latter was reading a sutra, he came upon the passage:
"Within a single hair-tip of a lion, ten billion hair-tips appear all at once. The Master pointed to it and asked: "As for this 'single hair-tip of a lion'..."

"How can one cause the hundred billion hairs on the body to manifest all at once? Da said, "You have only just entered the monastic community; how can you immediately concern yourself with such matters?

The Master, harboring doubts because of this, subsequently resolved to take up the position of *jingtou* (sanitation officer). One night, while he was sweeping, Yinyuan happened to be giving a night lecture.
Upon arriving, he encountered the conclusion of the session. Throwing down his staff, Yinyuan said, "If you understand, then even the tip of a hair can swallow a giant mountain."
"O Sea! Only now do I realize that the great earth is but a single mote of dust. At these words, the Master attained a sudden awakening.
He then traveled from Min to Mount Huanglong in Yuzhang, but his intellectual rapport with Sīxīn did not harmonize. He subsequently went to attend on Língyuán.

Whenever he entered the inner chamber for instruction and emerged, he would invariably weep and reproach himself, saying: "I see this matter very clearly, yet when the moment arrives, I cannot bring it forth. What can be done?"

Lingyuan knew that his teacher was diligent and earnestly told him that he must achieve a great penetration (*dachè*) before he could attain mastery. Not long after, he happened to observe a monk at the neighboring desk reading the *Extensive Record of Caodong*. "Ma! Shan drew his knife and made a gesture as if to strike. The Master suddenly smiled with delight and slapped a monk at the neighboring table.

In the four directions and eight corners there is no obstruction; the myriad phenomena all simultaneously reveal themselves. Later, he shared the teaching seat with Zhencheng and received the posthumous title Shangfeng.
His life was marked by frequent transfers between famous monasteries. While residing at Qianyuan Temple, he ascended the hall to address the assembly, saying:

"The myriad gates of hundreds of thousands of samādhis, the infinite treasury of merit and virtue—when let go, it is like opening a military arsenal where weapons flash and gleam in chaotic brilliance;

when held fast, it is like snow covering reeds, such that one's entire being cannot be discerned. Let those who see this lift themselves up and depart immediately; let those who hear this take up the single blade."
Directly enter! Each one possesses the true eye atop the head; every person hangs the numinous talisman from behind the elbow.
Sweeping away the perceptions and knowledge of Buddhas and patriarchs, they act as a calamity and harm to the monastic groves. I recall the day Bao-shou opened the hall:
San-sheng pushed forward a monk, and Bao-shou struck him immediately. San-sheng said, "If you act as a teacher in this way, you will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou."
Furthermore, for instance, today at the opening of the hall, if any monk comes forward, I shall strike him as well.
Not only will this story become widely circulated, but it is also intended to open the eyes of the people of the entire city of Fuzhou. Why?
Because "The sword leaves its precious scabbard because of injustice; the medicine emerges from the golden jar to save the sick. [Ascending the hall: Before Bodhidharma came to this eastern land...
Everyone cherishes the pearl from the waters of Maitreya; every single person embraces the raw jade of Mount Jing. It may be said that they stand like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms.
Yet, after the Second Patriarch performed his three prostrations, each one went south to seek instruction from their companions and north to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
"What a fine great man! There may be one or two who do not seek after the sages and do not prize their own spiritual nature;

'Since I have not yet returned, when I return it shall be attained; who can vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes? [He] ascended the hall: 'The proclamation of the Dharma-lineage is wondrous beyond words.'"

A single phrase is all-pervasive; heaven and earth are contained within its lid. It is like the central eye of Śiva protruding from his face, or like the three dots of a circle spanning the Dharma-realm horizontally.
Then, striking the meditation staff upright, he said: "If you can understand clearly beneath this very dot..."
"One's origins may still be changed; but to cast off the body and respond to the Way must be difficult. Again, he struck the meditation staff and said:

"If you can understand it beneath the third dot, the fish and dragons lock their doors and the Buddhas and Patriarchs hide their traces. Otherwise, let this one move pass by as it is."
There is. A single branch of spring blossoms with three or four flowers. [The Master] ascends the hall: "One Dharma has form, encompassing both the moving and the planted;
the hundred rivers rush and surge, competing to flow toward the source. The zither of Shaozhao is not struck, and the clouds and sky are serene; I imagine the old, sickly gentleman of Vaiśālī.
When Vimalakīrti is ill, Shangfeng is ill; when Shangfeng is ill, the staff is ill; when the staff is ill, all that is dense and vast is ill."
The myriad phenomena are ill. When the myriad phenomena of the forest and the stars are ill, then both the ordinary and the sage are ill.

Do you all perceive the place where the root of this illness arises? If you do perceive it, then the sentient and the insentient are of one and the same body; everywhere is identical to the true Dharma-realm.
If this is not yet so, then the sweet melon is sweet to its very stem, and the bitter gourd is bitter down to its roots.
Chan Master Tongzhao Hedefeng of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Hu family of Jing’an in the prefecture. He was born with thick eyebrows.
At the age of seventeen, he received the tonsure under Chan Master Jin of Shanglan and subsequently relied upon Linyuan, where he immediately realized the profound meaning [of the teachings].
Once, while ascending the hall, he cited the "Jiangshan’s Realm" koan and said: "Fayan merely had these words, yet he did not realize that Jiangshan..."
This old mountain man, being lightly pressed by this monk, was driven to his wits' end, with his feet shuffling before and behind him.
Even if one does not interpret this as a "boundary-phrase" (jinghua), one cannot avoid still being halfway there.

Chan Master Yingduan of Falun Monastery in Tanzhou was the son of the Xu family of Nanchang. In his youth, he relied upon Master Shanyue at Huadu Monastery, where he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He visited Chan Master Zhenjing Wen, but their karmic connection did not harmonize. Upon arriving at Yunju, he encountered Master Lingyuan, who sat on the high seat to inspire the assembly;
the Master questioned him regarding the essential meaning. However, he prided himself on having entered the various sutras with subtle insight. Master Lingyuan once gave him a severe reprimand.
The Master then cited the dialogues between Mazu and Baizhang, as well as the essential tenets of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, as his written testimony.
Yuan laughed and said, "Mazu and Baizhang were certainly mistaken; however, the tenets of the Avataṃsaka have no connection whatsoever with this matter.

The Master became indignant and wished to leave for another place, so he requested leave to depart. As he lifted the curtain, he suddenly attained great enlightenment, and sweat poured down his back. Yuan saw him—
He then said, "This man recognizes good and evil. Mazu and Baizhang—Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra—were nearly brought to ruin by you.

From this point on, his reputation spread in all directions, and though scholars vied with one another to entreat him to appear in the world, he declined them all. Toward the end of the Zhenghe era, he passed away.
The Grand Preceptor Zhang Gongsheng, having been firmly commanded by Baizhang to open the Dharma, could not refuse and finally complied.
He ascended the hall and, citing the story of the "Great Sui Kalpa Fire Blazing," said: "The six realms of existence overturn and come crashing against my face;
