Chan Master Zhongfang Tianlun of Baoning Monastery in Jinling was a son of the Zhang family of Xiangshan. He studied under Huiji, who asked him:
The lake and mountains are lush and verdant; the lake waters flow vast and wide. They soak and rot your nostrils; they block and pierce your eyes.
Why do you not know? The Master said: "Throughout the entire body there is no reflected image; at every step, all traces of movement are cut off. Jiji said: "Not yet—speak further."
The Master shook out his sleeves and departed. [Zhaozhou] subsequently sat at the teacher’s feet and repeatedly questioned him about this matter, but the Master never spoke of it.
He then went to the Peach Blossom Grove in Wuxing, where he thatched a hut. One day, upon hearing a clap of thunder, he attained realization and clearly saw the working of Master Huikai.
Ascending the hall: Three at the beginning, eleven at the end; nine in the middle, seven at the bottom. Seven times nine is sixty-three; nine times nine is eighty-one.
In the morning one departs for the Western Heaven; in the evening one returns to the Eastern Land. One horse gives birth to three tigers; the stone ox guards the ancient path. *Chan*.

Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month: Last night, seeing the morning star, he awakened to the Way. In the back garden, the wind blew and the fence fell down. At dawn, there is nothing.
The traces may still be followed; the Snow Mountains remain as they were, growing green grass. Entering the hall, he said: "The teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon.
Yesterday someone came from Xizhou and received news from Dongzhou, reporting that a man from the kingdom of Daśapura is selling incense and medicine upon his own eyelashes. He gave a shout.
Chan Master Zu Ying of the Stone Chamber at Yuwang in Mingzhou was the son of the Chen family of Wujiang. He entered the monastic life in his childhood and immediately went to visit Huiji;
upon their first meeting, they reached a profound accord. He offered this verse in response to Chan Master Pingshi Di’s inquiry regarding his illness:

"This body is without self, yet the roots of my illness run deep. I am ashamed that Mañjuśrī has come so far to visit me. There are naturally the mountain flowers discussing non-duality; the green lamp..."
Smiling broadly, he faced his end and addressed the assembly, saying: "For fifty-three years, I have been cleverly playing tricks until I became clumsy;
I have trodden through empty space walking barefoot. The myriad phenomena and all living beings cannot help but laugh."
Chan Master Niangchang Meiwu of Xiangfu Temple in Jiaxing Prefecture was the son of the Huang family of Huating. At the age of twelve, he received full ordination.

In the year Dushen of the Zhida era (1308), he went to study under Huiji. He happened upon Huiji ascending the hall, where Huiji cited the karmic anecdote of Elder Fu hearing the sound of a horn, and offered this verse:
"Qinsheng entered the vast ocean; the Grand Historian traveled to famous mountains. From this point on, outside the city walls of Yangzhou..."
On the road, the official Yan ordered that the gates not be opened early. Upon these words, the Master attained realization. He went to the abbot’s quarters to communicate what he had gained;

the abbot nodded in approval and appointed him as head of the secretariat. He served diligently for seven years. In the year of Bingchen of the Yanyou era, he presided over Xiangfu Temple and authored the twenty-two fascicles of the *Fozu Tongzai* (Comprehensive Record of Buddhas and Patriarchs), which was circulated in the world.
Chan Master Wuwai Zongkuo of Donglin in Jiangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Lingyin Yin. He was the son of the Wei family of Nanchang. He went to visit Yue Tang, who asked him:
"The sound of the mountain stream is entirely the broad and long tongue. Their spiritual resonance and dialogue were in perfect accord, and he was subsequently granted a seal of certification.
He first resided at Yunju and later moved to Donglin. His verse on parting from this world says: "At the age of seventy-one, my worldly ties have now come to an end.
Having pushed through to the five Sumeru mountains, the sun rises at midnight. He then passed away in silence.

Master Mengshan Yi, a dharma successor of Master Ningshan of Gushan, went to visit Master Wanshan. He investigated the "Mu" (No) kōan but had not yet attained realization. He then went to Chengtian Temple to pay his respects to Guchan Ying.
While the head seat was entering the hall to burn incense, the sound of him striking the incense box triggered a moment of awakening. His verse of realization says: "Gone..."

Setting out on the road, one reaches the end; treading it over, the waves are but water. The ancient Zhaozhou, who transcends all, has a face and features exactly like this. Next, he relied on Xutang.
Xutang pointed to a plum in a vase and said, "Those who can compose a verse may return to the hall. The Master said, "Having fought back the masses of darkness, I return with joy;
atop the hundred flowers, I am the champion of spring. Observe how his skillful means benefit others: he lets forth the spring.
When the wind and atmosphere shifted, the Master said, "Return to the hall. He later studied under Huanshan, where one day, while ascending the stone ladder, he attained great enlightenment.

He once set forth the "Three Barriers" to test his students, saying: "If a mosquito were to suck dry the vast ocean, where would the fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs find a place to dwell and establish their lives?
He also said: "If a water jelly were to fly up to the Ultimate Heaven (Akaniṣṭha), what would it do there?"
He entered the eye of Mahesvara and performed a dance; why was he not seen? He also said: "The Lotus Lake Bridge is a direct pointing for all people;
why did those with clear eyes fall into the well?"

The Chan Master Wuyong Kuan of Taho, Shuzhou, was a successor of the True Chan Master Jin Niu. When the monk Yiyuan came to visit him, the Master asked, "Where have you come from? Yuan replied, "From Tongzhou."
The Master asked, "Lately, how has the rise and fall of the Huai and Hai rivers been? Yuan said, "They flood the sun and overwhelm the heavens;
not a single drop remains. The Master said, "They do not follow the canals. Yuan said, "I ask the Master to speak. The Master then gave a shout.

On another day, he raised the verse on Realizing the Way and asked, "A flash of lightning comes flying; with no regard for one's whole body, in the space of a single thought, there is no path for sage or ordinary being."
"Quick! Quick! Yuan said, "When sparks fly and stars scatter, what room is there for deliberation? To meet face-to-face and act upon the occasion—this is not 'not,' this is not 'not.
The Master shook his majestic presence and let out a shout. Yuan asked, "What was that shout for? The Master replied, "Before the Melon Mountain, he swallows a扁担 (carrying pole);
he seizes the pure wind and strips it of its skin. Yuan could not help but break into a cold sweat all over his body and said, "Only today do I truly understand."
Regarding the Master’s point of application, the Teacher said: "Shut your mouth.

He was exceptionally intelligent. At the age of seven, his father taught him the "Opening the Sect and Clarifying the Meaning" chapter of the *Classic of Filial Piety*. The Master asked, "What is the 'opening' of the sect?
What is the 'clarifying' of the meaning? His father was struck with wonder and amazement. Thereupon, he took Zhongguan Zhao as his teacher. One day, while supporting Zhao as they walked, [Zhao] said:
Guǎn said, "Fǎdēng, you look at others' affairs while your own house is in chaos. Tell me, by whose power do you act? How do you understand this?

The Master seized Guǎn’s hand and pulled it away. Guǎn said, "You wild fox spirit! The Master said, "Yes, yes. Guǎn said, "You must still seek further elsewhere. Later, he took up his staff and traveled to Yān.
Meeting with rain, he stayed overnight beneath a cliff; striking a fire, he attained great enlightenment. He rubbed his face and said:
Today I have finally come to know that his eyebrows are horizontal and his nose is straight. I believe the words of the old monks throughout the world are never false.
He visited Zhonghe Zhang and subsequently received his seal of transmission (*kaji*). He presided over Qingshou Monastery. One day, while walking in the corridor, he encountered several monks.

Chan Master Nanshi Wenxiu of Jingshan, Hangzhou, a successor in the twenty-first generation under the lineage of Chan Master Wanshou Ren of Mount Nanyue, was a native of the Li family from Kunshan. He ascended the hall and said: "The ten directions are..."
"Different paths! Why seek Tiantai in the south and Wutai in the north? There is no different grass before one's eyes.
Why then is the peach blossom red and the plum blossom white? After a long silence, he said: "Break through the barrier of the patriarchs, and everything is simply your own."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Zen Master Zhenjing, who said: "Yesterday the weather was warm; today the sky is cold.
Heaven and earth both exert their power, yet the patch-robed monks’ eyelids remain wide open. To speak thus is still lacking awakening. Yesterday the weather was warm; today the sky is cold.
Do not run about upon the ground; withdraw your feet and ascend the meditation seat. *Duḥ!* Ascending the hall, the Dharma...
The body is without marks, yet it assumes form in response to things; Prajñā is without cognition, yet it illuminates in response to conditions.
The seventy-one or seventy-two peaks of Dongting Lake are shrouded in misty clouds; the thirty-six thousand acres of Taihu Lake have waves rolling on.
Jianjing Stream faces Hangkong Pavilion; Qin Terrace looks toward Qionglung Mountain. The sun shines upon the secluded crags, and the cuckoo calls in the ancient woods.
Muzhou suddenly picked up his staff and said, "This is the staff; which one is the Dharmakāya? Pointing to the incense table, he said, "This is the incense table;
which one is Prajñā? If you can see this clearly, then everywhere you return to the source and at every turn you follow the same path.
If you have not yet reached this realization, Lingyan’s staff will not yet be entrusted to you.
Ascending the hall: "The dust of emotion is easily dispelled, but the obstruction of principle is difficult to remove. Throughout the entire world of the ten directions, it is utterly empty and void;
if one seeks even a single dharma, it is completely unattainable. What dust of emotion is there to dispel? What obstruction of principle is there to remove?
Nevertheless, at the mountain gate or atop the Buddha hall, take care not to collide with a pillar. Ascending the hall: "Dust speaks, lands speak..."
He spoke of cutting off concealment without interruption. Leaning his staff across [his chest], he said, "Do you understand?
The vast water fields, white egrets fly; the deep summer trees, yellow orioles turn. He ascended the hall and raised an example:
A monk asked the Fifth Patriarch, "The entire Tripitaka is but a 'cutting foot' (a suffix). I wonder what it cuts? The Patriarch said, "Bharaṇī. The Master said, "Dongshan speaks of this..."
"Prāṇa. Again and again, those in the stream of Chan recklessly attempt to measure it; they are no more capable of recognizing the sword than was Zhang Hua.
They merely observe its light shining beside the Ox and Cow constellations. [The Master] ascends the hall, takes up his staff, and says:

"National Teacher Guoyi went to Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, Jambudvīpa in the south, and Uttarakuru in the north. Having traveled all about, he has now returned to this old monk’s hand."
He presented his body. Looking closely, it was originally just a black lacquer staff. Do you see it?

Even if you were to see it clearly, it would still be like a "car-degree-li-le" (a type of ancient drill) from the Qin dynasty. When a monk came to pay his respects and prepared to unfold his sitting mat, the Master said, "In my place, there is no leftover gruel or stale rice;
there is no need to use a worn-out cooking cloth. The monk said, "Out of compassion, Preceptor, please accept my prostrations. The Master said, "Ha! (Laughing).
The monk overturned the blue stone pillar in front of the gate and entered. The Master said, "You fellow who treads upon prefectures and counties—your heels deserve thirty blows!
The monk said, "I have not even asked a question, and you have already granted me a blow.
The Master said, "What would it avail you to wait until you open your mouth? As the monk hesitated, the Master shouted and drove him out.
Chan Master Xibai Lijin of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ming of Mount Jing. He was the son of the Yao family of Wu Jun.

Having visited Guding, Guding showed him the story of Deshan meeting Longtan, upon which he attained realization. In the winter of the fifth year of the Hongwu era, an imperial decree was issued to convene a great assembly, and [Lijin] was appointed.
The Master propagated the primary truth (*paramārtha*). When the princes, dukes, and officials listened, they rubbed their robes so that the sleeves would not come off.
One day he said to his disciples, "I have a karmic debt from a former life that remains unsettled; I must surely repay it. Do not constrain me with worldly appearances."
Before long, he manifested a slight illness and passed away in accordance with the natural course of things. He was enshrined in a stupa at the Huancui Aranya (Monastery) west of the city of Jiaxing.
Chan Master Xiangyuan Renshu of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou was a native of Taizhou. One day, he hurried through the gate and cried out, "The executioners have arrived!
The executioners have arrived! How can one evade them? Thereupon, he sat upright and passed away.

Chan Master Jueyuan Huitan of Tianjie Monastery in Nanjing was a dharma successor of Chan Master Longxiang Xun. He was the son of Yang of Tiantai. His mother conceived him after dreaming that she had swallowed a bright pearl.

At the age of sixteen, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*), studying the Vinaya and practicing the teachings. He listened to the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) methods at a time when Xiaoyin was proclaiming [the Dharma].
He traveled to India. When the Master arrived there, Baizhang Huaiyan asked him, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from traveling the mountains.

Huaiyan asked, "As for that which was thoroughly investigated by Luopu during his travels—how is it beneath your straw hat? The Master said, "It has already been presented before I even entered the gate.
Huaiyan asked, "Why do you not bring it forth now? As the Master hesitated, Huaiyan let out a shout, and the Master was suddenly liberated.
[Zhaozhou] had an awakening. On another day, Yunyan spread both hands out and showed them to the Master, saying, "I have opened it wide with eight characters;
why do you not consent to take it up? The Master said, "Stop trying to confuse me. Yunyan said, "Come closer, and I will explain it for you.
The Master covered his ears and went out. Yunyan nodded in approval. Later, when he presided over a hall assembly, he said: "A single phrase—pitch black, without a handle, yet possessing a standard."
After a long silence, he said, "Do you understand? The pestle pounds toward the southeast; the millstone grinds toward the northwest. Entering the hall, he continued:

"Before the Peak of Shaoshi and beneath the gate of Caoxi, the lamps have been passed down in succession, transmitted with absolute clarity. From antiquity to the present, not even a hair’s breadth has changed."
Furthermore, by what means is this verified? From the top to the bottom of the towers and terraces, the fire illuminates the chariots and horses as they pass back and forth;

people look upon people. Ascending the hall, he said: "The sutras have masters of the sutras; the treatises have masters of the treatises. Today, I shall let loose a single thread from the Dragon River to divide the sections and arrange the segments.
He took up his staff, struck it once on the ground, and said: "Tell me, what chapter or verse is this? Ascending the hall again, he said: "It is simply this very thing, already perfected."
This public case (gong’an). Among the assembly, there are many who have attained understanding, yet not a few who have misunderstood it.
Consequently, gold and brass are not distinguished, and jade and stone are not differentiated. Here at Longhe, I intend to distinguish them clearly. As for Venerable Zhang and Venerable Li:
"One arm is long; one eye is large. It is always as it is today. "To whom does the Dharma of Bodhidharma entrust its transmission?
He let out a single sigh and descended from his seat. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The spring breeze blows vast and wide; the spring days linger on.
The yellow oriole sings upon the branches of the hundred flowers. Within this, there is boundless meaning—whose message can know it? At that time, a monk stepped forward.

A question was asked: "When the mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot be suppressed or restrained, what then? The Master said in a stern voice, "Who is there to suppress them? He then addressed the monks in the hall:
"During the twelve periods of the day and night, you have no share in chewing and swallowing, nor do you have any share in moving toward or away. Do you understand?"

The monks were at a loss. The Master said, "If you do not understand three, eight, and nine, it will be difficult to avoid deep reflection. In the summer of the Gengxu year of the Hongwu era, he was commissioned as an envoy to the Western Regions.
Upon arriving at the kingdom of Shinghala, the King attended upon him at the Fo-shan Vihāra. In the ninth month of the following year, he manifested illness.
Calling his attendants to him, he said, "I shall no longer be able to return to my mission. He sat cross-legged, and at midnight, he asked:
"Has the sun risen? he asked. "Not yet," was the reply. He questioned him two or three times more, and finally said, "The sun has risen. With a serene expression, he passed away.
He was interred alongside [his predecessor] at the Pratyekabuddha Stūpa in the capital.

Chan Master Zongle, whose style name was Jitan, of Tianjie Monastery in Nanjing, was the son of Zhou of Linhai. From the moment of his birth, he sat in the full lotus posture; people marveled at this.
At the age of eight, he followed Xiaoyin to study the Buddhist canon; he could recite it from memory upon a single reading.

One day, Xiaoyin asked him, "When the National Teacher called out three times and the attendant responded three times, what did you make of that? The Master replied, "How can one carve away flesh to create a wound?"

Chuangyuan said, "I thought you were extraordinary; it turns out you have nothing to show for it. The Master gave a shout. As Chuangyuan reached for his staff, the Master shook out his sleeves and departed.
At the end of the Yuan dynasty, Chuangyuan went to Mount Jing; in the first year of the Hongwu era, he was transferred to Zhongzhu. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
The Vajra King’s sword is brandished horizontally; a thousand demons vanish from sight. The Śakara eye is brilliantly clear; ten thousand things conceal their forms.

Reaching this point, rolling up and unfolding are within one's own power; killing and giving life are applied according to the occasion. It would be enough to make the Thousand-Year Rock leap and bound, and for the waters of Qiantang to surge eastward against the current.
Do you all know that this exists, or not? He then held up his whisk and said: "In front of the courtyard..."
The stone bamboo shoots forth its branches; soon we shall see the high boughs where phoenixes lodge. Later, he was summoned by imperial decree to preside over the celestial realm.
When Empress Gao passed away and the time for her burial approached, wind, rain, thunder, and hail broke out. The Emperor was deeply displeased and suddenly summoned the Master.

Upon his arrival, the Emperor said, "The Empress Dowager is about to be interred; you should compose a verse for her. The Master immediately responded with these words: "Rain falls as Heaven sheds tears; Thunder roars..."
The court observed a period of mourning. The various Buddha-sons from the Western Heaven escorted Mafu (Ma Ru) Tathāgata together. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
In the twenty-fourth year of the Hongwu era, he retired due to old age and crossed the Yangtze River. Upon arriving at Shifo Temple in Jiangpu, he manifested illness.

Calling to his attendant, he said, "This, you see? The attendant was bewildered. The Master said, "Suffering," and then passed away. He was interred in a stupa behind that of Master Xun at Tianjie Monastery.
Chan Master Yuezhi Chong of Jiuzhangfu was a native of the Chen family of Piling.
He went to visit Xiaoyin, who brought up the koan of Linji’s "True Person Without Rank" and interrogated him, saying, "Do you recognize him yet? Without hesitation, the Master prostrated himself.
Yinyou asked, "What have you seen that you prostrate? The Master replied, "The one who bows is not another.
Yinyou said, "One who enters through the gate does not possess the family treasure. The Master said, "Venerable Monk, please do not deceive people. Yinyou nodded in agreement.

In the autumn of the fifth year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned to the private audience hall. The Emperor questioned him on the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and the Master presented a verse. The Emperor—

The Emperor was greatly pleased. He presented food before the Master; at times, the Master would doze, and his breathing would emit a faint sound. A neighboring monk pulled at the hem of his robe to alert him.
The Emperor laughed and said, "This old man has no artifice in his heart; he is truly a good spiritual friend. Later, when he manifested his passing, he was interred in a stupa on Shier Peak.
Chan Master Yongzhen Fuliang of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou was a native of Wuxian County, Suzhou. He was a tenth-generation descendant of Fan Wenzheng Gong.

At the age of fifteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination, whereupon he declared: "I study the Buddha-dharma in order to clarify the mind; without a teacher, there will be no way to reveal its essential points.
He subsequently went to attend upon Xiaoyin at Longxiang Monastery. Upon first seeing him, Xiaoyin recognized his potential and held him in high esteem. On another occasion, [he] again...
Question: When the Master’s words became increasingly severe, Yinyue laughed and said, "You have attained it indeed, but in the end, it remains within the second meaning.
After some time, he finally realized the Dharma of the Mind. Later, he appeared in the world at Zisheng Monastery in Jiaxing and resided late in his life at Lingyin.

Addressing the assembly, he said: "The single school of Bodhidharma has declined until it is nearly extinct. You all must apply yourselves with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire. Nevertheless, there are hundreds of thousands of dharmas..."
The immeasurable and wondrous meanings of the gates can be fully understood within the tip of a single hair.

If you understand them as such, you may transform the great earth into gold and accept it without hesitation; otherwise, you will incur the shame of eating the bread of idleness. Time flows like a flash of lightning.
As for matters that transcend the mundane, you all must urgently advance in your own practice. On the sixteenth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Hongwu era, he passed away.
Chan Master Qingyuan Huaiwei of Baoxiang Temple in Shaoxing Prefecture was the son of the Wei family of Nanchang. He was a disciple of Xiaoyin.
He was my nephew. At birth, a divine *lingzhi* fungus grew in his courtyard; as he grew up, he was exceptionally brilliant. He could recite the scriptures without waiting for a teacher’s instruction.
Hearing of this while staying in seclusion at Longxiang, [the Master] said with joy, "This is a 'thousand-li colt' of our lineage. He summoned him to his presence.
One day, Baizhang Conglin was secretly exhorting his disciples, but none of the assembly had an answer. The Master stepped forward and spoke at length.

Lin manifested his majestic power with a single shout (*he*), yet the Master’s spirit was not the least discouraged. As they engaged in a back-and-forth exchange of difficult questions, Lin smiled and said, "You may enter my chamber.

He then appointed him as the Secretary (*jishi*). Later, while the Master was traveling to propagate the Dharma, a woman of the Chen family requested instruction. As she was doing so, she suddenly felt as if—
She attained awakening. Before the Master had walked even a hundred paces, the woman took her leave of her family and passed away while sitting.
Chan Master Gudong Mingde of Daochang Monastery in Anji Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhutian Lin; he was a son of the Zhu family, whose ancestral home was Changguo in Mingzhou.

His father had a close friendship with Puto Jie. Having heard the sound of a rooster, Jie entered the Way; whenever he preached the Dharma, he would invariably flap his wings to mimic the crowing of a rooster.
Long after Jie had passed away, the mother dreamed that he came to stay with her as a guest. Upon waking, she conceived and gave birth after fourteen months.
From childhood, she delighted in sitting in meditation (dhyāna). Someone asked her, "Child, you do not read books; sitting here in a daze, what do you hope to seek? The Master replied:

He sought only to become a Buddha. At seventeen, he received full ordination and went to visit Zhuxi. Zhuxi asked, "From where have you come? The Master replied, "I have come from Golden Goose Mountain.
Zhuxi asked, "How high is Golden Goose Mountain? The Master replied, "Its peak is not to be seen. Zhuxi rebuked him. Next, he visited Huiji.
Huiji asked, "What kind of person comes in such a manner? The Master replied, "The madman Zhang San and the black fellow Li Si. Huiji asked again.
"From morning until evening, while you are putting on your robes and eating your meals, do you still recognize yourself? The Master replied as before. The teacher raised his staff;

the Master shook out his sleeves and departed. Later, he visited Zhutian. It happened that Zhutian was ascending the hall and citing the koan of Yinshan’s "Mud Ox Entering the Sea," his voice thundering like a roll of drums.
Unconsciously, the Master felt a sense of profound joy and clarity, and all his lingering doubts were suddenly resolved. He then presented a verse to him. Zhutian—
He sighed and said, "The eyes of the human and heavenly realms remain solemnly present. From this time on, his reputation became universally renowned. He presided over four monasteries in succession.
In the second month of the fifth year of the Hongwu era, he wrote a verse and entered parinirvāṇa. A stupa was erected at Donggang; he was seventy-nine years of age.

Chan Master Zhishan Cheng of Daci Monastery in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Tianchi Xin. When Jiefeng went to visit him, the Master asked, "Where did you see those gods and ghosts come from?
Jiefeng said, "I have caught the thief. The Master asked, "Where is the stolen property? Jiefeng gave a shout. The Master said:
"Neither opening the mouth nor closing the mouth is it. Bring forth a single phrase that goes beyond this. Feng said, "The entire world is clearly manifest, never concealed.
The Master raised his bamboo staff and said, "To call it a bamboo staff is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a bamboo staff is to turn one's back on it. What do you call it? Feng then overturned the meditation seat. The Master struck the bamboo staff three times and said, "Blind!"
"Han, you dare to come here and pull at a tiger’s whiskers! Feng then prostrated himself and attended him for three years.
One day, the Master said: "The ancients sought teachers and chose friends; one must not let their time be wasted in vain.

Although you have attained the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, you have still not yet been able to turn yourself over toward the ultimate. Have you not heard how Fenyang saw Shoushan and said: 'Ten thousand ages, the blue abyss is empty'?"
"Jièyuè (Realm-Moon), stir it again and again until you finally understand. At this, Fēng was suddenly enlightened.
Chánmāster Tiěguān Fǎshū of Tiānbǎoshān in Jiànníng Fù was the son of the Lín family of Píngyáng in Wēn.
At the age of seventeen, he paid homage to Zhūxī as his teacher and received full ordination. He studied under Zhōngfēng and Ān but found no resonance; he subsequently went to see Yuánwēng.

Shimen instructed [his disciples] to contemplate the saying, "The three 'nots'. One day after the midday meal, as he stepped down from his seat, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and composed a verse:
"Not mind, not Buddha, not thing; Pressed out, the very bones of empty space. A golden-maned lion cub— How could it linger in a wild fox’s den?"
"Bravo! Bravo! [The Master] immediately went to the abbot’s quarters. The old man asked, "What is it? The Master said, "Nanquan has been caught by me.
The old man said, "It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing. What is it? The Master said, "A set of bones for teeth;
two pieces of skin for ears. The old man said, "Do not speak of anything else. The Master said, "The warbling of the oriole, the chatter of the swallow, the cawing of the magpie..."
Crows were cawing. The old man said, "Wrong. The Master also said, "Wrong. The old man asked, "Where is Nanquan right now? The Master gave a shout.
The old man said, "Apart from this shout, where is Nanquan? The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Later, he traveled south to Jianzhou.
The regional commander invited him to head Tianbao Temple, and he subsequently resided at Puzhai in Songxi. Above.
"Empty. Not, not, not. Still, still, still. Erroneous, erroneous, erroneous. He looked at his attendant and asked, "Does this old monk still have a tongue?
In the third year [of his retirement], he returned to Tianbao. On the Mid-Autumn Festival of the sixth year of the Zhizhi era (1270), he wrote a verse:
"Fundamentally there is no coming or going; one phrase is fully raised. Red clouds pierce the azure void; the white sun circles Mount Sumeru. Having cast aside his brush, he passed away.

Chan Master Zhuyuan Shuisheng of Miaoguo on West Lake was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wunengjiao. When he first visited Master Yueting Zhong at Jiangshan, Guzhou Ji was serving as the First Seat (Dazuo).
[Shuisheng] was shown the words from the "Instruction for Mount Meng" by Mount Wan. Five years later, he attained realization.
Ji said, "Mongshan once remarked that the one who planted the pine trees did not possess the two conditions [of body and mind] when he was born.
When Bodhidharma was buried at Xiong’er Mountain, his single shoe later returned to the West. Was this truly due to supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), or is the Dharma simply such?
The Master said, "This is merely a case where both form and spirit are wondrous. Ji said, "Not so. You shall know this for yourself in the future. Later, the Master encountered Wuneng.

He recounted the previous conversation. Neng said, "It was because you did not understand. At these words, the Master suddenly attained great realization. In the year Jisi of the Tianli era, he presided over Miaoguo Temple.
He passed away in the summer of Dinghai of the Zhizheng era.

Chan Master Yongning Yiyuan of Longchi in Changzhou was a successor of Chan Master Wuyong Kuan. He was the son of the Zhu family from an official lineage in Tongzhou. From birth, he was exceptionally intelligent.

At the age of thirteen, he received ordination papers and tonsured himself to become a monk; shortly thereafter, he received full precepts. Traveling on foot through various regions, he encountered many... [text continues]
The Master’s speech was often unconventional. Later, he went to Huai-xi to visit Wu-yong. As soon as he stepped through the gate, Yong shouted at him with a stern voice and drove him out.
The Master prostrated himself outside the door and stood there with palms joined. After a long time, Yong finally permitted him to enter.
The Master withdrew to his meditation cell and did not sleep the entire night. One day, hearing Yong cite Yun-men’s saying, "A single thought does not arise," he attained realization. He hurried—
Yong urged him to seek realization immediately and struck him. Knowing that the Master had attained sudden enlightenment, Yong commanded him to compose a verse on Zhaozhou’s “Mu” (No).
The Master composed it on the spot, saying: "Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; The myriad phenomena all beg for their lives.

An bottomless basket filled with dead snakes— Add much or take little, there is nothing left over. Yong laughed heartily. After a long while, [the Master] took his leave. Yong instructed him, saying: "You..."
Whenever he encountered a dragon, he would stay; whenever he met a pond, he would dwell. In the year of Jihai during the Hongzhi reign, he was invited to reside at Longchi (Dragon Pond).

The Master, seeing that his name corresponded to the prophetic record, joyfully accepted the invitation. Within a year, disciples from near and far had all gathered, and his monastic seat was moved several times.

He entered the imperial presence for an audience, where he was granted purple robes and a posthumous title. In the summer of the Jiyou year of the Hongwu era, he manifested illness and requested that a paper robe be made for him, saying: "I..."
He was about to pass away. On the seventeenth day, he donned paper robes for his mourning period and wrote a verse, saying: "For seventy-eight years I have guarded my simplicity;
clearly, this has been one great failure. The clay ox turns over in the depths of the sea; in the blazing heat of the sixth month, snow falls.
Having finished writing, he passed away in peace.
Master Zhen of Mount Jingyun in Chongqing Prefecture was visited by Biluofeng for an audience. The Master drew a circle on the ground;
Biluofeng brushed it away with his sleeve. The Master drew another circle; Biluofeng added a stroke across its center.
He wiped it away again. The Master drew as before. Xuefeng added another stroke to form a cross. He wiped it away again. The Master drew as before.
Xuefeng added four corners to the cross, forming a *svastika*. He wiped it away again. The Master then drew thirty circular marks in total.
Xuefeng answered each one in detail. The Master said, "Only now do you understand the vast superiority of the Buddha-dharma."
Thus it is. You should go to the north to extensively propagate my Way.
[He was] the twenty-second generation successor under Mount Nanyue, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Yin of Shuanglin.
Chan Master Yuejiang Zongjing of Mount Jingshan in Hangzhou was the son of the Ni family of Lanxi. While reciting the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained a realization upon reaching the passage:
"It is like a finger pointing at the moon. He went to study under Shuanglin, who asked him: "When Huangbo struck Linji, what did you make of that?"

The Master said, "It is like pressing down a cow while it eats grass. At the time of his passing, he spoke this verse: "A guest at the gate of the Patriarchs, Opening my mouth to discourse on non-arising.
In my old age, I understand nothing at all; At midday, I strike the third watch. Thereupon, he passed away.

Chan Master Dingyan Jingjie of Linggu Monastery in Nanjing, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Tantan of the Heavenly Realm, went to visit Chan Master Jueyuan. Jueyuan raised the kōan concerning the bursting of a wooden barrel hoop and questioned him.
Before the Master could answer, Jueyuan said in a stern voice, "It is already eight *ke* late! At these words, the Master attained great realization.
Wu. The Master subsequently carved the *Lianzhu songgu* (Linked Verses on Ancient Cases) for circulation in the world.
Chan Master Jiefeng Shiyu of Wushan Mountain in Quzhou, a dharma heir of Chan Master Daci Cheng, was the son of the Yu family of Xian County in that same prefecture. He traveled extensively...

Finding no satisfaction at Congshê, he heard that Yan was expounding the Great Compassion teachings at Zhiyan. He went there to pay his respects. Yan raised the phrase: "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not things.
One night, sitting until the second watch, he heard a neighboring monk recite the *Song of Realizing the Way*:

"Neither eliminating delusive thoughts nor seeking the Truth... At once, he felt as though a heavy burden had been lifted. He composed a verse: "Moment by moment, face-to-face, yet they do not meet..."
Feng encountered [his teacher]. Having consumed his mother’s vital energy until it was exhausted, at midnight he suddenly forgot the finger pointing at the moon.
A red solar disc burst forth from the void, and he went to see Yuanwu. Yuanwu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Daci.
Yuanwu said, "How deep is Daci’s nostril? The Master struck his staff once. Yuanwu said, "If you break the staff, with what will you strike? The Master made a gesture.
The *Ritual Code* says: "Today I have personally seen the Elder Master. The Master said, 'I am mindful of you, my disciple and grandson;
I grant you thirty blows of the staff. When Yanzhao returned, the Master went to pay his respects. During the night, he raised the case of Fenyang seeing Shoushan, who said:

'The moon in the empty realm of the eternal green pool—only after repeatedly searching for it will you begin to know it. Only then did [Yanzhao] attain a sudden flash of realization. Later, while presiding over the assembly in the Dharma hall, there was a person..."
Regarding "practice without reaching" and "reaching without being able to speak": there is one who reaches but cannot speak; there is one who reaches both in practice and in speech;
and there is one who fails to reach both in practice and in speech. Tell me, who is this person?

The Elder Śākyamuni preached the Dharma for forty-nine years—this is reaching through speech without reaching through practice. Master Bodhidharma faced the wall at Shaolin for nine years—this is [reaching through] practice...
Reaching yet not reaching; the cat and the white ox recite the *Mahā*. Reaching and speaking both reach;
the pillar and the lantern join their palms together. Neither reaching nor speaking; tell me, among these four people, which one is most intimate?
If you can discern this, I grant that you possess a single eye. If not yet so, I shall call forth the wooden monk to come out and [join] you all.
A person conveys a message. [The Master] plants his staff on the ground and says: "Last night, the sound of thunder shook the universe;
rain poured down from heaven to earth in vast torrents. He lets out a shout. He ascends the hall and says: "The autumn wind whistles; autumn leaves fly. The fierce heat has just now subsided."
The summer heat is but slight; on high mountains the sun rises late, and across the vast sea the waves arrive slowly.
Raising the three eyes of Maheśvara, the entire trichiliocosm is but a single hair’s breadth. [He] ascends the hall. Linji and Deshan possessed great capacity and great function:

their shouts were like thunderclaps, and their staffs were like gusts of wind. They shook the five sacred peaks and the three mountains, startling and dispersing the great assembly at Ling Shan. There was release...
There is gathering; there is seizing and releasing. A hundred circuits and a thousand layers, without a single crack or seam. Does the assembly see Deshan and Linji?
*Shoo!* In broad daylight under the blue sky, do not speak of dreams. Entering the hall: Today in all quarters the furnace is opened, its red flames reaching to the heavens.
Zen monks vie with one another to step forward toward the fire; each one is warmed until their heads turn yellow and their faces turn crimson. Although they act according to their own nature—
At that moment, alas, he was seen through by the deity who guards the furnace. Here at Longmen, there is no need to open the furnace, nor is it necessary to tend the fire;
let it remain as pure as jade and as clear as ice, drop by drop, frozen to the very core—frozen to the bone and to the marrow.
Suddenly, from within cold ashes, a single bean pops with a loud crack. It startles heaven and shakes the earth; it brings a sense of lifelong joy and fulfillment. Why is this?
Because one knows that on this day one sits by the hearth, yet does not recall the man standing in the snow of years past. Entering the hall:
On the eighth day of the twelfth month, eating chicken soup—just as doubt arises, calamity is born. The shadows of willows by the stream do not hinder the passage of the fishing boat. Ancient.
When people speak in this manner, they say that great enlightenment is not constrained by minor details; yet they cannot avoid providing a ladder for thieves, leading the heterodox into the orthodox.

Xingguo was not like this: on the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ate red fermented rice; his spirit in the monastic community was bold and grand. Drunk to the point of collapse, he no longer stirred up any fuss.
He ascended the hall and said: "On this day every year, dragon boats race; the drum of the crocodile roars across the waters."
Ascending the hall, he recalled the events of Qu Yuan’s day: “Where the mournful wind blows, all is chillingly still; who is there to repay this sentiment?
Through ages past and present, how many autumns have passed? Where are the lands of Han and Chu? The Yangtze River flows east as it has always done. Ascending the hall, he said:
“If one discusses this matter, it is like a person climbing a mountain: taking one step, one sees one [peak].”
He walked. When he reached the midpoint of the mountain, he saw the realm of the midpoint. When he reached the summit of the mountain, he saw the realm of the summit.
If he had not walked at all, there would have been nothing seen. "Great assembly, tell me: are you now on the summit of the mountain, or on level ground?
Is there something seen, or is there nothing seen? He stood his staff upright and said: "Seeing, seeing, seeing."

"Time is not this seeing. Zuo leaned on his staff and said: "Where there is hearing upon hearing, there is no further hearing. The eye atop the head opens wide, transcending the three periods of time;
the great earth, mountains, and rivers are swallowed in a single gulp. Leaning on his staff, he rose from his seat. At the conclusion of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said:

"The mountains of Eastern Zhejiang and the waters of Western Zhejiang; the springs and the south of Fujian—whether treading on the head or underfoot, even if one roams throughout the entire world, one does not go beyond [this]."
Within the vast net of the heavens—ha ha ha! Li lo li! Throughout the hall, there is boundless wind from white artemisia;
it is clearly manifest, yet does not arise from the autumn river. A monk asked, "I have a stringless lute that has long resided in the wilderness.

It is not that I do not know how to play it; it is simply that I have not yet met one who understands it. "What is this stringless lute? the Master said. "The high mountains and flowing waters. [The monk] said, "How so?"
"How do you play it? The Master said, "The *Yangchun* melody amidst the snow. The monk said, "If that is so, then: 'A single note of the painted horn at dawn in the Dragon Tower;
hand grasping the golden whip, celebrating peace. The Master said, "This is a matter within the jurisdiction of the Military Commissioner.

The monk asked, "What about when the student takes full responsibility with his whole shoulder? The Master said, "If you try to hear it with your ears, it will be difficult to understand; you must hear it with your eyes."

[The Master] said, "It was only upon hearing the sound that I first knew. [The monk] asked, "At midnight, you broke off a reed and crossed the river; for nine years you faced a wall—what was your intention? The Master said, "A total failure.
[The monk] asked, "The Second Patriarch stood in the snow up to his waist and cut off his arm to express his sincerity; what did he seek?"

The Master said: "If one does not undergo a thorough freezing to the very marrow, how can one obtain the fragrance of plum blossoms that strikes the nose? [A monk] asked: "Sin arises from the mind; one should repent with the mind.
But in repenting for sin, how is it better than not giving rise to the mind at all? Why did the Third Patriarch seek the Second Patriarch to repent for his sins?"
The Master said: "Doubt in the mind gives rise to dark demons; eye disease causes one to see floating flowers. [The student] asked:
"One might rather endure the cycle of samsara for eternal kalpas than seek explanations from the various sages. Why, then, did the Fourth Patriarch request the Dharma-gate of liberation?

The Master said: "It is like gouging a sore into healthy flesh; it is to bind oneself with one's own rope. [The student] said: "With hair hanging white, I descend the green mountains; having returned at seven years of age, I have changed."
The old face has become youthful again, yet the pine is already aged; from this point on, right and wrong shall fall back into the human world. "In the end, what is true and what is false?
The Master said, "The sun rises in the east and the moon sinks in the west. [The monk] said, "On the day the flower blooms at the pestle-head of Huangmei."
"At midnight, the robe was passed south of the ridge. Is this matter truly definitive? The Master said, "Originally there is not a single thing; the two shoulders cannot bear it.
[The monk] asked, "'It is not the wind moving, nor the banner moving; it is the mind of the noble one moving. What about that?
The Master said, "Know that the lamp is originally fire; believe that water does not depart from the waves. [The monk] asked, "Ultimately, how is it?"
[The monk] requested confirmation. The Master said: "When you meet a swordsman on the road, you must present your sword; if you are not a poet, do not offer your poem. [The monk] asked:
"As for the Master’s single phrase for the sake of others, how would that be? The Master said: "A slap across the cheek, a blow behind the head.
[The monk] said: "If it is so, then the grandmotherly heart is too earnest. The Master said: "If one does not cast fragrant bait into the white waves, how can one catch the golden fish?"

On the tenth day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Hongwu era, while on a fishing boat upon the scales [of the water], the monk prostrated himself and wrote this verse to bid farewell to the assembly:
"Birth is fundamentally not born; extinction is fundamentally not extinguished. Casting off my hands, I go forth; the sky is one bright moon. Having cast down his brush, he passed away.
Chan Master Xuefeng Niche Zhishun of Fuzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tianbao Shu. He was born into the Chen family of Ruian, Wenzhou. He left home to become a monk at the age of seven.

As he grew up, he traveled through the monastic academies, where he was consistently esteemed for his exceptional brilliance. Suddenly, moved by the impermanence of worldly phenomena, he entered [the mountains].

Min Shan was practicing under Tieguan. After more than a month, while using the toilet, he had an awakening. He presented his realization to seek certification, and Tieguan said, "This is merely entering the gate;

the supreme vehicle is still far off. He further instructed him, saying, "You must completely discard your previous intellectual understandings and exert yourself solely in the practice of *can* (investigation) and *ti* (raising the question).
Then you will naturally enter the innermost depths. One day, while attending Tieguan’s evening discourse, Min Shan prepared to leave his seat.
Suddenly and completely enlightened, he called out to Guankou in a stern voice, "Nanquan has defeated you; I have already seen through it.
Guankou said, "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing. What is it? The Master replied, "The ground is paved with bricks, and the roof is covered with tiles.
Guankou asked, "Where is Nanquan right now? The Master said, "A hawk has flown off to Silla. Guankou said, [nothing further].
"Wrong," said the Master. "Wrong," said the Master again. Guanzhi said, "Wrong, wrong. The Master performed a prostration and withdrew. Guanzhi said, "Not yet.
He struck the bell to assemble the community for an examination. The Master laughed and said, "Before a single word was uttered, we were already not involved with one another.
Where are the Master’s eyes? Are you still putting on such a theatrical performance? Guanzhi said, "I want everyone to know. Later, he left.
The Great Dragon of the World traveled as far as Xuefeng, visiting five major monasteries in total. In the sixth year of the Hongwu era, he responded to a summons to the capital;
after only four months, he passed away while sitting in meditation.

Chan Master Bijing Baolin of Lingjiu on Mount Wutai in Daizhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhinyun Zhen. He was the son of the Shi family of Yongshou. From childhood, he was constantly afflicted by illness;

his parents believed that because his birth had been accompanied by auspicious omens, it was fitting to entrust him to the Buddhist order. When he was only six years old, they sent him to rely upon Yunji.
When Master Wen reached adulthood, he received full ordination and traveled extensively among lecture halls. Later, changing his robes, he entered Jinyun to pay his respects to Ruhu Hai.

Hai showed him the essentials of the Way, which caused the Master to give rise to a great state of doubt. Once, while carrying a basket and following Hai to gather vegetables, he suddenly sat motionless in meditation.
Only after half a watch did he awaken. Hai asked, "Are you in samādhi? The Master replied, "Yes. Hai asked, "What do you see?"
The Master raised the basket. Xuefeng was unwilling. The Master set the basket on the ground and stood with his hands folded. Xuefeng remained unwilling. The Master let out a shout.

Xuefeng lunged forward and struck him in the chest. The Master did not yield in the least. Xuefeng laughed and said, "My worldly afflictions have been briefly stilled, but my power of meditative concentration is not yet deep enough.
Only when the path of the mind is severed and the Patriarchal Barrier is penetrated can the Great Dharma be clarified."
Later, he stayed at Mount Emei, where for three years his side did not touch the mat. One day, hearing the sound of wood being hewn, he attained great enlightenment.
He hurried to seek verification from [Zhao]hai, who questioned and cross-examined him repeatedly. The Master dragged the meditation bench over and walked out.

During the Zhizheng era, Emperor Shun summoned him to the capital of Yan three times; he was granted a golden-patterned *kāṣāya* robe and the title "Jizhao Yuanming" (Tranquil Illumination and Perfect Clarity). The Hongwu...
At first, the Taizu also summoned him for audiences on several occasions, bestowing upon him double the usual honors and favor. Before long, he manifested illness.

When the assembly requested a final verse, the Master said, "The Dharma-treasure of the Tripitaka is still but old paper; what would my words accomplish? He passed away with serene composure at the age of sixty-five.
His body was cremated at Mount Zhubao, where countless five-colored śarīras were obtained.
Chan Master Lizhong Cheng of Ciguang Temple in Hangzhou, a descendant of the twenty-third generation under Nanyue, was the dharma heir of Chan Master Liaojian of Jingci Temple.
He was the son of the Sun family of Qiantang. Having visited Liaojian at Jingci Temple, Liaojian—

He brought up the story of the mountain fire in the sixth month. The Master composed a verse, saying: "The white clouds obscure the old tracks; In the twelfth month, the mountain fire burns a brilliant red.
Once again, the breeze of compassion comes to fan it forth; Where it was cold and frozen, it now blazes with warmth. Lian Shen regarded him as a vessel of great capacity.
Chan Master Wuya Feihuan of Linggu Monastery in Nanjing was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wushan Yu. He was a native of Xi’an in Quzhou and left the household life under Master Jiefeng.

When Jiefeng asked him where he had come from, the Master replied, “Empty space has no front or back. Jiefeng then pointed to the monastery bell and instructed him to compose a verse about it. The Master said:
Rolled forth from within a furnace of a hundred refinements; empty space originally never soils itself with dust.
Now suspended upon the human head, it meets the profound resonance that pervades the nine realms. At the age of twelve, Master Feng took a liking to him and immediately ordered him to shave his head.
In the Dinghai year of the Yongle era, when Emperor Taizong Wen was attending to matters at Changling, he summoned the master to an audience; the master’s responses pleased the Emperor. Great...

The Emperor praised him highly and bestowed gifts upon him, decreeing that he reside at Linggu Monastery. In the spring of the Gengzi year, the Emperor convened a great assembly. When the Master appeared indifferent to it, his disciples questioned him.
The Master smiled and said, "I have a matter of my own that is most urgent; how could I have leisure for anything else? He then wrote this verse: "Life and death drift on, severed from worldly ties;
Having received the Emperor’s grace, I rejoice forever in years of Great Peace. This time, I let go of my hands into the void."
He returned home. The snow had cleared and the clouds vanished as the moon was at its full. He then passed away.
Chan Master Taichu Qiyuan of Sanfeng Temple in Luoyang was a native of Japan.
At the age of nineteen, he visited forty-five eminent patriarchs in the Land of the Superior (China). Finally, he received the Dharma from Jiefeng. Later, he resided at Sanfeng. One day, he wrote:

The verse says: "In life there is an iron face; in death there is an iron face. Struck by a single blow, one is shattered into a hundred fragments, wandering by day around the Iron Encircling Mountains.
Having cast aside his writing brush, he passed away. His stupa was erected to the south of the monastery.
The Five Lamps Adorning the Lineage, Volume 212;
The Five Lamps Adorning the Lineage, Volume 213;
Linji School.

Chan Master Qianyan Yuanchang of Shengshou Temple on Fulong Peak in Quanhua Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben of the twenty-third generation under Nanyue. He was the son of the Dong family of Xiaoshan and possessed a natural disposition.
He was intelligent and quick-witted; upon seeing a text, he could recite it from memory. At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

During a ceremony where the Chancellor’s administration provided a meal for the monastic community, the Master entered with the assembly. Zhongfeng was seated there and called out to him, "How do you spend your daily life?

The Master replied, "I practice the Buddha-recitation. Zhongfeng asked, "Where is the Buddha now? As the Master hesitated, Zhongfeng rebuked him with a stern voice. The Master then knelt and requested the essentials of the Dharma. Zhongfeng...
He was given the "wordless koan. The Master lived in a thatched hut in the mountains of Lingyin for three years, his side never touching the mat.
While traveling to Wangting, he heard the cry of a magpie and attained realization. He hurried to see Feng and fully explained the cause of his awakening, but Feng again rebuked him.

The Master returned home in indignation. In the stillness of night, a rat suddenly overturned the cat’s feeding bowl; as it fell to the ground, it made a sound. At that moment, he attained sudden enlightenment. He went back once more.
He stayed with Feng. Feng asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The Master said, "A mouse eats the cat's food. Feng said, "Not yet.
The Master said, "The vessel for the food is broken. Feng asked, "What after it is broken? The Master said, "I would smash the square jar to pieces. Feng smiled.
Later, while presiding over the assembly in the Dharma hall, a monk asked, "What is the first phrase? The Master said, "Having a mouth like one who is mute."
[The monk] asked, "What is the second phrase? The Master said, "To have eyes yet be like one blind. [The monk] asked, "What is the third phrase?
The Master said, "Even if the staff were broken, I would still not let you go. The Master then threw down his whisk and said, "This is the old monk’s second phrase.
What is the first phrase? He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "This Dharma abides in its own place; the world..."
Phenomena are eternally abiding: mountains are mountains, waters are waters, monastics are monastics, and laypeople are laypeople.
Throughout the entire universe and the great earth, there is not a hair’s breadth of fault or affliction. Yet, under the gates of Deshan and Linji, it is otherwise. How is it, after all?
They stubbornly love to bind themselves to mortal enemies and gouge out the three eyes at the crown of their heads. Bestowing the Dharma robe, he ascends the hall; [this is] from years past.
The worn-out robe is tattered and frayed; newly crafted, this golden brocade robe descends from the heavens. It wraps the void with not a bit left over;
the mountains and rivers, flower by flower, break into smiles. Ascending the hall, he said:

"O assembly, I do not like to hear the single word 'Buddha,' let alone speak so many idle words and long phrases that corrupt the sons and daughters of families. They deserve thirty blows of the staff. Why is this?"
The mosquito was struck by the fan; it was solely because its mouth harmed people. [The Master] stood for a long time. He ascended the hall and said:
"This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination. The Old Man Śākyamuni said: "For twenty-one days, I contemplated such matters as these."
Can it be called "not thinking"? Master Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my marrow. Can it be called "non-discrimination"? Heh!

Everyone who meets them says they have retired from office, yet not one person has ever been seen beneath the forest trees. [Ascending the hall: Can it be called "not thinking"? Master Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my marrow. Can it be called "non-discrimination"? Heh! Everyone who meets them says they have retired from office, yet not one person has ever been seen beneath the forest trees. [Ascending the hall.]
The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. On every side, the green mountains unfurl their smiling brows. The Sutras have masters of the Sutras; the Shastras have masters of the Shastras.
Do not take umbrage that this old monk has no Dharma to speak; it merely tires you all to stand here for a short while. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "A wild horse enters a cow pen. The monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "A wild horse enters a cow pen."
The Master said, "I lack the strength to raise my fist. [The student] asked, "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his servants;
I wonder, who is he? The Master said, "A broom grows from atop a heap of refuse. [The student] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Ask the janitor.
[The student] asked, "What is it to take away the person but not the environment? The Master said, "The sun shines upon mountains and rivers, and their shadows sway."
He asked, "What is 'seizing the environment but not seizing the person'? The Master said, "When the battle array is set against the water, courage and strength increase.

He asked, "What is 'seizing both the person and the environment'? The Master said, "Even if it were a sharp blade, it would always be level; even if it were a lethal poison, it would remain indifferent.
He asked, "What is 'neither seizing the person nor seizing the environment'? The Master said, "The rustic old man knows nothing of the efforts of Yao and Shun."
The drum thumps as the river deity is worshipped. He addresses the assembly, calling out: "Do you know where this old monk has landed?
He then speaks on the practice of releasing captured fish while addressing the assembly; picking up his staff, he says: "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away.

Do you people still want a second ladle of foul water? With that, he strikes the ground once. He addresses the assembly again: "If the狂心 (wild mind) does not cease, even in the heavens it is [unrestful]."
If it does not accord with your wishes, even becoming a Buddha is but a hollow pretense. Once the frantic mind ceases, one would not even wish to be a Buddha;

what more need be said of heaven and hell? Have you all ceased [this striving] yet? To the assembly: Today is the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month. Yunmen’s single melody has never had a musical score.
How can it compare to the Unconsciousness (avidyā) tune, which rises ever higher? It is encountered in the midst of the ordinary.
He sings out the dance of a thousand mountains. Taking the great earth as a lute and empty space as a drum, beat after beat they follow one another;
sound after sound they assist one another. You people must listen well: how could the "White Snow" or "Yangchun" melodies be worth counting?

Who among you knows the true essence within this? Through the long, silent night, the pine wind passes by. While the assembly was looking at the sutras, the Master held up the sutra and said, "What is this?"

[The Master] said, "What sutra? No one in the assembly could respond. The Master spoke on their behalf, saying, "Chapter One: The Introduction. After a long silence, he asked, "Do you understand? The subsequent text is extensive.
Once, when a secular official saw a cat, he asked, "Does this cat eat meat? The Master replied, "It does not eat meat; it only eats mice.
The official asked, "How can a person of good knowledge tolerate such a thing? The Master said, "Tell the official not to come here again."
He attained [enlightenment]. On the fourteenth day of the sixth month in the Dingyou year of the Zheng period, he manifested slight illness.

He gathered the assembly and wrote a verse, saying: "Throughout my life I have been loquacious; today I am undone. One phrase roars through the heavens—the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished. Thereupon he threw down his brush and passed away.
His disciples used a ceramic casket to enshrine his remains and buried them at青松庵 (Qingsong Hermitage). He was posthumously granted the title of 佛慧圓 (Fohui Yuan).
Chan Master Jian.
Chan Master Lintu Weize of Shizi Forest Monastery in Suzhou, a native of the Tan family of Yong’an in Jixian, addressed the assembly, saying:
“Zhaozhou uttered the word ‘Mu’ (No), opening his mouth to reveal his very heart and liver. Why, then, do you all create obstacles for yourselves?”
At that time, a monk asked, "All sentient beings, down to the smallest crawling insect, possess Buddha-nature. Why is it that the dog alone has none?
The Master said, "Do not speak only of the dog. Even if you were to ask Śākyamuni or Maitreya whether they have Buddha-nature or not, they too would say 'no'.
The monk said, "Zhaozhou’s Chan rests upon his lips. Why then does he only say the word 'no'? The Master said:
"Zhaozhou’s realization reached no further than this. [A monk] asked, "Does the Master not approve of Zhaozhou?
The Master said, "Yes. [The monk] asked, "Zhaozhou was an ancient Buddha; for what reason does the Master not approve of him? The Master said, "Where is Zhaozhou?
He then gave a shout. Addressing the assembly, he said: "A tiger painted on a paper screen, its two eyes glowing red like fire-pearls."
Last night, a pair of horns suddenly emerged, goring to death Yangqi’s three-legged donkey.

You all—whether climbing onto your beds, descending to the ground, leaving the door, or entering the room—must each take care of your own wretched lives. To the assembly, he said: "I cite Linji’s words:
'In my place here is the living meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West; everything is to be used as it is required for the moment. The Master then brandished his whisk.
The Master swayed back and forth and said, "What I have here is also alive; it is used when needed, entirely according to the occasion. Now tell me, is this the same as Linji’s, or is it different?
He struck once, threw down [the staff], and said, "Linji still lacks this one point. He addressed the assembly: "For the lame, life depends on the crutch;
for those crossing water, life depends on the boat. There is a source from which they come, and there is no source from which they do not come."
Byo. Within a single body there is yet another body of sorrow. In the school of the patch-robed monks, food is snatched away and oxen are driven off.
If you attempt to look with your eyes, they immediately close the doors and windows; if you attempt to speak with your mouth, they immediately block your throat.
When there is no moon on the night corridor, do not light a lamp; let the pillar be free to smash its head against it. To the assembly: Old Tianru is but a single dull-witted monk.
Alas, how can people fail to recognize him? They say he stands tall and majestic, yet he remains humble and unassuming.

He appears as if he were dull and indistinct, yet at other times he is exceptionally distinguished and towering. Sometimes he assumes the guise of a spiritual mentor (*kalyāṇamitra*), discoursing on the profound and the subtle;
at other times he manifests three heads and six arms, displaying anger and malice.
In all such instances, you fail to recognize him one by one. Little do you realize that this old fellow does not reside within your eyes, but rather within yourselves.
"Inside the nostrils. People did not believe him, so he reached out his hand and touched them. "Even if you cannot touch those, you will surely touch your own nostrils.
He addressed the assembly, raised his whisk, and said: "This very thing is not worth half a cent, yet it commands Buddhas and Patriarchs and issues edicts to gods and humans.
Now I am entrusting it to you all. He then cast it down, gave a shout, and departed.
Addressing the assembly: What is there within the mountains? Upon the peaks, many white clouds. Hehehe! This is the property of the entire community; who would dare possess it privately?
Nevertheless, though this may be so, it can only serve to delight oneself; it is not fit to be presented as a gift to another.
Addressing the assembly: The Elder Śākyamuni cannot be pushed open; Master Bodhidharma cannot be driven out. Thus, he has led one [to this realization].

On three acres of land, there were three snakes and nine rats. Everyone said that while it was easy to call out for the snake, it was difficult to drive it away. [The Master] struck his knee and said, "What difficulty is there?
If one has the *Bai Ze* (White Deer) Chart at home, such monsters will certainly not exist. On New Year’s Eve, he addressed the assembly:

"If you wish to realize the meaning of Buddha-nature, you must contemplate the conditions of time and season. The old official calendars of former times are not worth the price they fetch. — Lion Forest Monastery.
Below, there is another explanation. Once the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month has passed, tomorrow morning will certainly be New Year’s Day.
On the Buddha’s Birthday, he addressed the assembly: "The plum rain plays at clearing the sky; the plum wind blows with moisture. Prince Siddhārtha is born! Raising his whisk, he said:
"He is now upon the tip of this whisk, looking toward the four quarters and walking seven steps, bringing turmoil to the world."
"Everyone! From this day forward, Hūṃ Hūṃ! Do not say that there is no Yunmen in the world; no one dares to deceive you. I shall pour foul water over your heads;
the handle of the ladle is in the old monk’s hand. Later, he passed away and was interred in a stupa at Suixi Yuan.
At Kenchō-ji Temple in Sagami Province, Japan, there was the former Zen Master Ingen, whose secular surname was Fujiwara. He was a member of the national nobility.

At the age of thirteen, he shaved his head and traveled extensively throughout the various monasteries, yet found no realization. Consequently, he embarked on a ship and traveled south to visit Mujaku.
Upon meeting him, Mujaku directed him to visit Zhongfeng. He attended Zhongfeng as his attendant and repeatedly presented his insights, but Zhongfeng rebuked him, saying, "Your roots..."
"Dust does not cease; how can it be like a binding shackle? The Master neglected both sleep and food. Guifeng, pitying his sincerity, said: "This mind encompasses all phenomena.

In delusion, there is birth and death; in awakening, there is nirvana. The delusion of birth and death is indeed not easily cast off, yet the awakening of nirvana is still but a speck of gold dust before the eye. You should know that Prajñā is like a great mass of fire."

To draw near [to such delusions] is to risk having one's head scorched and forehead blistered; therefore, maintain only the single thought of non-retrogression. Whether born, be born together; whether dying, die together.
Thus, you will naturally accord with the Way. Even if, in the interval before awakening, there were a thousand Śākyamunis and ten thousand Maitreyas—
"Empty out the waters of the four great oceans and pour them into your faculty of hearing; all of these are but false, worldly afflictions, none of which are ultimate matters.

Upon hearing this, the Master was so overcome that he broke into a cold sweat. One day, he attained a realization and told Feng, "Yinyuan has already crashed headlong into the silver mountain and iron wall.
Feng said, "Since you have entered the silver mountain and iron wall, why have you come here? The Master leaped [into the air].

Having thus grasped the essential meaning, he later accepted invitations to appear in the world. On his eighth transfer to a famous monastery, his disciples wished to paint a portrait of the Master and requested a eulogy in advance.
The Master drew a perfect circle and inscribed upon it: "The wondrous marks are perfectly luminous; suchness is unmoving. Meeting [it] at every point—what face is this?
In the spring of the Jia-yin year of the Hongwu era, as he was about to enter nirvana, he called to his attendant, saying: "The time..."
"It is complete. Bring a brush and inkstone. When they arrived, he said again, "My stupa is finished; only the plaque has not yet been inscribed.
He wrote the two characters "Xinyin" (Heart-Seal) in large script, entered his room, sat upright, and passed away.
The Chief Seat Shou of Jiufeng attained the essential meaning under Zhongfeng. Later, when he was about to pass away, he spoke this verse:
"Seventy-two years, here and there, Eating the food of the ten directions, Studying the Chan of Bodhidharma. This morning, with one cast, I turn my body and depart;
I laugh until half the mouth of the onlookers is split."
Chan Master Guimei Zhengyou of Gaoyang Mountain in Jianning Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Chengyan of Shengshan. He was a native of the Ding family of Guiyi in Guangxin.
Having left home at a tender age, he traveled extensively to consult senior masters as he grew up. One day, while urinating and touching the ground, he attained a point of entry.
He requested further instruction on the "study of cessation" (*juexue*). Later, upon arriving at Xueyan, he read the *Recorded Sayings* of Fachang;

when he reached the passage "driving away the oxen and seizing the food," he was suddenly overcome with perspiration. He then composed verses on several *gong'an* cases and sent them to Xueyan for inspection.

Xueyan remarked, "This man has received the vital power from my third bamboo staff, yet he merely lacks the shedding of the shell. Three years later, while passing through the hall during the meal, he struck the alms bowl.

Suddenly he attained great enlightenment. He ascended the hall and said: "The sword of wisdom is raised alone; the clear and correct command is issued. If you hesitate or deliberate, you will lose your body and forfeit your life.

Is there anyone here who can face this head-on? After a long silence, he said: "Just right—a single sail passing over the sea on a favorable wind. Yet within this, one does not meet the man who rides the surging waves.
In a small assembly (xiaocan), he said: "The moon has fallen behind the mountain peaks; clouds hang across the valley mouth, shrouding it in gloom. If you wish to clarify birth and death..."
Regarding this matter: he directly pointed to the original mind. Is there anyone who can realize this original mind? When the night is still, there is no need to borrow the moon again;
the jade hare is always suspended within the great void. In the summer of the Renchen year of the Zhi Zheng era, he passed away.

Chan Master De-yin Purin of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yizi. He was a native of Lanxi; his secular surname was Zhao. Having studied under Liao Ran, their spiritual dialogue reached a state of mutual resonance.
During the year of Yiwu in the Zhi Zheng era, he resided at Xifeng in Jinhua. When Emperor Taizu captured Wuzhou, he visited the monastery.
He was appointed to reside at this temple by imperial decree. Later, while presiding over Jingci Monastery, he suddenly manifested slight illness.

Counting on his fingers, he said, "It is now the fifth month of summer. His attendants replied, "Indeed. The Master said, "The eighth day of the eighth month is most auspicious; I shall depart from this life then."
When the appointed time arrived, he adjusted his robes and passed away while seated.
Chan Master Zhizhan Dexiang of Hangzhou, a successor of Chan Master Pingshan Lin, was a native of that same prefecture. One day, leaning against his seat, he said: "A pack of wine-drinkers..."
"You wretch! How can I possibly be like you? He did not speak further, and remained silent.
Chan Master Lan-yun Zhian of Bai-lan Temple on Mount Bian in Huzhou was a successor of Chan Master Hai-men Ze. He was the son of the Shen family of Jiaxing. He addressed the assembly, saying:
The myriad dharmas return to the One. An iron hammer without holes is hurled right before one’s face. Where does that One return? It sweeps past the Western Heaven and this land alike.
The Lin-chi robe from Ching-chou weighs seven catties; on cold crags and ancient trees, the jade flowers bloom in spring. You, O worthy one, inquire earnestly for the ultimate point:
the nostrils born of one’s mother have always been straight. If you can understand where to return beneath these words, then the nine-times-nine will be resolved.
In the eighty-first year of the Ming dynasty, he entered nirvana. His stupa was erected at Nanqian on Mount Cangbian.
Chan Master Baiyun Zhidu of Fulin Monastery in Chuzhou, a successor of Chan Master Dushan of Huading, was the son of the Wu family of Lishui in the prefecture. He reached the age of twenty.

He received his provisional ordination from Zhongkong Jigong and subsequently underwent full ordination. Later, he traveled south on foot, visiting monasteries throughout the land, yet none could satisfy his mind.

He returned once more to the ruins of Baibuyun, where he built a cloister to reside. Daily, he took up the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*, but he found them merely mired in literal words;
his own insights did not accord with them. Upon hearing that Master Wujiandu had expounded [the teachings], he went to seek him out.
Fazheng of Tiantai went joyfully to pay his respects. He asked, "I do not yet understand the hidden meaning of the West's coming;
how should I regard it? Jian said, "Wait until Mount Śāla nods its head, and I will tell you. The Master shook his hand as if about to answer. Jian then gave a shout.
The Master said, "Atop the peak of Mount Śāla, white waves overflow to the heavens. Flowers bloom after芒種 (Mángzhǒng); leaves fall before立秋 (Lìqiū). Jian said, "My..."
"There is no leftover soup or stale rice in my home. The Master said, "How can this not be leftover soup and stale rice? [The official] nodded in agreement.

Later, he presided over various monasteries with universal compassion. In the spring of the Gengxu year of the Hongwu era, he felt a profound desire to return home, but the assembly firmly urged him to remain.
The Master said, "Leaves fall and return to the root; this is my wish. He then returned to Folin. One day, he wrote a verse: "There is no world to bid farewell;
there is no assembly to part from. In the vast void of space, why is it necessary to drive in a stake? Having cast down his brush, he passed away.
From the remains of the cremation, five-colored śarīras were obtained, along with his incorruptible sacred bones and other relics, which were interred to the west of the monastery.
Chan Master Yuanming Yuanliang of Tiantong in Mingzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Biyuan. He was the son of the Zhou family of Ninghai. A eulogy for him by Chan Master Hongzhi reads:
"Alas! It is because the mountain does not reject the dust that it can achieve its height; it is because the sea does not reject the flowing streams that it can achieve its vastness."
As for its profundity: were it not for the Master’s long-prepared wheel of vows for the six perfections and ten thousand practices, how could such merit for this Great Dharma have been established?
Among the sages who appear throughout antiquity and the present, acting as teachers for a hundred generations, there is but one occasion in a thousand years; only our Master has attained this.
This majestic stūpa now anchors this eastern valley, restoring the true regulations of the Dongshan school and making them ever more manifest. I hereby offer this humble announcement.
Epitaph: Deeply inscribed upon cliffs and valleys, it is my wish that the Master would return once more to establish the standard for the Dharma.

Chan Master Da’an Puzhuang of Yunju in Fuzhou, a dharma successor of Chan Master Tiantong Yi, was a native of the Yuan family from Xianju, Tai prefecture. His mother dreamed of a Brahma... [text continues]

The monk was born into the Sangha. At one year of age, he was precocious and exceptionally gifted. Carrying his book-bundle, he entered the local school; having been taught the texts, he could recite them from memory.

In his youth, he relied upon Zuo’an at Tiantong, where he shaved his head and received full ordination. He then traveled to Tianning Monastery in the prefecture to attend upon Liaotang. When he arrived, Liaotang questioned him:
"Where have you come from? the Master asked. "From Tiantong," the monk replied. "You have braved the rain and the cold; what such desperate urgency do you have? the Master asked.
